A comnrratum for the scientists who think they know all about it—Will the last shoe be made on a ohne last ? " Iner's what beats me !" as the boy said when he saw his father take the skate-strap down from its accustomed nail. "I SUPPOSE you are interested in 'Gems of Thought,' Matilda ?" "Yes, Angelina; but not so much as in Thoughts on Gems." IT is said that the girls " adore " the present style of feminine apparel—Derby hats and nobby jackets. It makes them so boy-ant. An the philanthropist remarks: "When Charity asks her due, she doesn't get what's odor, if you don't give her a scent." A RURAL CONUNDRUM.—" What did the snow- storm say to the farmer ?" It said: "If you've any steers to shed, prepare to shed them now." "ON whom shall we call," exclaimed an orator, "to 'cure the evil effects of bad legislation ?" "On a doctor of laws," cried one of the auditors. A MAN much addicted to snoring remarked to his bedfellow in the morning that he slept "like a top." "I know it," said the other; "like a humming-top." A CELEBRATED wit was asked why he did not marry a young lady to whom he was much BA-Leached. "I know no reason," replied he, " except the great regard we have for each other." A BAD NUT.—An officer having been spoken of as "a poor colonel," a bystander remarked that he "knew nothing about his kernel; but he always thought the fellow was a bad nut." FULL OF HAYPINESS.—A little girl, attending a party, was asked by her mother how she enjoyed herself. "Oh," said she, "I am full of happiness. I couldn't be any happier unless I could grow." " I en armed so strong in honesty that I have no fear," said a street-corner politician, but when the terrible cry of "mad dog !" broke upon the air, he didn't dare trust to his honesty, but fled like a common thief. "Was he held for ransom ? " a man asked when told of a traveller being captured by brigands. "Ha would have been if he hadn't rim,som," was the ready reply. A MAN, unable to choose a wife from three girls whom he admired, sent duplicate letters of proposal to all, intending to marry the one who assented first. The trouble that he did not foresee was that the two too-late ones would sue for breach of promise. Damn X. Is a bad hunter as he is a physician, but this does not prevent him regularly as the bunting season comes round from spending a fortnight in the fields with his dog and gun. "And that's the only period of the year when he doesn't kill anything, said one of his colleagues kindly. A searievr old miser surprised his friends by appearing in the street with a new coat. On being rallied on the subject he said: " Well, yes, my wife has long wanted me to get a new coat, and as this is her birthday, I thought I'd get me one as a present for her." "1 BEE a good deal about a celebrated Beef Steak Club' in London," said an old lady, as she laid down her paper; and then she musingly added, "I don't see why they can't pound their steak with rolling pins, as we do in this country." Tavo officers observing a fine girl in a milliner's shop, the one, an Irishman, proposed to go in and buy a watch-ribbon in order to get a nearer view of her. "Hoot, mon," says his Northern friend, " nae occasion to waste siller ; let us gang in and speer if she can give us twa sixpences for a shilling." "WHAT do you say to a lady when you are at a ball ?" asked a young gentleman who went to a ball for the first time. "Talk to her about her beauty," replied the friend, who had been there before. "But suppose she hasn't got any ?" "Then talk to her about the ugliness of the other women who a.rapresent." "ISN'T there some way of gettrng a verdict out of that jury ? " exclaimed a Texas judge, after the "sworn twelve" had been out over sixty hours. "Yes," answered the clerk of the court; "Let the officer in charge of them mention that a circus has come to town." That was done, and it brought a verdict in ten minutes. AN old Scotch lady was told that her minister used notes, but would not believe it. Said one, "Gang into the gallery and see." She did so and saw the written sermon. After the luckless preacher had concluded his reading of the last page, he said, "But I will not enlarge." The old woman called out from her lofty position, "Ye canna, ye canna, for your paper's give out." ALMOST A HIT.—For Some months past Miss Esmeralda Longcoffin has been trying to get Gus de Smith to pop the question, but he has fought shy and dodged the issue. A few evenings ago, while conversing in a leafy bower, she used the familiar quotation, "Man proposes," &c. "Miss Esmeralda," replied the wretch, "I don't believe there is a word of truth in those old proverbs."— Texas Siftings. BfewE's little brother to bridegroom—" Did it hurt you much when she did it ? " Bridegroom— " What hurt me ? " Bride's L.B.—"The hook. Did it go in your lip ? " Bridegroom—"l don't know what you mean, Johnnie." Bride's mother Leave the room this instant, Johnnie " Bride's L. B.—" What for? I only wanted to know Uit hurt him. You said Sis had fished for him a long time, but she hooked him at last, and I wanted to know If--" Brides L. B. is carried out of his chair and hirried from the room, and the bridegroom beeomes meditative. IT is said that the celebrated Lord Chief Justice Holt was in early life very dissipated, and belonged to a club of wild fellows, nearly all of whom went tolPruin. One day when his lordship was engaged at the Old Bailey, a man was convicted of highway robbery, whom the judge remembered to have been one of his old companions. Moved by curiosity, Holt, thinking the prisoner did not know him, asked what had become of his old associates. The culprit, making a low bow and fetching a deep sigh, replied, " Ah, my lord, they are all hanged except your lordship and me." "Bon, where is the state of matrimony ?" "It Is one of the United States. It is bounded by hug- ging and kissing on one side, and cradles and babies on the other, its chief products are population, broomsticks, and staying out o' nights. It was discovered by Adam an Eve while trying to find a north-west passage out of Paradise. The climate is rather sultry till you pass the trophies of house- keeping, when squally weather commonly sets in with sufficient power to keep all hands cool as cu- cumbers. For the principal roads leading to this Interesting state consult the first pair of blue eyes you run against." COLONEL PETERITY met Jim Webster a few days ago. Jim was recently married. "How do you like matrimony, Jim?' asked Colonel Peterby. He shook his head dubiously. "What's the matter "Yet. see, boss, before we were married, when I knocked at de dore, she use ter say, Am dat you, hoheysuckle V Now, when I comes home, she bawls out, Clean off dem hoofs before you comes in dat dore, you black moke I'" Limit Joniory wanted to go to church; his mother WU afraid to take him lest he should make a noise; but his father said, "Johnny knows better than to make a noise in church, does he not ?" " Yes, papa, me will be dood." So they tookbim with them, and he kept very still till the last ptayer, by which time he had grown so tired that he got up on the cushion of his seat and stood with his back to the pulpit. When the lady in the seat behind bowea her head for prayer, Johnny thought she was crying, so he leaned over, and laid to a lady in a tone which was meant for a whisper' but which was only too plainly heard, "Poor, dear lady 1 what ee matter Do oo belly ache?"

In regard to Mr. Goschen's statement about the new coins, it is explained that he included the five- shilling piece, as well as the sovereign and the half-sovereign, in naming the only coins of new de- sign that would not have their explicit value plainly marked upon them.

Lady Henry Somerset's arrangement for the issue of her new weekly, "The World's White Ribbon," are so complete that it is expected to appear forth- with. It will advocate not only temperance but woman suffrage and kindred subjects, and a staff of qualified writers has been engaged worthily to carry on the crusade. It will also be the organ of the World's Woman's Temperance Association.

It is rumored that Countess Russell has decided to follow the lead of other society beauties and adopt the stage as a profession. Whether melo- drama or fin-de-siecle terpsichorean exercises will engage her ladyship's attention does not yet appear. But before the Countess seeks her fortune on the boards she is going to try her hand at fiction, for a short story from her pen will shortly appear in the columns of the "Thames Times," a new paper de- voted to to the interests of river residents and visitors.

Mr. G. D. Giles, the artist whose sporting pic- tures are just now on view at Raymond Groom and Co.'s gallery, is a man with a history. He ought to become the De Neuville of Britain, for he is about the only living artist who has been under fire not once but many times. He was in the Indian cavalry, and he was in command of the Egyptian cavalry at both the El Teb engagements, and will doubtless in due time give, the world not the conventional artist's ideal, but the soldier's real production of the grim norrors or warrare. _ _ _

7_The workmen's branch of the Sunday Society pro- tested on Monday night against the shutting of our great national institutions on the one day. of the week in which the working-classes have the leisure to visit them. The British Museum, the South Kensington Museums, the Bethnal-green Museum, and the National Gallery are supported by public money, but the working-classes who contribute half of the taxation are deprived of the pleasure and the Instruction which follow from visiting these educa- tional institutions. The duty of opening them on Sunday lies with the Government, and not with the trustees of the institutions, who are understood to be favourable.

7*Naval men are laughing at Lord George Hamil- ton's speech to his parliamentary guests at Ports- mouth. The first Lord spoke of the perfect condi- tion of the boilers in our men-of-war. Did he in- clude H.M.S. Thunderer ? This great warship was re-engined at enormous cost only last year, and yet if she were in action at this moment, she would have to stand stock still as a target to the enemy's guns, owing to the breakdown of Lord George Hamilton's " perfect " boilers. The original cost of the " Thunderer," which is fifteen years old, was .£350,060. Last year's repairs ran the bill up to over half a million.

The return on Irish emigration,which was issued on Tuesday, shows that happy, loyal, and contented Ulster contributes largely to the exodus from Ire- land. Between 1851 and 1891 no fewer than 55.4 of every hundred of its people—a total of over a million—have emigrated. Antrim, one of the most loyal of counties, since it returns four Tories to Parliament, has lost over 60 out of every 100 of its population. Tyrone, notwithstanding that it sends T. W. Russell to Westminster, has been de- pleted to the exent of 57.3 per cent. The total num- ber lost to Ireland and the Empire during the forty years was 3,467,576, and this does not include the Irishmen who have emigrated from England or Scotland. These are some of the fruits of Unionism. raftStlit'c' If we may believe the story told by the ex-Court Photographer Mr. Vernon Heath in his recently published "Recollections," there is at Raby Castle what is known as the " terrible book which is pur- posely kept for visitors to contribute some impres- sions of their stay." After dinner this book is placed in the hall, and each guest as he leaves is expected to write his name and address and to fill ,in answers to queries under certain headings. There are many quaint and amusing entries, and mg thc, moct oweioua mr,a rh, fnllnxving lines, which are believed to have been inscribed by Lord Bennet : " A pity at Raby There Pant a baby." Had there been one the chances are that the ownership of the famous castle would not have been in dispute as it is at the present moment.

There is once more a Duke of York. The title, as announced on Wednesday morning, is conferred upon Prince George of Wales, together with that of Earl of Inverness and Baron of Killarney. The new Duke will thus bear the titles of two of the Queen's uncles. The last Duke of York was Prince Frederick, the second son of George 111., who was 80 long Commander-in-Chief, and who died in 1827. The title of Earl of Inverness was borne by the Duke of Sussex, the brother of the last Duke of York. There is something peculiarly interesting in the revisal of a title which belongs to the history of the British Monarchy. If the associations which gather around the Dukedom of York are not all of them such as the world cares to cherish, the name is at least a link between the present and the past, and the new Duke of York will no doubt give it all the lustre it needs.

The Gladstone Library received some we ll- deserved compliments at the annual meeting of the National Liberal Club. The library has become a valuable adjunct of the club. It is one ot the best managed and cosiest in London, and Mr. H. W. Hutton is the most courteout and competent of librarians. Mr. John Morley recently complained that the House of Commons library was an absurd collection of books, which did not contain a copy of Mill. The working politician, or the student of political and social questions could make no such complaint against the Gladstone Library, for it is well stocked with the class of books which he is likely to consult. Ancient history and belles-letters are not well represented, but there is a very large collection of books dealing with questions ot cur- rent interest. It is also well supplied with works relating to London and London questions.

The Grand Old Man is a marvel—always a sub- ject for wonder as well as admiration. For over five hours on Monday he sat in Committee, con- centrating his attention on the Clergy Discipline Bill. Young men were fagged out with the strain. and protested that the hours' discussion in a close Committee-room on a hot day was enough at once for .human nature. But not too much for Mr. Gladstone. He held on unflinchingly, taking as much interest apparently in the proceedings as if be had been tracing parallelisms between Homeric theology and the old Testament, or discussing the committee stage of the Home Rule Bill. The meeting was a lively one, and there was a good deal of wrangling and obstruction by the Welsh Radi- cals, but nothing disturbed Mr. Gladstone's deter- mination to stick to stick to his self-imposed duty of seeing the Clergy Discipline Bill through the Grand Committee.

div.head: ATTEMPTED TRIPLE MURDER.
div.p: ATTEMPTED TRIPLE MURDER.

On Saturday afternoon, a triple attempt at murder took place near Huddersfield, George Graves, aged 23. a smith's striker, but lately out of work, who has been living apart from his wife, went to her father's house, where she had taken refuge, and during an altercation, it is alleged that be drew a six-chambered revolver and shot her in the right temple. Her father, Luke Berry, and her brother Albert Berry, rushed to her assistance. A desperate struggle ensued, during which Albert Berry was struck by one shot in the bridge of the nose and by another in the chest. He fell to the ground, and Graves is stated to have fired at and wounded his father-in-law, at the same time drawing a pocket knife and stabbing the unfortunate man under the left shoulder blade, the knife penetrating the lungs. The three victims were removed to the infirmary. At Huddersfield, on Monday,George Graves,23,striker, of Rastrick, was brought before the borough magistrate charged with attempting to murder his wife and her father and brother. On the application of the Chief Constable the accusad was remanded for a week. At the Infirmary on Monday it was stated that Luke Berry, the father-in-law, whose lungs are injured are slightly better, and the other patients are making satisfactory progress.

THE TORY GOVERNMENT A LABOUR QUESTIONS. HOW THE TORY GOVERNMENT TREAT LABOUR QUESTIONS IN PARLIAMENT. The Tories claim that the interests of labour are always more secure in their hands than in those of the Liberals, and English working-men are always being told by them that no reforms in that direction can be hoped for from the Liberals, because every- thing will be postposed indefinitely in order to pass a Home Rule Bill for Ireland. But Home Rule does not stand in the way while Tories are in power, and so we may fairly ask, How have the Tory Govern- ment treated Labour Questions? Now during the session of 1891 questions directly affecting labour have come to the front more than usual. How have the Tories faced these questions? The first question that came up was SHORTER HOURS FOR RAILWAY SERVANTS. On January 23rd, Mr. Channing (Liberal member for East Northamptonshire) moved a resolution declaring that the excessive hours of labour imposed upon Railway Servants are a grave social injustice, and that legislative powers ought to be put into the hands of the Board of Trade to compel the Railway Companies, where necessary, to limit the hours of work. The Tory Government opposed the resolution and defeated this effort of the Liberal party by 141-124 deferring the whole question by referring it to a Select Committee, who could not report till 1892. The next question that was debated was the treat- ment of

TRADE UNIONISTS AS CONSPIRATORS. In the end of 1890, the surprising decision of the Recorder of Plymouth called attention to several doubtful phrases in the Law of Conspiracy, under which Trade Unionists might be treated as criminals for exercising their rigut to combine. In mtier to place the matter beyond all doubt, Ur. Robertson (Liberal member for Dundee), introducing a Bill amending the Law of Conspiracy, by making no combination criminal except for a criminal purpose. The Government declined to accept the Bill, and it was rejected by 179-143. THE AMENDMENT OF THE FACTORY ACTS (which should lessen the evils of sweating) is a subject that has been much discussed in and out of Parliament. Mr. Sydney Buxton (Liberal member for Poplar) brought in a thorough-going measure aimed at this evil, but the Government brought in a Bill of their own, not half so advanced, and Mr. Buxton's Bill was consequently shelved. THE EMPLOYERS' LIABILITY BILL. Nothing has been done by the Government to help the settlement of this Bill since 1868, and the Par- liamentary Committee of the Trades Congress say in their report:—" It would be better in our opinion to retain the law as it is than to accept the arrange- ment proposed by the Home Secretary in the Bill of 1888." The most important piece of work that the Tories have done for labour in 1891 has been the appointment of .

THE LAI3OI//t COMM/881011. But this has not entirely given satisfaction. The Parliamentary Committee of the Trade Union Con- gress say in their report :—" We regret that our representations were disregarded and a very consid- erable balance of power given to capital in the constitution of the Commission. We therefore forwarded to Mr. W. H. Smith our protest against the indifference which has been shown to the interests of labour as compared with capital. . . . The Government declined, however, either through entreaty or protest, to give way on this point, and thus in the opinion of your Commit- tee have wilfully biassed the inquiry on the side of the employers." Bu t there are other reforms which though not exactly what are called " Labour Ques- tions," yet affect workmen quite as much. In Agricultural Districts especially the question of LOCAL COUNCILS is of first importance. On April 14th, 1891, Mr. Arthur Acland (Liberal member for Rotherham), with the support of the Liberal party, proposed a motion in favour of Parish Councils and ,Reformed Vestries. The Tories not only rejected this, but have thrown obstacles in the way ot independent politi- cal action in English villages. On July 7th, 1891, Mr. Cobb, (Liberal member for the Rugby Division of Warwickshire,) moved in the House of Commons that all schools in receipt of public money might be claimed as a matter of right by the inhabitants of the district for meetings, so that Trade Unions, Co-operative Societies, and Political or other Asso- ciations of woramen roignt meet, there. But. the Tories united to reject this proposal, and the excuse was made that the " village roughs" might damage the property. But the Liberals also want workmen to take their share in the Government of the coun- try. They tried June 14th, 1888. to get the travel- ling expenses of Ceunty Councillors paid out of the rates, so that workmen should at least not be losers by being on the Councils, but the Tories would have none of it. After this we cannot expect Tories to be in favour of
on

PAYMENT OF MEMBRES, and,indeed, they voted against it when Mr. Fen- wick (March 23, 182,) proposed it in tke House of Commons, and several of the leading Tories have spoken against it. But the Liberals have declared in favour not only of paying travelling expenses for County Councillors, but also of giving members of Parliament a salary, so that workmen can choose one of their own number to represent them. This is the way the Tories treat Labour Questions, even when they have a free hand, 'and mulct pretend that Ireland blocks the way. It is the Liberals who first propose reforms, and who are constantly obstructell in trying to get tnem carried.

div.head: LA.TE MR. EDWARD GREENALL,
div.p: THE LA.TE MR. EDWARD GREENALL,
OF GRAPPENHALL THE FUNERAL.

On Saturday afternoon, the funeral took place of the late Mr. E. Greenall,of Grappenhall. The funeral procession left Grappenhall Hall, at 25 minutes past two. Owing to the close proximity ot the hall to the church there was no hearse, the coffin, which was almost hidden from view by the beautiful wreaths which had been placed upon it, being con- veyed on an ingeniously constructed bier with wheels. The order of the procession was as follows: —First came several men carrying a stretcher, on which many other wreaths were placed, then the coffin followed by the mourners, who were as follows : Mr. Frank Greenall, Mr. Alfred Greenall, the Mayor and Mayoress (Mr. and Mrs. Edward Greenall), Mr. and Mrs. Peter Greenall (London), Mr. and Mrs. Henry Greenall, Mr. and Mrs. W. C. Jones, the Rev. Richard Greenall, Colonel Greenall, Mr. W. Pilkington, and Mr. Peter Stubs. The pro- cession was met at the church gate, by the Rev. Canon Cross, of Southport, and Prebendary of Clonfert, who read the first part of the service. A large congregation had assembled in the Chtisch, amongst whom were Mr. J. C. Parr, the Rev. Canon Dodd, the Rev. H. V. Pigot (Warrington), the Rev. J. C. Pigot (St. Helens), the Rev. F. Slater, the Rev. E. D. Garven, Mr. James Marson, Mr. T. H. Lyon, Mr. Lsgan Wright, Mr. Robert Davies, Mr. John Dun, Mr. Pierpoint, Mr. Gilbert Greenall, Mr. Cyril Greenall, Mr. R. I. Wynne Jones, Mr. Alderman Francomb, Mr. William Long, Mr. W. C. Tinsley, Mr. James Tinsley, jun., Mr. Hugh Tinsley, Mr. P. Carlaw Walker, Mr. Wth. Owen, Mr. Henry Milling, Mr. Dunn (Clifton), Mr. Harrison Tinsley. Mr. R. A. Naylor, Mr. John White, Mr. R. Fenton, Mr. A. Crossthwaite, Mr. John Chidlaw, Mr. Joseph Taylor, Mr. Geo. Dakin, Mr. John Laithwaite, Mr. E. J. Hall, and Mr. Peter Edgar. The service inside the church was conducted by the Rev. H. V. Pigot (vicar of St. Paul's, Warrington). Hymns 231 and 401, "Forever with the Lord" and "Now the labourer's task is o'er," were sung in a very impressive manner. The service was concluded at the grave side by the Rev. Canon Cross. The following is a list of those who had forwarded wreaths :—Mr. and Mrs. F. J. Coleridge Boles, Mrs. WIWI. Eckersley, Mr. Hugh Tinsley, Mr. and Mrs. Lyon, Mrs. Turner, Mrs. Litton, Mrs. R. Parry Jones, Mr. and Mrs. Harrison Tinsley, Mr. and Mrs. Logan Wright, Miss Beal, Mr. and Mrs. T. G. Rylands, Miss Rylands, Mr. and Mrs. T. P. Norris, Mr. and Mrs. James Eckersley, Mrs. T. Carter, Mr. and Mrs. W. C. Jones, Miss Jones, Mr. and Mrs. John Reid Walker,Miss E. A. Barratt, Mrs. Benjamin Davies, Miss Davies, Miss Lilian R. Davies, Mr. James Tinsley, Mrs. Davies, Mr. and Mrs. Walter Scott, Miss Litton (Southampton), Mrs. Fenton (Dutton Manor), Mr. and Mrs. H. Greenall, the Rev. Canon and Mrs. Greenall, Mr. and Mrs. Edward Greenall, and Mr. and Mrs. Peter Greenall (London). Wreaths had also Wen forwarded from the Distillery in Bridge-st., the servants at Grappenhall Hall; and others bore no names. A particularly beautiful cross bore the following inscription :—" In loving remembrance of husband and father from Annie, Alfred, and Frank."

On Sunday the morning service at Grappenhall Church was taken by the curate, the Rev. A. Nield,who briefly referred in the course of his sermon to the death of Mr. Edward Greenall, of Gra ppenball Hall. His was a familiar figure in that church, and he would be deeply missed. The sermon at the evening service was preached by the Rev. Richard Greenall, brother of the late Edward Greenall. The rev, gentleman took for his text the words : " This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation." The sermon was very im- pressive, and was attentively listened to. At the morn- ing and evening services the Dead March in " Saul " was played by the organist, Mr. Arthur Miller, A.C.O. Suitable hymns were sung at both services by the cheir.

div.head: G DA
div.p: G DA
MEETING IN THE NATIONAL SCHOOLS.

A meeting of the representatives of the various Sunday schools in the town for considering at the request of the principal manufactures, the desir- ability of changing Walking Day from the 24th of June to the Ist of-July, was held in the National Schools, on Monday evening. The Rev. F. W. Willis presided, and there was a good attendance. The Chairman said he had received a letter from Mr. Morris, as repreeenting the Dallam and Bewsey Forges, begging him to use his influence to post- pone Walking Day for a week. He had read the letter to a meeting of the Sunday school teachers of his church on the Monday previous, and con- sidered it carefully, and they all felt it was too late in the day to make any change. He wrote to Mr. Morris to inform him this, and on Tuesday morn- ing, Mr. Morris and another gentleman waited upon him as a deputation from various large manufac- turers, and told him that if Walking Day were to be on the 24th June, it would be a loss to the town of between £2,000 and ..E3,000. The manufacturers, he believed, took stock on the lst of January and the Ist of July, and if Walking Day were the 24th of June it would necessitate having two holidays, thus causing the loss. He felt that it would be very impolitic and wrong not to give due consideration to such an important matter, and 'agreed to call a meeting through the papers for that evening, to consider whether under the circumstances it would not be better to postpone Walking Day for a week. (Applause.) Mr. WALLINGTON thought this matter had already been discussed in the town, and be felt that Mr. Morris's sug- gestion was a reasonable one and was sure that Sunday School teachers would be disposed to fall in with it. He proposed that it be acceded to and that Walking Day be Friday, July lat.—Mr. THORNTON seconded the motion. —The Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON supported. He thought no inconvenience would be caused by postponement for one week. He thought that when they had settled this, it would not be a bad idea to agree who was the proper body to settle this question in the future for all time. They had had meetings in that room before, on the subject of Walk;ng Day, and then had a town's meeting with the Mayor in the chair, and everything had been over-ruled, and that was a very unsatisfactory state of things. He thought it would be a good plan for manufacturers and trades- people who had got any idea upon the subject to settle the matter amongst themselves, and then confer with I the Sunday School teachers, and decide the matter.— Mr. Wm. Ronanrs approved of this suggestion, and of the proposal to fix July let as the date this year. There was, he thought, almost complete unanimity in favour of the alteration. A number of the manufacturers had for two or three years refused to contribute to any of the schools, but they, if that meeting saw its way to meet their wishes would pay up. (Applause.) In his opinion the matter should in future be in the hands of the Sunday School teachers alone. The manufacturers, if they were going to give their workmen a treat would not consult the teachers. Walking Day was first insti- tuted by the then Rector of Warrington, and the records of the town would show that the Mayor and Corporation had nothing to do with the fixing of the date.—ln reply to a St. Anne's teacher. the Chairman said it had been decided to break up the church day echool the week be- fore Walking Day, because it was found that parents kept children at home preparing for that day.—The Chairman read a letter from Mr. F. Monks, of the firm of Monks, Hall, and Co., Limited, who said that some years ago he urged the adoption of the first Friday in July or the last in June, to avoid extra stoppage for stock-taking. He again suggested one of these, asking that the one might be selected the most convenient to manufacturers, and involving the least loss to working- men. To change the date this year only, without set- tling the question altogether, would be unsatisfactory, and he thought some consideration was due to the manu- facturers from the teachers in this matter. Holidays were much more frequent than they used to be, and it was not desirable to have two breaks coming SO closely together at the end of June. The motion before the meeting was put and carried, with but two dissentients.—The Chairman said the manufacturers had stated that they could not be ex- pected to give subscriptions if the fourth Friday in June were fixed, but that if the first Friday in July were fixed they would double their subscriptions. (Applause.) The Chairman then made some remarks as to fixing the date in future. He objected strongly to Whit- son week, proposed by some, because sometimes it would come early when the days were shorter, and even cold for children. He suggested that the first Thursday in July would be a good day.—The Rev. F. Slater said that Friday having in a certain degree something of the character of Good Friday ought not to be chosen. Now- a-days Sunday was rightly being looked upon as a more joyous and less gloomy day, and there was the more room for keeping our Fridays as they ought to be kept.— Mr. A. J. Jolley said his churchmanship was of a more ..bust character than that of the previous speaker, and urged that there wete many reasons why Walking Day should be on Friday. If earlier in the week it would stop work in the town for the remainder of the week. If this question of Friday being done away with were to be opened up, he, for one should not be sorry to see Walking Day abolished. It was instituted as a counter-attraction to Newton Races, but they were not so much frequented now; and the number of holidays in the year now were very much greater than formerly, and the means of getting to the coast and places of resort infinitely better. They used to have a general united church procession. Now many church schools did not join in the procession except for a very short distance. Many people would not regret to see the festival done away with, and there were many reasons which could be brought forward in favour of its abolition. If anyone else would move in that direction he would support him. He should per- haps be in a minority of one. (Hear, hear, and ap- plause.)—Mr. Dewhurst thought it would be a very great pity to do away with Walking day. It Was an old institution, and the children looked forward to the day with great pleasure. Many of them got provided with new clothing which they would not have but for that occasion. He hoped Walking Day would be a fixture.—After some further remarks by Messrs. W. Roberts, and Stansfield, the latter endorsing Mr. Slater's reason for objecting to a Friday being selected, and other gentlemen; it was, on the motion of Mr. Roberts, seconded by Mr. Carleton, left to the Rector to call a meeting at which the school teachers could confer with the manufacturers as to th • fixing of Walking Day in. future years.—A vote of thanks to the Chairman con- cluded the proceedings.
LOCAL VOLUNTEERS AT LIVERPOOL

--- On Saturday afternoon a grand march out of the various volunteer forces of Liverpool and neigh- bourhood, took place in celebration of the Queen's nirthday. At three o'clock the Warrington Volun- teers (Ist Battalion South Lancashire Regiment) assembled on the lawn in front of the Warrington Town Hall, to the number of about 330, of all ranks, and marched to the Central Station, where they left by train for Liverpool, reaching that city about 4.25. The Commanding Officer, Col. Greenall, was unable to be present, owing to the funeral of the late Mr. Edward Greenall taking place the same afternoon, and Captain F. A. Adam, the battalion adjutant,was in command. The other officers present were Captains J. C, Ridgway, J. D. Buckton, 11. J. Widdo ws, and R. W. Baynes; Lieutenants F. M. Appleton, R. J. Chorley and J. D. Fairclough, and Captain and Quartermaster Hutchinson. Arrived at Liverpool the Warringtonians proceeded at once to the rendezvous, Abercromby Square. Here the whole of the troops, with the exception of the Ist and 4th Lancashire A.V. (which to the disappointment of many, were not included in the procession), were divided into three brigades, each battalion being headed by its own band. Col. Twentyrnan, who was in command, and hie staff headed the troops, and following him came the 2nd, eth, and Bth L.A.V. and the Ist L.V.R.E., which comprised the Ist Brigade, Colonel Wilson being the brigadier and Lieutenant-Colonel Clay, the brigade major. The second 'brigade, for which Colonel Heiden, Ist Liverpool, acted as brigadier, included the Ist, 2nd, and sth, Liverpool ;. and the remaining battalions, the 1 4th and 6th Liverpool, the Ist (Warrington) V.B. South Lancashire, and the Cadet Battalion Liverpool Regiment formed the third brigade, Colonel S. F. Pilkington, 4th Liverpool, being brigadier ; Lieu- tenant-Colonel W. Cooper, 2nd Liverpool, brigade major, and Lieutenant W. H. Cooper, 3rd battalion Liverpool Regiment, A.D.C. The route taken was by way of Oxford-st., Hope-st., Hardman-st., Leece-at., Church-st., Lord-irt., Castle-st., Dale-st., Cross- hall-st., Victoria-at., St. Jehn's-lane, and Lime-st. In front of St. George's Hall Colonel Twentyman and his staff were drawn up, and the whole of the troops marched past him, afterwards proceeding up London-road to 'Monument Place, where the regiments separated and marched to their respective headquarters. At St. George's Hall the military spectacle was seen at its bast. The Warrington Volunteers arrived home at their headquarters at 9.30, where they were met and ad- dressed by Colonel Greenall, who said he was very pleased to see the men turn out so clean and in such good numbers. He hoped to see a very good muster at the coming encampment, and he thought that every per- son who possibly could should make every effort to attend these encampments in order that they might be- come perfectly efficient in their duties, which could scarcely be attained otherwise than by manceuvreing with the troops.
The men were then dismissed, and partook of refresh- ments provided by the officers in the Drill Hall.

div.head: CURSE OF THE CALLERLEYS. By LILLIAS WASSERMAN, Author of "Some Fisher Folk," "Judith," "When the North 'Wind Blows," &c., dec.
div.p: THE CURSE OF THE CALLERLEYS. By LILLIAS WASSERMAN, Author of "Some Fisher Folk," "Judith," "When the North 'Wind Blows," &c., dec.
CHAPTER XLIV. THE DIJEL ON CALLERLEY SANDS.

Undward, a red ball of sullen fire was drooping behind the sandhills ; as three men namely, Sir Lancelot Callerley, his second, Mr. men, and Dr. Denny, whom they had requisitioned, picked their way across the said sandhills to the rendezvous upon the beach ; where already Jack Breamish and Teddy awaited them, the latter pacing about im- patiently, fussy and important. The baronet, for a short space of time after his interview with his wife, had found his mood strangely softened and subdued. Her sweetness and patience were not without their effect upon his stubborn spirit. But alas, the demon of jealousy had him too firmly in its grasp, and would not let him go; and he soon got the better, or the worse, of his momen- tary hesitation. The suitability of time and place struck him for- cibly as he and his companions neared CAllerley sands. A wilder and more solitary spot could not have been selected for such a meeting. The beach was a continuation of those shifting sands over which Yarrop Burn flowed ; and being judged unsafe and treacherous, was seldom visited, save of necessity, by the natives of the district. Long, fiat; monotonous; unbroken by rock or shingle, they stretched their dreary length for a couple of miles to the northward of the Yarrop. Upon the low sea banks the vegetation was of the thinnest and poorest description.

_ "As for the grass, it grew as scant as hair. In leprosy ; thin dry blades pricked the mud. Which underneath looked kneaded up with blood." "It will do," thought Sir Lancelot with a sonit bitter satisfaction. "A fit spot indeed to was% out in blood my shame and his treachery. We s.re safe in one way, for there is small fear of our being interrupted. And since he knows the ground better than I do myself, there need be no stumbling into quicksands by mistake !" "Mr. Bremmish you are punctual !" he said aloud, with a dignified bow. Jack was pale to the very lips, but his was cer- tainly not the pallor of cowardice or irresolution. There was a look of high resolve and determination upon his face which enobled it and gave to it the strength needed to perfectits comeliness. Even his adversary noticed and wondered at this exalted look. What right had a man who had irrvo- cably the happiness of another to wear an expres- sion that might very well have belonged to a hero or a inartyr Not that high or exalted looks went very far to prove innocence. Else were both Silvia and Jack the most angelic and wronged of Ituraan beiffg.C-- 4 But Sir Lancelot knew Letter than to be deluded by a fair outside. The world was full of whited sepulthres ; and of this sad fact he was quite persuaded. In the meantime Teddy was fussing about, laying down the law to the other second, pacing across, measuring the ground, objecting to something about the pistols provided—altogether quite in his element. At length all was ready, and the opponents faced each other, waiting for the signal. A moment of utter stillness and suspense and then the dropped handkerchief, and two shots fired simultaneously. Just as Sir Lancelot, taking steady aim, raised his hand, a sudden scream and the flap of a sea bird's wing overhead caused him Is. start involun- tarily, and his aim swerved slightly from its original intention; and he imagined, to his great vexation, that he had missed altogether. Jack had done the thing which lie had planned and intended from the first, viz., fired into the air. Teddy went close up to remonstrate with him upon this proceeding. "Why should you do such a foolish thing as that. Lucky for you lie missed his aim—why what is this. By Gad ! if he hasn't hit you after all ?"
Jack Breatnish staggered forward a pace or two, put his hand to his side suddenly, and fell, face for- ward, upon the sand.
iy hurried. i

examined him carefully. Although Sir Lancelot's deadly aim had swerved, it had not yet done so sufficiently to miss alto- gether, and falling a trifle lower, had hit poor Jack somewhere in the region of the ribs. The blood was welling out of the wound, and encrimsoni,ng the sands; and the doctor cut away his coat in a very hasty manner, and proceeded to try and stop the hemorrhage, though pronouncing it to be im- possible to do more than this at the time. Slowly Sit Lancelot went up also, and stood by the prostrate form of the man whom he had hated with such bitter, vindictive hatred, and for whose life he had eagerly thirsted. Did he feel content now, when evil wish had been translated into evil deed? Now that the Antinous- like face and figure, of which he had felt so bitterly envious, were bowed to the ground and their beauty blotted out, per,chance for ever? No. Humanity is not altogether diabolical, and seldom derives supreme satisfaction from the fulfil- ment of its revenges. As he stood there, silently watching Dr. Denny busy at the work of stanching the wound he him- self had caused, the baronet could think of nothing save the bright winsome gladness of the young life he had done his best to quench. Visions of Jack Breamish and his frank honest manhood rose before him, in place of that horrible, motionless form he saw with his bodily eyes lying there. Visions of a shy, country lad, blushing and awkward, but ever with a joyous, genial smile; visions of the same country lad transformed by the magic of a velvet coat into a gay gallant, and yet by the utter4sim- plicity of his manner subduing any effect of un- wonted finery; vision of him, simple and loving, with his little nephew—all these rose up before Sir Lancelot reproachfully. As he thought of it the innocent blood he had shed became an unSea.rable reproach. Duelling was not adjudged a crime by people of the ordinary mould ; but Sir Lanceiot Calleirley wae. in the matter of thought :and philosophy, some- what in advance of the period ; and during these few minutes of suspense, it seemed only another name for murder.

Ths,,n Teddy, who was also kneeling on the opposite side from Dr. Denny, gave a cry of glad- ness; a,nd. Sir Lancelot, looking down and awaken- ing from his self-accusing dream, saw that a faint colour had stolen back to Jack's face under the in- fluence of the brandy Teddy had been administer- ing with unsparing hand; and that soon after his eyelids quivered and opened. He gave a deep sigh, and then immediately appeared to recognise the face looking down at him. "You Will—believe—me----now, Callerley '1" he said, in a faint, quivering voice. " I—could—not—help—it—but--/there— was— no—harm—for—she—she loved you all the while— she loves you now—and I knoW it, never mivl how." Something rose in Sir Lancelot's throat, and choked the words he would fain have uttered; but after a moment's hesitation he too knelt down, and took Jack's hand in his, "You believe me now ?" gasped the wounded man, and for answer Sir Lancelot pressed the hand he held. "God forgive me, I have been blind and mad too, I think 1" said the baronet remorsefully, and at the words a pallid smile beamed faintly for a moment upon poior Jack's face. But the effort to speak had been too great for him, and he lost consciousness again immedi- aOly. "I wonder whither we ought to have him re- moved ?" mused Teddy, wonderingly. Much as the little man admired the fine physique of the Mistress Of Breamish Hall, he had his doubts either as to her capabilities as sick nurse, or as to her willingness for the post. It would not be exactly comfortable for Jack to be left to the tender mercies of busy, bustling Bessie Carr at the Fisher- man's Rest, though without doubt the kind-hearted woman wOuld do her best for one so dearly beloved by the fisher-folk; and yet even that might be pre- ferable to the alternative of troubling his sister-in- ILw. As for his own little room at Farmer Toad's, it was decidedly much too far distant for the con- veyance thither of a wounded man. But Sir Lancelot Collerley came to the front and rescued Teddy from his dilemna. “He ,shall go to SeatourCallerley !" said the bar- onet decidedly; and though Teddy glared in an utterly astonished manner, and would fain have stickled a bit upon the, point of etiquette, Sir Lancelot's stronger will swept away all objections as of no acccount.

,4 • His blood is on me and on my house, and if he (lics, it is there he must die," he exclaimed in a gloomy tulle; as he hurried off home to make arrangements for the most comfortable conveyance timmami. ibialata apecacutal.

lirial:ll6 the docl6r still busied himself with his t* t ; the seconds, who had got through their ut ies in much too speedy a manner for their own immediate satisfaction, eyed each other, like two dogs kept in check by circumstances, but longing for an opportunity of attack. Teddy was still using his eyeglass, and now in that calmly •eritical way which irritated Tom Scott; made him keenly conscious of his long, awkward limbs, and, still more, his badly cut coat. " Not worth calling a fight, you isn't, to my way o' thinking," the latter growled out, after a pause; during which he racked his brains for some excuse to get up a quarrel on his own account; "hardly worth coming all this long way for, say I 1" Teddy cocked his hat a little .more over one eye, and brisked himself up, like as a small terrier does, when It hears the challenge of some powerful mas- tiff, and prepares to show that it is pluck-Land cheek—not brute force, which rules the world.

"By gad,-sir, Ido not know what you want, if that does not satisfy you! Here is my prinfipal laid. low, and perhaps—who knowSl—dying=by the fire of yours; while he himself, as fine a fellow as ever breathed, is too chivalrous to make any defence, against an unjust accusation," here Teddy apparently forgot that in the first instance he him- self picked the quarrel with poor Jack, "and I can only say this, sir, that if you are not content, I am ready and willing—yes, 'pon my honour, willing and glad, to carry on the warfare, whenever and wherever you think fit." But second thoughts are best. Teddy looked so absurdly like a game bantam cock as he perked up his little head, and fussed, and ruffled his feathers; that instead of closing with his tempting offer, Tom Scott burst into a mighty guffaw, and held out his brawny fist in humorous amity. , "What sir? Will you not fight with me? Do you not consider me yottr equal in skin; then? Let me ten rut, air, that I have had considerable prac- tice in Emelt matters, and no one is more proficient either with the rapier or the pistol," went on the little man, who suspected and resented bitterly the real reason for the North-countryman's re - fusel. "Very like! Ye're a game un though ye're a little un, but aw'm none for fightin' thee all the same," said Tom bluntly, and Teddy—much alf= the grain,was forced,,at length, to shake and part in peace.

div.head: CHAPTER XLV. TOGETILER.
div.p: CHAPTER XLV. TOGETILER.

The wild looks and excited manner of Sir lance- lot had alarmed his wife exceedingly; and of his strange words she. could understand little, save that he had no longer any faith in her, or any belief in her goodness. What manner of evil did he suspect, then, to make him so hard and. bitter towards her, and not• only towards her, but also towards the whole of humanity? She had not been a perfect wife, that she knew .only too well. But surely to some extent her youth and ignorance excused this? And even now, bitterly as she blamed herself for her lack of sym- pathy and apparent coldness to him—for of real coldness there had never existed a trace—she could li2,..ft_tz dmit thm the whole of the ntisunderstanding . ' - bUtfeseii\ku_.• hu_stand and Wulf arose so ely. cugi this fault of ti'.: Looking back, Act recalled with pain and yearn- ing regret what her own fresh enthusiastic feelings had been, when she first entered this gloomy old house as a young bride. How, even then, she had admired and respected her husband as the grandest, handsomest, most chivalrous gentleman it had ever been her lot to nieet ; an.kl,how fi,lgni.al2y.kg had stood the contrast when she compared hiff—witlire crowd of frivolous, ieather-headed youths, who Were her adorers while she was under Lady Ormskirk's not too ,strict chaperonage-, Not one of these had excited even a passing "entotion within her breast ; save perchance one of amusement and contempt, when some more than usually silly ad- venture had reached her ears concerning them, or some vapid compliment had been paid toiler by one or other.

' That her grave guardian should condescend to ask her to be his wife was, however, a very differ- tilt matter from any of these slight love affairs. That was a conquest worth making, a compliment worth having. In those days of her inexperience, it would have been too much to expect that he would step down from the pedestal whereon she-had raised him, and condescend to woo her like the rest.

She was quite content without that. The ideal she had formed of him could not have so far for- _gotten his own dignity, and would undoubtedly have loaf more than he -gained by lowering himpifilf to the level of COllllllOll humanity, He• was some- thing 'quite apart and sacred from the ordinary run of mortals.

It may seem strained and exalted in the highest degree, and perhaps a trifle unnatural also that a girl of light, and gay, and shallow temperaßent, ich as Silvia Wynne undoubtedly was at the time of her marriage, should set up and worship such a high-minded, unemotional, passionless abstraction; but if it is thought out it is in reality the most likely of all things to happen to the little spoilt beauty. She was sick to death of the fopling and the petit maitre, and every fresh admirer seemed to her merely &repetition of the original type. There was &grave manliness about the north-country baronet by direct opposed to these, that appealed to her at once, and as his ward, she obeyed him, even in the smallest matters, with an alacrity very differ- ent to the wilfulness she usually displayed with Lady Ormskirk and Teddy. This was, ia some ways, a pity, for it gave , Sir Lancelot Callerley an entirely erroneous impression of her character! He imagined her to be a gentle, submissive, yielding girl, without much will of her own, and probably also without much mental force or stamina, but dowered with a happy, sunny, joyous nature, a nature that would render her contented anywhere, and under any circumstances; asking little, and giving less in the way of affection. Occasionally he saw a flash of something that he could not quite square with this preconceived notion, but in his ignorance of girls, be set this down to petulance, and thought little of it. It was not until after his marriage that he began seriously to doubt whether Silvia was really formed of such yielding material after all. It stande to reason that the wear and tear of daily life and the familiarity of constant contact would cause a revulsion of sentiment in Silvia's case with regard to her husband; and when she found that her beau ideal was but made of ordin- ary clay, and was developing moods and tempers, and unreasonable jealousies, there is no manner of doubt that her hero worship received a sad check.

A man may, without doubt, remain a hero to his wife, but it is not in the nature of things that he should remain a faultless, bloodless, superhuman sort of hero, gifted with all the virtues and none of the vices of mankind.

But Silvia was of the age and enthusiastic tem- perament to which hero worship is almost a neces- sity; wherefore had all gone well, her sentiments would have changed insensibly as she grew older, and she would have grown to love the man, where before she only adored the abstrac- tion. '

Grown to love him! Why she loved him now, loved him with all the passionate fervour of a nature widened by experience and deepened by Pain- If by bowing her head to the, dust in supreme contrition and self surrender she could undo the past and make him ailnowledge her repentance to be sincere, how gladly would she so humble her pride? But, alas, had she not already don% all that woman could do to show him that her heart was aching for his affection? How had that concession affected him?
Her face burnt with shame as his stinging cruel words, and still more cruel embrace rose to her remembrance. He neither loved nor'reepected her. 911. that was the worst of it.

61 Oh Lancelot, my husband, why will you so =raw r_tderstand me 2 Why do you banish me from your aeart t" she cried aloud, pacing the floor of her oom in thesad autumn twilight. As she reached the end nearest the door her wila puestioning seemed to awaken there an echo, and this caused her to stop suddenly, and peer into the tarkness. Was that sad figure standing there the hmsband she apstrophised, or was it merely a phan- tom conjured up by her own excited imagination? As she wondered, the figure advanced into the room, and resolved her doubts. "Silvia," it said, in a low, melancholy tone, "if you knew what Manner of man your husband really was, you would thank him for keeping apart from you. "Never, Lancelot! I love you so dearly that it matters little to me what you do either, or what you are. I know you will not believe me, but that I cannot help. I am a woman now, a woman who sees things as they are, and does not any longer ex- pect impossibilities. But oh, if my husband would but overlook the past, and have a little patience with my shortcomings, we might be happy yet. But they might say that was matter of sentiment, let them come to matters more of substance. Well, he poided to hr. friend Mr. Thomas A. Dickson, an Ulster Presbyterian who had been returned to Parliament by a Catholic constituency. (Applause.) Be could illustrate that by other cases, such as that of Mr. Swift McNeil. But, coming to matters in Which the pecuniary interests of Irish Catho- lics were involved lw pointed out that in Limerick, which was overwhelmingly Catholic and Natiopalist, they had over and over again elected Protestant Mayors and appointed Protestant officials. In Dublin, ' the Corporation of which was overwhelmingly Nationa- list, the public analyst with £I,OOO a year, the chief engineer, with £BOO a year, and the city treasurer, with £5OO, were Protestants, and in some cases Tories. (Hear, heat and applause.) Turning, h ' )wever to Protestant Derry and immaculate Belfast—(laughter)—in those two cities not one single official was a Catholic. (" Oh "and " shame.") Yet, those were the people who talked about the Catholics of Ireland being prepared to oppress and persecute and plunder the Tories. He asked them to take a pattern by the people they calumniated.
