div.head: TUE TALE ABOUT CIVIL WAR
div.p: TUE TALE ABOUT CIVIL WAR

in Ulster they had heard that before. (Laughter) When Catholic Emancipation was talked about in the year 1828 there was much of that warlike talk, and it amounted to just as much as it did at the present day. There were certain clubs established called the Brunswick Clubs, desperate fire-eating bodies who.usually burst into song. In his reading the other day he came across a verse which had been composed by one of these Brunswickers whose name was Butler, and he would read it :
• " Surrender I Nn we never will While Bruaswickers have blOod to spill; Our muse is glorious, and for that we'll fight, • For George's title and for William's right."

(Loud laughter.) He was bound to say that, notwith- standing his poetry and his martial ardour, Mr. Butler died peaceably as a law-abiding citizen in his little bed. (Loud laughter and applause.) The same sort of thing went on when the Irish Church was going to be disestab- lished. One reverend gentleman talked about immersing the Queen's crown in the Boyne if they attempted to disestablish his Church,-and there was a gentleman who went by the name of the Rev. Leslie Canter—(laughter) —who declared that the Protestants of the North would march across the Channel—(loud laughter)—to the House of Commons. Then there was a Rev; Mr. Mc, Ginnis who burst into song in this wise :

" Our bosoms we'll bare to the glaring strife, Our vows are recorded on high, To prevail in this cause is dearer than life, Or crushed in its ruing to die," (Laughter). Then there was the Right Hon. David Plunkett who became pathetic as well as warlike, but the Hon. David plumkett had never lined any ditch that he (Dr. Houston) had known, though' he had lined his purse pretty well. (Laughter.) There was another Queen's Council, Mr. Faulkner,who declared that if they did not succeed at least they would nobly die, but he was happy to say that Mr. Faulkner had not died nobly or otherwise seeing 'that he was alive and very well, was recorder of Dublin and got through £1,500 a year. (Laughter and applause.) Well, they were accustomed to that sort of thing in Ireland. At one time when the church was about to be disestablished, somebody adver- tised for 20,000 Minie rifles, and a wag advertised for 20,000 rotten eggs. (Laughter.) After that they beard nothing more of the Minie rifles. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) Another speaker had said lately twit he shed the last drop of Ilis blood in defence of the Irish church, and be was prepared to shed it again in defence of the Unien. (Laughter and loud applause.) LETTRR FROM THE REV. T. RIGBY. _ . . _ . _

The CHAIRMAN at this point said that he had received a letter from the Rev. T. Rigby, vicar of St. Peters, which read as follows :- " I regret lan unable to be present at the meeting. With every wish for Dr. Hous- ton's success." (Applause.) Letters of apology for non-attendance had also been received from the Rev. F. K. Freeston, Mr. A. H. Crosfield, and Councillors Bea- man and Shaw-Green. MR. DICKSON'S SPEECH.

Mr. T. A. Dicxson, M.P., who was received with loud applause, said it gave him extreme pleasure to be there that night and to stand upon that platform with his old and valued friend Dr. Houston, as the candidate for Warrington. They were met upon the eve of one of Ithe most critical contests that would occur, he believed, in their memory or in this generation, and he ventured to predict that befose five weeks had passed that con- test in Warrington, would have been decided. He was there that night to ask what side Warrington would take. He remembered their old member, Mr. McMinnies. (Loud applause.) He remembered when Mr. McMinnies entered the House of Commons in 1880, and replaced a Tory. Now the question was, would Warrington go back to its old Liberal-Radical principles,, or would it remain under the tjaraldom and dominion of the Tory party ? (" No, no.") The question before them was not whether Dr. Houston or Mr. PierpointWas to represent them, but what prin- ciples were to prevail at the coming election. (Hear, hear.) They in Dublin had their eyes fixed upon War- rington.-- Every English election was now a matter of the deepest importance to them in Dublin, and all over Ireland every victory for the Liberal party was regarded as a victory for their country. In coming there that night he asked them not to disappoint them at the com- ing contest. (Applause, and a voice : We will not.) He found that at the recent Tory meeting some of the speakers had said.,

WHY SHOULD THEY VOTE FOR AN IRISHMAN, for a stranger, and that they might as well vote for the King of the Cannibal Islands. He asked if the old cry was going to be raised in Warrington that "no Irish need apply" (" Never " and "No.") Was that the Union that the Tories were so anxious to maintain? Was that their idea of union, and no separa- tion between the two countries, that an Irishman of the eminence, of the ability, of the culture and of the talents of Dr. Houston—(applause)—was to be declared by the Tory party at a Tory meeting, to be ineligible for an English constituency, because he was an Irishman. (Cries of "Shame.") He thought they were dealing with the United Kingdom. (Loud applause.) As an Irishman he asked, was that the way to maintain the Union, and was that the way to create good feeling in Ireland, that when an Irish candidate and a Protestant • came there amongst them to ask for their suffrages, he was to be denounced in that manner by those who wanted to maintain the unity of the Empire. (Hear, hear.) Be noticed at that Tory meeting an old friend of his from Ireland, that old friend being

Du. RENTOUL. (Hear, hear. and laughter.) He had one curious objec- tion to Dr. Houston, and that was because, he said, the name,of Houston was difficult to pronounce. He (Mr. Dickson) was not there to analyse the differences be- tween " Pierpoint " and "Houston," but be would say that he remembered Dr. Rentoul when he was living in the wilds of Donegal, and that the Donegal people had a great difficulty in knowing whether they should call him . " Rentowl" or "Rentool." (Loud laughter.) Just fancy a gentleinan with the pre- fix to his name of Dr., coming all the way from London to an enlightened constituency to advocate the claims and the merits of the Conservative candidate, and tO base his objection to tbe Liberal candidate upon the fact that his name was difficult to pronounce. (Hear, hear.) Dr. Rentoul objected to Dr. Houston coming to England because he waS an Irishman. Dr. Rentoul thought Dr. Houston should not leave Ireland to look for a constituency in England, but what had Dr. Rentoul done himself?; Dr. Rantoul, who was an Ulster Presby- terian like himself (Mr. Dixon), found it convenient to leave the wilds of Ulster to find a congregation and go to where ? To Woolwich. (Laughter.) Yet this Irishman who found it advisable to cross the Channel, to leave his native country—he would not say for his country's good but for his own good—(laughter)—came to Warrington to find fault with Dr. Houston for standing for the borough of Warrington. (Laughter and applause.) At that Tory meeting some of the speakers said that those Gladstonian Liberals could swallow any- thing, but he could tell them one thing Dr. Houston would never swallow—he would never swallow the prin- ciples he professed there that night. If they wanted to know who it was that had swallowed their principles in the past, he would just refer to the Tory and Liberal Unionist parties. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Dixon then quoted from the past speeches of Mr. Chamberlain, Mr. Balfour, the Home Secretary, with regard to Ireland, to sh6w the inconsistency of their present position. He was himself. he said, an Ulsterman to the backbone, and an Ulster Presbyterian, but because he was a Protestant he did not consider that any reason or argument that he should be in continual conflict with, and should insult his Catholic fellow-countrymen. (Hear, hear.) He

DEFINED NOISE ROLE as giving to Irishmen the right to manage and control their own purely domestic affairs in a Parliament in Dublin, subject to the supremacy of the Imperial Parliament. (Hear, hear.) That was Home Rule, but let him tell them it was not separation. A Separatist was a disloyalist, and lEIS an Ulsterman and a loyal sub- ject of Queen Victoria he would give his right arm rather than be identified with any scheme or plan that would weaken the Union between Ireland and England. (Loud applause.) He not only wanted to see the Union main- tained but he wanted to see it strengthened ;at present it was not a Union. Separation was impossible, even if there were a score of Irishmen wild enough to dream of separation. They in Ireland were a poor country, with- out an army. without a navy, without resources, and they were to separate from England the most powerful country upon the face of the earth! They were within twenty miles of the English shores, yet they were to separate from a country that could stretch her arm to India 7,000 miles away, and hold in subjection 250.000,000 of people, and they in Ireland only 4* millions of people. Why, one gunboat and one man-of war would settle the question. (Hear, hear and laughter.) SEPARATION WAS NOT ONLY IMPOSSIBLE

but to Ireland it would be ruin. Englishmen did not realise that in Ireland they had only one industry, and that was agriculture and England;7as the market for all their produce. Separtition frbm England would to Ireland mean commercial ruin, for out of £21,000,000

of exports £19,000,000 came to England. vrear, hear.) He asked sensible Englishmen not libtbdl96, the (,) THREATS OF CIVIL. in Ulster. He knew his countrymen, and he would tell I them this, that if the Imperial Parliament passed a just and fair measure of 110111 e Rule his countrymen would, like loyal men, in the future as in the past obey the law and the Act of Parliament to which the Queen had given her Royal assent. (Hear, hear.) Such men as Dr. Rentoul and Mr. T. W. Russell came over to Eng- land speaking about fire and blood and all that would happen, but these men had not one sixpennyworth of property in Ulster. Mr. Russell had not, as they said in Ulster, as much land as would give a "sod to a lark." (Hear, hear and laughter.) There was not a shilling that Dickson) was worth that was not invested in Ulster manufactures, and therefore if Home Rule was to bring all the disasters it was said it would he had everything to iose by it, but he knew there was not one atom of foundation for the statements that were made. (Hear, hear.) In Ulster. if they excluded Belfast, 55 per cent. Of the population, was Catholic, and if they in- cluded Belfast 46 per cent. of the population was Catho- lic. Excluding two of the counties all the rest of Ulster contained a population of which 62 per cent. was Catholic. (Hear, hear.) They heard a good deal about the

PROSPERITY OF ULSTER, but he knew that while Belfast was increasing in pros- perity the rest of the province was decaying year after year. His own native county, Tyrone, had at one time a population of 315,000 but had now only 170,000. If they had all that prosperity, why were both the Protestant and Catholic population flying from Antrim, Tyrone, and Down, and seeking a home In foreign lands in order to earn the bleed they could not do in Ireland? (Hear, hear.) They were told that if they had Home Rule they would misgovern themselves, but he would say this—that no matter how badly they managed their own affairs, they would not do it half so badly as It was done at the present time. (Hear, hear, and loud applause.) THE RESOLUTION.

Mr. Rang WALKER then moved "That this meeting heartily welcomes Thomas A. Dickson, Esq. M.P., to Warrington,strongly condemns the. vacillating, extrava- gant and unconstitutional. policy of Lord Salisbury's government, and records its unabated confidence in Mr. Gladstone and the other -Liberal leaders, and pledges itself to do its utmost to secure their triumphant return to power at the approaching general election, in order that they may do full justice to our Irish fellow subjects and press forward the other urgent reforms set forth in the Newcastle programme." (Applause.) Mr. T. BIRCHALL seconded this proposal which was carried with acclamation. , A vote of thanks to the Chairman, moved by Dr. Hou- ston, brought the meeting to a close.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 28, 1892.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 28, 1892.
CROWDED MEETING IN THE EMPIRE
THEATRE.

SPEECHES BY MR. T. BURT, M.P., DR. HOUSTON, Q.C., 3I R. JOHN CROSFIELD, &c. On Tuesday evening a Second meeting was held in the Empire Theatre, Sankey-Bt., and the capacious building was crowded to the doors with an enthusi- astic audience. The principal speaker of the even- ing was Mr. T. Burt, M.P. for the Morpeth division of Northumberland, and addresses were also given by Dr. Houston and others. Mr. John Crosfield presided and amongst those on the platform, besides the gentlemen named, were Mrs. Houston, Miss Daly, Mrs. Winser ; Rev. J. W. Varley, Councillors H. Roberts, Plumpton, A. Browne, Green, Blackhurst, and Beaman; Dr. Gornall, Messrs. W. Pierpoint, A. H. Crosfield, T. Morris, C. J. Holmes, G. A. Severn, J. Walker, J. Winser, W. Roberts, J. Heyward, R. Storey, Benjamin, C. Plinston, Dunn, T. Birchen, Hayward, A. H. Lee, S. Dunbobbin, J. G-andy, J. Albinson, D. Tinnion, T. Pemberton, T. B. Kiernan, E. Plmston, J. Podmore, 5, B. Stringer A. Black- burst, E. Ford, G. Clay, T. Malkin, and .1. Clayton (Liberal agent).

div.head: CHAIRMAN'S SPEECH.
div.p: THE CHAIRMAN'S SPEECH.

The Cilanimae,who was received with much cheering, said he had not been able to attend any meetings for some time past owing to ill-health, but he was deter- mined that he would tome there that night—(hear, hear)—if it was for nothing else but to show his sympathy with the Liberal party and his support of Dr. Houston. Some people might think that he wad a little jealous of Dr. Houston being the candidate. Such was not the case. His feelings towards Dr. Houston were 'full of friendship and sympathy, and he wished him success with all his heart. He was very pleased to hear from Dr. Houston that his CANVASS SO FAR HAD BEEN VERY SUCCESSFUL, and that he had been well received by the Liberal elec- tors in Warrington. It made him think better of his fellow townsman when he found them show sympathy with an Irish gentleman from Ireland. (Loud applause.) That sympathy. was what had been wanting for a great many years past between Englishmen and Irishmen. The Irish were a sympathetic people and they relished and enjoyed the sympathy and the society of those who were friendly towards them. That was the reason why their great leader, Mr. Gladstone had put confidence into the hearts of the :Irish people, and that they believed that, through him, they would have justice done to them when he came back to power. (Applause.) That was the secret why Ireland had been more peaceable and quiet during the last five or six years, and not that vile and contemptible Coercion Act of Mr. Balfour, which was brought iota the House of Commons contrary to the terms that were made by the Tory candidates in 1885, when they premised there was to be so more Coercion. (Hear, hear.) They got into Parliament under false pretences, and every one of them deserved to be kicked out. (Laughter and loud applause.) They bcasted and they bragged about their policy in Ireland, but they had nothing to boast of. Look at the

div.head: ATROCITIES OF MITCRELSTOWN.
div.p: ATROCITIES OF MITCRELSTOWN.

Nothing was more abominable than the treatment of Irish people at that meeting. (Hear, hear, and A Voice: "it is not forgotten.") It was not forgotten, and he hoped it never would be forgotten'. (Applause.) At Mitchelstown, they would remember, the police shot in cold blood, three innocent Irishmen, as innocent as he was on that platform. They knew the whole of the in- cidents of Mitchelstown from his friend% Mr. Brunner. (Hear, hear and applause.) Be sheuld just like to say a word or two about Lord Salisbury. (Applause.) Lord Salisbury had made two remarkable speeches. In the first one he

div.head: INCITED THE 'MEN OF ULSTER
div.p: INCITED THE 'MEN OF ULSTER

to civil war. It was a wicked and a vicious thing to do. It was a thing which had never been done, he should think, in the memory of any man by any Prime Minister in England before. (Hear, hear and a voice : Why not prosecute him.) But he (the chairman) did not think the men of Ulster would be such fools as to listen fo the advice. (Hear, hear.) He himself thought that a Prime Minister who made a speech like that, to incite rebellion in Ireland,ought to be hooted and hissed and driven from the position that he holds. (Hear hear, and
YEAST§
'oon" Br

ing to the House of Commons, to bear another distin- guished Irishman, sent by an English constituency, Sir Charles Russell—(applause)—company, that eloquent and distinguished Irishman who was now appealing to them for their suffrages. (Loud cheering.) He had been asked to say a word on the subject of mining royalties—(loud applause)—and he learnt by the recep- tion they gave to that item in the Liberal programme that they considered that a question of very great im- portance. (Cries of "Hear, hear.") On this subject he had to speak with a certain amount of reserve. On a motion that he brought before the House of Commons, accepted by the present Government, a Royal Com- mission was appointed to inquire into the question. He was a member of that commission. The evidence before that commission was now, he thought, almost complete, and very shortly they should have to prepare their report. It was assumed that a member of a royal commission was in a judicial capacity until the report was completed. He bad thoroughly well made up his mind upon a few points ; but he considered it would hardly be proper for him to enter into detail upon them. What he would say and he felt quite free to say was this, that with regard to mining royalties in connection with several kinds of minerals they undoubtedly were paying a higher amount than many of their competitors on the continent. (Hear, hear.) This meant to a considerable extent handicapping them in their competition with other coMitries. He was a coal miner himself, and had been for 25 years past, and was now general secretary of the Northumberland Miners' Association, and was president also of the Miners' National Union, and he knew that sometimes Id. or lid. per ton made all the difference between work and idleness. He had known a colliery stopped, laid off altogether, and the men dismissed to seek employment elsewhere, and the colliery had been stopped for months when the difference between the employer and the workman was only id. 11-d. per ton. (" Shame.") The amount paid for royal- ties on coal amounted to some sd. to 63. per ton. ; and in the case of ironstone with which they were very much interested, about two tons of coal were required for the production of a ton of pig iron. There was a royalty to be paid on the ironstone, and, there was one paid also on the coal, and in the aggregate these must amount to a considerable sum. In most countries—in France, and he believed in Belgium, and in parts of Germany the greater portion of the amount paid as royalty went to the State, and not to private indivi- duals. (Applause.) If we were beginning afresh lie would say that minerals should never be private pro- perty—(applause)—but always owned by the State— (hear, hear)—and he would apply the same principle to land. (Cries of" hear, hear.") But we were not begin- ning afresh. Ours was an old country, and there things were established, and minerals and land were recognised and legalised as property, and you could not now take take them from the owners without compensat- ing them, which would require a very large amount of money. But there were landowners claiming to have absolute power over the minerals, and who said they would not open their mines but would keep them for future generations. No man ought to have that power. The speaker then dealt at some length with the subject of way-leaves, which he said were more extravagant than mining royalties. He applied his remarks on these royalties to ground rents. He instanced the case of land in London worth £3OO an acre a few years ago and now £5,000 per acre, and that of some land in Bermondsey, about 4134 superficial feet in extent, for which the owners asked £1,250,000, or at the rate of £13,000,000 an acre. He maintained that it was by the skill and industry of the community and not of the owners that land was so largely increased in value, and that the com- munity, and not the owners who neither created, nor enhanced the value of, land ought to enjoy the benefit. (Applause.) In concluding be said some people looked forward with dread forebodings to the future, but he had faith in the future—(applause)—and above all in the working people of this coantry. He believed that special privileges and monopolies would have a hard time °fit, but everything founded on justice and reason would stand more firmly rooted than it had done in the past—(loud applause)—and with a sober, intelli- gent and law-abiding people this cld country would increase in lustre and in glory. (Load applause.) Another song was given by Mrs. Houston, which was clamorously encored, on which she sang" What Paddy gave the drum " for which she was enthusiastically applauded. The Rev. W. VARLEY proposed a resolution welcoming Mr. Burt to Warrington, which was identical in terms with that passed in the case of Mr. Dickson the previous night with the addition " and pledges itself to do its utmost to secure their [the Liberals'] triumphant return and the return of Dr. Houston."

Mr. R. STOREY seconded the motion, dealing largely with the question of mining royalties. The resolution was put and carried unanimously. Dr. HOUSTON then moved a vote of thanks to the chair man. He remarked that the Crosfields had always been a tower of strength to the Liberal cause in that consti- tuency. (Applause.) , Mr. HENRY ROBERTS, who was well received, defended Mr. Crosfield from the Tory accusation that he was cold in the Liberal cause, pointing to his presence that night as a proof to the con- trary. He (Mr. Roberts) claimed that as far as public meetings in Warrington were concerned the Conservatives had not been in it ; the Liberals had knocked them into a cocked hat. (Laughter.) He urged strongly however, that the result of the election would I depend not merely upon public meetings, but also upon the individual work of each man present. Dr. Houston put the resolution, which was enthusiastically carried, and the Chairman's reply brought the meeting to a close.

div.head: laughter.) The next speech that Lord Salisbury made was perhaps more monstrous still if it were possible, and that was at Hastings, where he advocated that they should
div.p: laughter.) The next speech that Lord Salisbury made was perhaps more monstrous still if it were possible, and that was at Hastings, where he advocated that they should

COME REM DO PROTECTION and abandon Free Trade. He wanted them to put on what were called retaliatory duties. But they had tried retaliatory duties in the time of Huskisson and Sir IRobert Peel, and Sir Robert Peel said they were a dead failure, and Sir Robert Peel as they knew, brought in the irepeal of the Corn Laws in 1846—(applause)—and swept away those retaliatory duties. He just wanted to ask them to remember that if any import duties were put on ia this country the people that pay the import duty are the consumers, and therefore it any duties were put on it was they who consumed the article that had to pay the duty. It was not the country that the article came from. (Hear, hear.) It was a monstrous thing that a Prime Minister should at this time of day, after they had reaped all the advantages of Free Trade for nearly 50 years, dare tostand up in England and advocate such a policy as that. (Hear, hear.) But what did all that show ? It showed that Lord Salisbury saw that his game was up. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He saw that the Tories were going to be licked at the next general election, and he was driven to get up some cry or "another that he thought might please the electors. (Hear, hear.) They in War- rington knew very well that they had nothing to ex- pect from a Tory Government. It would not give them anything but what was forced upon them by fear, but a Liberal Government brought in measures because it trusted Use people. (Applause.) If they wanted

INJUSTICE, TYRANNY, AND comicloN, well, they could vote for the Tory candidaßt in War- rington. He was one of that sort. (Laughter and ap- plause.) He (the Tory candidate) was a particular friend of his own, but they did not quite agree in their political opinions, that was all. (Hear, hear.) But if they wanted freedom, and justice, and conciliation, let them vote for Dr. Houston. (Loud applause.) They could trust him to stand shoulder to shoulder with Mr. Gladstone in.the House of Commons. (Applause.) He was a sound Liberal at heart, and he (the Chairman) would guarantee that he would always vote right, and that they should not find him doing as Mr. Joseph Chamberlain and one or two others of that sort had done. (Hear,hear.) What they wanted was t 9 sweep away that curse of coercion, and to see Ireland made free. They wanted to see Ireland have her own Parliament and to manage her own affairs, not independent of England— for they were not Separatists—but under the supre- macy of the English Parliament. He believed that there was in store yet for Ireland such a future as they could none of them realise. (Loud applause.) Mrs. Houston and Miss Daly then sang with fine effect the duet, "My heart's delight." DR. HOUSTON'S SPEECH.
Dr. HOUSTON, Q.C., on rising to address the meeting was received with continued cheering. He said that magnificent meeting was a significant contrast to the

div.head: SHRIVELLED STARVELING MEETING
div.p: SHRIVELLED STARVELING MEETING

that the Tories held on the previous night—(laughter and applause)—and the splendid reception that they had been pleased to accord him, and the kindly and sym- pathetic words in which their chairman had been pleased to refer to him augured well for their success in that momentous conflict, provided they worked as men who were conscious of the great issues that depended upon their actions. That was the most momentous conflict of the 19th century, and upon its result would depend the welfare and the well-being of that nation and empire for a generation. (Hear, hear.) He believed he was pretty well acquainted with the feelings of the electors, and especially of the workingmen of ‘Varrington, and he was satisfied that when the day of battle came they would not be wanting in their duty. (Applause.) That day was approaching with rapid strides. They knew not the hour when the trumpet would sound, and when it sounded he believed every Liberal elector of Warring- ton would be found At his post. (Hear, hear.) His opponent, Mr. Robert Pierpoint, had in his wisdom and his larger political foresight been pleased to say that he thought the Liberals had been
PREMATURE IN OPENING THEIR CAMPAIGN.

To use his own language, they had lighted their bon- fires too soon, and that before the general election arrived their fuel would be exhausted and their fire would be black out. He took leave most respectfully to differ from Mr. Robert Pierpoint. (Hear, hear and applause.) He believed they commenced their campaign in the nick of time—(applause)—and he told Mr. Robert Pierpoint that, let the general election come sooner or come later, the flame which had been kindled in War- rington would burn bright on the day of polling. (Loud applause.) Their opponents had given them some idea of the treat that they had in store for them should they be returned to office again. Lord Salisbury was a man who had the courage of his prejudices—(laughter)—and he had let the cat out of the bag. He had informed them in unmistakeable language of a good many things that they had to expect from him and from the Tory party, and amongst other things they had to expect was one that had been alluded to by the Chairman—they might expect from him the

LIIRCRY OF A RETURN TO PROTECTION. The Prime Minister of England had declared himself a Protectionist. The principle of Free Trade was to be insiduously attacked, and they were to have a squalid, a mean, and a stupid war of tariffs. The campaign was to be opened by the light artillery of silks and satins and laces—(laughter and applause)—but did any man of sense suppose that the fight was to stop there, and that if they succeeded in applying the principle of pro- tection to luxuries, it would not extend to the necessaries of life? (Hear, hear.) Protection was like the daughter of the horse leech ; she was never satisfied ; she was always calling for more. They would be told, when they had protected silks, and satins, and laces, and articles of duxury and refinement, that they had not done enough, that they had not succeeded in benefitting themselves or inflicting any loss upon foreign countries, and that they must go a step or two further if they were to succeed. Having taken one step in the downward course they should be called upon to take, and if the Tory party were in power, they should have to take another step, and another step, until at last they should be involved in that slough and in that quagmire in which other nations of the world were at the present moment floundering. (Hear, hear and ap- plause.) As in former times England held the fortress of human liberty against all comers, she now held the citadel of Free Trade against the nations of the world— (applause)—and the Liberal electors of the United King- dom were never Failed upon to stand together more closely, or more firmly, or to show a more determined front than they are at the present day, when the great principle of Free Trade was insidiously attacked and assailed by the suggestions thrown out by Lord Salisbury in the speech alluded to by the Chairman. (Hear, hear and applause.) If little was to be expected in Great Britain from another lease of Tory power, nothing at all was to be expected in Ireland. Mr. Balfour had once more proclaimed authoritatively the

DOGMA OF COERCION. He had announced not merely that he was not ashamed of it, but that he gloried in it. Why, if he had but one particle of shame in his composition he should blush to hear the thing even named. The his- tory of coercion was the chronicle of broken pledges and of violated faith from the beginning to the end. (Hear, hear.) Then Mr. Balfour said they had succeeded in tranquilising and pacifying Ireland, and had made it prosperous to a degree that was never seen in the past ages. But they had heard that story before. That was

the account that every tyrant and oppressor that had trampled Ireland under his heel had told ths English people. He should like to know what suecess lVtr. Balfour had achieved ? Had Irish nationality quailed before the Coercion Act? Had any man receded from the position that he occupied, had any man turned tail, or had any man lost courage or confidence in the principle of Irish nationality? (Cries of" No," and loud applause.) No, coercion had failed as it had ever failed for seven centuries, and as coercion amongst every people worthy of the name of people must fail. (Loud applause.' In conclusion, Dr. Hous- ton referred to the attempt that was being made by the Tory Government to disfranchise Irish illiterate voters, and pointed out that if they succPeded in doing this they would next proceed to disfranchise the same class of English, Scotch and Welsh voters. (Hear,. hear and loud applause.) Mr. Taos. Haar, M.P. then rose, and was received with enthusiastic and continuous cheering. After some preliminary remarks, he said Mr. Roberts had been kind enough to send him some specimens of

ELECTORAL LITER/MIER that the Tories were disseminating very widely in that constituency. He did not intend to deal with it very elaborately, but he noticed that one leaflet gave an account of working class legislation, and gave side by side the Conservative and the Liberal legislation of this kind. He found that while the Conservative legislation went over three or four pages, the Liberal legislation only went so far into the second page. Now, they did not expect very high morality in politics ; even in the House of Commons he feared, political morality would hardly square exactly in every point with the decalogue, but he thought political, and especially Tory literature sank to the very nadir of immorality. The first thing he noticed in connection with this circular was that it began in 1874. It gave two long Tory Parliaments of about 12 years ; and it only gave between five and six years of Liberal legislation. Why did not the compiler go back to the Parliament of 1888—(applause)—if he: wanted to make a fair comparison ? Why did he not compare Mr. Gladstone's Parliament from 1868, to 1874 with the Parliament of Lord Beacons- field from 1874 to 1880 ? Well, then, he noticed further that a great number of the measures claimed as having been passed by the Conservatives were not measures that specially affected the working-classes, but questions affecting the general community. He found that the Mines Regulation Act, for instance, was men- tioned as passed by the Tory Government in 1887. Well, that was an admirable measure; he gladly admitted as he had said publicly before, that it was one of the best measures of of the kind that had ever been passed. But it was not a party measure. The Bill as it was intro- duced by Mr. Matthews and Mr. Stuart Wortley was, substantially, word for word and line for line, the Bill that had previously been introduced by Liberals, Mr. Childers and Mr. E. Broadhurst. The amendments embodied in the Bill were moved by the working- men's, the miners', representatives, by Mr. Fenwick, Mr. Wilson, Mr. Pickard, himself, and others. (Ap- plause.) He found also that in the Tory pamphlet there were mentioned as Conservative measures, The Conspiracy and Protection of Property Act, 1875, and the Employers' and Workmen's Act, 1875. These two were very admirable measures. Bills, however, bearing upon this question had been introduced by Liberals, and had been carried through certain stages. Sir Wm. Harcourt—(applause) Mr. Mundella—(renewed applause) —Sir Henry James—who at that time was associated with the Liberal party, and had always been sound and helpful with regard to labour questions—and others brought forward several amendments that were de- feated in theyllouse of Commons by the Conservative Government, and these, had they been accepted, would have prevented much of the agitation, expense, litiga- tion, and dissatisfaction which the workmen had properly felt in connection with this Act—(hear, hear)-- especially with regard to the definition of intimidation and coercion. They might test the views ef the present Government on these questions by what had ,taken place during the present session. Mr. Robertson, the member for Dundee, brought in a Bill to do the justice to the working-men of defining conspiracy, so that no- thing which done by one man in the way of picket- ing or in connection with trades union was not criminal would be criminal when done by two or more men. That Bill was defeated by the present Government by 36,and if the Liberal Unionists who voted against it had voted for it, and if the absentees, of the Liberal Union- ists had been present on that occasion the Bill would have been carried by a majority of 53. (Applause.) These leaflets spoke about what the Tories had done in giving the people
FREE EDUCATION.

He did not want to minimise that boon—it was undoubtedly a great boon—but far more Liberals than Conservatives voted for the Bill in favour of free education. (Applause.) If it had been left to the Conservative party it would have been defeated. They all knew how the Tory party, when Mr. Forster brought in his Education Bill, endeavoured to mutilate and weaken it to the utmost possible extent. He him- self was one of the first members of the National Educa- tion League formed in Birmingham about 1869, and the members of the League were then for compulsory and unsectarian education ; while the Conservative party had until recently opposed these principles. Why did they pass free education ? Because they knew the Liberal party would pass it in a much more through and democratic form. (Applause.) It would be one of the duties of the Liberal party when they got into power to complete the system of educa- tion by adopting School Boards everywhere, and give the people, through their properly constituted represen- tatives, absolute control over the teaching of their children. (Applause.) Then, what was the Conserva- tive programme for the future? They were on the eve of a general election, and what had they promised to do in the future! Well, as Dr. Houston had stated, what Lord Salisbury promised was a return to Protec- tion, and practical civil war in Ulster. These were the only positive statements he had made. The Conserva- tive creed seemed to be a creed of negation. So far as it was one of affirmations it was affirmation of a bad kind. (Hear, hear.) Referring to the Conservatives having carried Coercion and Land Purchase Bills after pledging themselves strongly against both, Mr. Burt asked, when they once broke their pledges could they be trusted to keep them in the future. (Cries of " No.") He went on to refer to the great meeting at ' Newcastle in October, which he said was attended by Dr. and Mrs. Houston, and at which he himself had the honour, the greatest honour of his life, to second the motion of welcome to their great leader on the occasion of his visit to Newcastle. (Loud applause.) He cited the eleven points in the Newcastle programme, the last mentioned being the ending or mending of the House of Lords, the ending he should rather say, hb remarked. I (Much applause.) He referred to the taunt against the Liberals of keeping Home Rule, in the background more than formerly, that it was because they have made up their minds. (Applause.) That question dwarfed and dominated every other political question which divided parties. It was not only intrinsically important, but important from the consideration that it was the dividing line of the political parties, I and until that question was settled no great democratic question could be settled in the House of Commons. The two great democracies of England and Ireland now understood each other as they never did before—(applause)—and what he wanted that constituency to do was to give the visible and out- ward sign of the consummation of the union by return-

GIPSY SMITH AT WARRINGTON.

On Sunday and Monday,large congregations were drawn to Bewsey-road Wesleyan Chapetto hear the well-known evangelist, Gipsy Smith, who gave ad- drecises of an earnest character, and afterwards met and conversed with penitents in the vestry. On Monday evening every available seat in the chapel was occupied, to hear the story of his life. After hymn and prayer, the Rev. A. Freeman briefly intro- duced the lecturer,who, on rising,was loudly applauded. In his remarks he said there were gipsies and imitations of gipsies. A great many people looked in the wrong place for them, and very many had all sorts of preju- dices against the people to which he belonged. Mr. George Smith, who had written about them, did not un- derstand them or he would never have said the foul things he had said. He had looked in the wrong place for them. The gipsy is away in the country lanes,fields, and forests, and does not know anything of town life. He believed there were about 20,000 gipsies in England, and, in his opinion,they were one of the lost tribes. They had no record, no bible, no churches, and no educa- tion, and he thought it:would be better if we had put education is in the hands of the gipsies instead of put- ting guns in the hands of the soldiers. They had no re- ligion, but they believed there was a salvation some- where. He said he was proud of their morals in private life ; we never have read of them committing murder, or running away from their wives, or a gipsy divorce suit, or elopements. They drink occasionally, but there were not many habitual drinkers. Swearing I was one of their greatest sins. They also' pilfered, but as regarded the statement of their stealing chil- dren, it was only a nursery story, as they had plenty of children of their own. He maintained they were worth saving for Christ, and he was hoping the time would come when he would be able to send two gipsy vans into the country to live among them and evangelise them. He said we spent hundreds of pounds in trying to save the heathen in foreign lands, but not five shillings in saving the gipsies in our own country. The lecturer afterwards gave in a most hu- morous manner an account of his early tent life, he hav- ing travelled with his father's van through most of he southern counties. When quite young he accompanied his father, in the evenings, to the public-houses where he assisted him as the caterer of amusements, his part being to sing and dance, his father playing the violin. In speaking of the drink trade be said he had hated it from his earliest days, and if lie had the power he would make it impossible for a man to be in the ministry, or a steward, or local preacher, or even to be a member of the Wesleyan body who was not a teetotaller. Ile then related the manner of his conversion, and his transition from gipsy tent to pulpit. His success is the more remarkable considering he had no education to begin with. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded Mr. Smith for his admirable lecture, the meeting afterwards terminat- ing by the singing of the doxology and the pronouncing of the benediction. The collections were in aid of the chapel trust, and during the collection Mr. A. Baker contributed a solo. The collections amounted to £27.

TEAM. What is feared to have been a sad boating fatality occurred in Port Philip on Saturday evening. Fifteen members of the football team secured the services of two fishermen to take them across the bay in an open boat. They never reached their destination, however, ana on Sunday morning the boat was found floating bottom upwards, having evidently been capsized. The body of one of those who lost Saturdaythei la r lives i s beenintll e boat accident at Port Philip on found. Boats are out searching for the 14 bodies not yet discovered. It is supposed that a heavy sqnall struck the boat and swamped her.

THE WARRINGTON WoUNDING CASE.

At the Liverpool Assiz-ts on Wednesday, before Mr. Justice Cave, James Kelly, forty-eight years of age, was charged with having, at Warring on, on the 15th inst., unlawfully, maliciously, and feloniously wounded his wife Mary Kelly with intent to do her some grievous bodily harm. Mr. Kinghorn prose- cuted. From the evidence given by the prosecutrix, it appeared that the prisoner resided in apartments with his wife in Warrington. On the day in ques- tion he did not come home from his work as usual. His wife, who was afraid of certain threats which he made against her, did not go to bed but lay down on the sofa. At four o'clock the next morning the prisoner came downstairs and found his wife lying, on the sofa. He began to pommel her with his fists about the head and body. The landlady, hearing the woman scream, came downstairs and found the prisoner assaulting his wife by striking her. The prisoner next went to the table drawer, and obtaining a knife stabbed his wife on the left side of the head. He then threw the knife down. A lodger named Henderson then came into the room, and found the knife lying upon the hearthstone with blood upon it. The prisoner again tried to attack his wife, but was pre- vented by Henderson. A policeman then arrived, when the prisoner was taken into custody. When arrested he said he did not care whether he had killed her or not. Before the magistrates he said he was very sorry for what had taken place. Prisoner denied that the woman was his wife. He never put a ring on her finger or went to church and chapel with her. In the course of a long ' statement he denied the offence.—The jury found the prisoner guilty of unlawful wounding—lt was stated that the prisoner was a farm labourer, and that he had been convicted nine times for disoiderly conduct.—His lordship said the prisoner appeared to be a man of quarrelsome nature. He must go to gaol for nine months with hard labour.

THE WA R RINGTON WORKINGMEN'S PERMANENT BENEFIT BUILDING SOCIETY. The twenty-second annual meeting of this society was held on Monday evening, in Golborne-street, schoolroom, Warrington. Mr. JohnHatton presided, and amongst those present were Messrs. Grove, Unsworth, Wallington, Isherwood, Parsons, Harding, Fenton, Norbury, Baxter, Ruberts, Grealey, Mills, Sudlow, Lee, Ashley, Frank Hesketh, Peter Dalton (secretary), and Josiah Longland (solicitor to the society).—The report of the Committee read as follows : —" The managers have pleasure in laying the twenty- second annual statement of accounts before the share- holders, as shown in the annexed statement. The sum of £2,328 4s. 11d, has been received as subscriptions dur- ing the year, and £1,741 10s. Bd. for repayments, making the total receipts £4,069 15s. 7d. The with- drawals during the year amount to £1,735 19s. 3d. The sum of £2,087 10s. has been advanced to members during the year. There are 213 subscribers holding 3191 shares and 36 borrowers holding 171 shares, makini, 249 mem- bers, holding 490,12 shares. The profits for the year, in- cluding £5 15s. 3d. from last accfiamt, after deducting working expenses, amount to £5lO 6s. ld., out of which the managers recommend a dividend of 41 per cent., which will take £444 Bs. 5d., leaving a balance of £65 17s. Bd., which they direct shall be dealt with as follows :—£so to the reserve fund, and the remaining £l5 17s. Bd. to be carried forward to next year's account. The reserve fund amounts to £5OO, and the contingent fund to £2OO. The whole of the managers retire. Messrs. Harding, Wellington, Fenton, Isher- wood, Bouchier, and Baxter are eligible, and offer themselves for re-election. Six additional managers will be taken from the register in rotation." The report was adopted.—Mr. Isherwood moved that a dividend of 4:1- per cent, be paid to inves- tors on their deposits. This was seconded and carried. —Messrs. James Harding E. Wallington, Edward Fenton, Robert Isherwood, J. W. &udder, and James Baxter were re-elected managers. Messrs. J. E. Wright and William Bodle, jun., were re-elected surveyors to the society for the ensuing year, and Messrs. William Ford and Samuel Albinson auditors It was decided, on the motion of Mr. Longland, that an allowance of is. be paid to each manager for his attend- ance at each meeting during the past year. A vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Hatton for presiding, and the meeting terminated.

div.head: CHARGE OF STEALING FURNITURE AT WA RRINGTON.
div.p: CHARGE OF STEALING FURNITURE AT WA RRINGTON.

At the boroughs magistrates' court on Wednesday, George Woodfine, alias George Huntley, shopkeeper of Pinner-brow, charged on a warrant with having fraudulently converted to his own use a bedstead and spring mattress, value £3 4d., hired from Messrs. Pendlebury and Co., Winwick-street. Mr. Browne appeared for the prosecution, and the prisoner was remanded after evidence by Inspector Spinks, till Thursday, when Mr. Browne again prosecuted, Mr. P. Davies appearing for the defence, and to watch the case on behalfjof Mr. Brooks, mentioned in connection with it. Mr. Browne stated defendant signed the usual hiring agreement with the firm for the articles, the document prpviding that he was not to remove the goods from his address, 3, Pinner's Brow, without the written consent of the owners. They discovered on Monday that the articles had been removed, and the firm's manager went to a Mr. James Brooks with whom he had seen the prisoner, and Mr. and Mrs. Brooks denied haying ever seen him or the goods ; but which, never- theless went to their house in 27, Wakefield- street. The prisoner was apprehended about four o'clock on Wednesday morning at the Brooks's house where he had slept overnight, intending to catch the train for Liverpool early in the morning, to go to America. He was arrested while trying to escape with nothing but his shirt on and his passage ticket and .£4 ss. 31d. were found upon him. He had obtained the goods in the name of George Huntley, though his real name was George Woodfine. It was admitted by Mrs. Brooks that she had bought the articles for £1 15s. and. I produced her receipt for £1 15s. for them. The pri- soner had paid £ll7s. 6d. on account to Messrs. Pendle- bury. The man pleaded guilty.—Mr. Browne thought steps oueht also to be taken against the liro&ks's. It was stated that it had been sworn by the police that he admitted his guilt.—Mr. Davies said that prisoner hav- ing admitted his guilt to the police, cleared his case to a certain extent ; but denied that there was any compli- city on the part of the Brooks's. His brother who had lodged with the prisoner, came to their house and offered the articles for sale as his. He was going to America on Wednesday, and they knew he was going and bought the goods off him for 355. The prisoner was never seen in the transaction at all, and they did net know they were doing anything wrong They were much astonished when the prisoner was found in their house; and it was admitted by T. W. Brooks that he let the prisoner into the house between one and two in the morning. The prisoner had meant to go to America with him, there was no doubt that he had been put up to do what he did by T. W. Brqp.ks,who had it townne It was America.(Laughter The story was Browne.) aowromsntic one, was true. stated that the prisoner's wife had left him.—Mr. Davies contended that under the agreement the pri- soner could not be prcsecuted, but the Beneh held a contrary opinion and considorinr, the case proved sent I e Brooks's though there was something very him to jail for 14 day's hard labour. The Chairman said as to t suspicious, he did not think anything could be done against them. They might have had no bad intention.

Weeks ago by an elector, he would have had to re-' sort to the familiar expedient of " spinning without Yarn." As it was, his answers to the questions were . au exposure of the political nakedness of the Tory Party. All he can promise as to amending the Em- Pleyers Liability Act is that if he sees an amend- ment which suits him he will vote for it. He does aPparently know that the Government have failed in thejl promise to amend the Act; and lamely auggests that this is in consequence of Liberal Obstruction. But what of the fact that the House has been counted out ten times during the present Sion? Does that look like obstruction? Or does it not show that the Government are negli_ gent, and that their supporters are idle? With ten kard to the proposed abolition of property quali- fication for members of Boards of Guardians, Mr. PgItPOINT is so very high and dry as a Tory that he prefers to leave the old bad system as it stands. Let working-men note this. No property quail- cation attaches to the office of Town Councillor °r even to that of a member of Parliament; but, cording to the Tory candidate for Warrington, were must continue to be a rating and property qualification to render a citizen eligible for a seat on the Board of Guardians! It goes with- !ut saying, after finding such a fossil, that _dr. I."aPonir is not in favour of the" one man one tote" principle, and that he is opposed to "pay- merit of members." As to the latter, he objects to the heavy tax which it will involve. Heavy indeed, When the total cost—a quarter of a million—to be Paid for the services of 670 State Servants will be actually less by £lOO,OOO than the sum paid to the 9pileeu—to say nothing of "the rest of the Royal `,4131i1.Y." No; it is not the cost which is the chief °ejection in the eyes of Tory candidates. It is the fear that, if equality becomes the rule, thoughtful and capable working-men may find their way into the Rouse of Commons to the exclusion of the thou g5B idlers who have nothing to recom- mend them but long purses and readiness in tesponding to the party Whip. There are too ljanY of that class in the' House of Commons wrrady. Why, therefore, should working-men 32iieck at their own order and stultify themselves by voting for Mr.ROBERT PIFRPOINT who deCiill3S IO help them to seats either in Parliament or on the Board of Guardians?

WHAT CHARLES LAMB called the Warringt on Walking Da, "holiday rejoicing spirit" has various ways of asserting itself. In B°ree districts it displays itself on May Day; in Others at Whitsuntide; while in Warrington it breaks out at what is known as Walking Day. It ,11aPPen5, however, that Walking Day has partaken "uo much of the character caf a moveable feast; been attempts to make it a fixture have usually a case of "out of the frying pan into the fire." It was originally instituted as a t°nter-attraction to Newton Races; but it has 1 li°flg since ceased to be governed by Race i,ix,r"ek; and of late years the only question at 'sane has been the fixing of a date which could be 4441 to be convenient. It was understood to be aettled the last time the matter was under con- ,,aideration that Walking Day should, for the future, ne held on the 4th Friday in June; but it has been Icqind that that is not convenient for the leading nnfacturers, seeing that it necessitates a stop- page a week before the half-yearly stock-taking. This important consideration was mentioned last week,when the Rector of Warrington presided over a meeting of the Sunday School teachers in connec- tion with the Church ; but it was then thought It was too late to make a change this year. How- ever, at a representative meeting of Sunday,School teachers over which the Rector presided, on Mon- daY night, the subject was more fully considered; and it was ultimately, and wisely as we think, de- cided to hold Walking Day on the first Friday in 413% Curiously enough, the Rev. FRANCIS SLATER ,66eined to think Friday should be regarded as a lioly rather than a Holiday, and suggested Thurs- claY for the Walking Day; but his peculiar views /iiia.st with small support. Perhaps he did not do himself justice. He should have explained whether be regards Friday as too good for work as well as or play. "St. Monday" is observed in some trades; and if "St. Friday" can be added, the &!V• FRANCIS SLATER will stand a good chance of r,"e,illg canonised. Mr. A. J. JOLLEY, although a "Inrchman, did not fall in with the saintly sug- gesti" of the reverend gentleman. Instead looking upon him as his spiritual pastor Master, he actually had the temerity to say that his own Churchmansbip was of a more robust jPe than that of the Rev. F. SLATER. Really a lowly, not to say "low," laymen is to be per- illtitted to speak in this way, what is to become the " high " Churchman ? The question is rieYtl:endr ; and so we pass on to state that a pro- Was mooted to abolish Walking Day alto- ; but this met with no favour . It was 15:411Y decided that in future years there should a joint meeting of Sunday school teachers and Illilatinfacturers, and that the date should be fixed 19Y.ptheni in conference. This, it is to be hoped, a„1,!. Prevent misunderstandings, and give general tTlefaction. It certainly seems a reasonable way ,n arriving at a result which will least divide the .ninmunity.

Candles have gone out, but they will come in again, if there be not before long an improvement in Warrington gas. Where should, the pressurd be applied—on the gaspipes, the gas manager, or the Gas Committee ?

With regard to the provision of a new Public Hall for Warrington there seem to be lions in the path; but let them be faced, and perhaps they will flee. We should like the opinion of our readers on the proposal to utilise the old Market Hall. It will never do to build a new Town Hall in order to get a hall for public meetings.

The execution of Deeming has closed one source of morbid and degrading interest. It is to be hoped there will be no publication of the papers he has left, for, as his last hours and latest speeches show, he cannot have written anything worth a moment's consideration. There is suffici- ent garbage in the world without spreading broael- cast what Deeming may have left behind him

There has been another Unionist demonstration in London. Neither the Duke of Devonshire nor Mr. Chamberlain thought it good enough to be there, but the latter sent a letter in which be said —" the flowing tide was with them." Has "Joseph" suddenly become "kinder sarcastic" to his "brethren?" Or is it that he means "the flowing tide" is with them, and about to over- whelm them?

It turns out that the sensational account of the four duels fought in succession last week by M. Roulez is an entire fabrication. It seemsthat the weather has been warm, and tho imagination of the Frenchman became lively. His explanation is that his object was to hoax the Press ; but his friends suggest "mental aberration." Byron says that "Cervantes smiled Spain's chivalry away" ; and if M. Roulez can smile French duelling away, his hoaxes will ensure him immortality.

On Thursday evening, while Dr. Houston was canvassing, along with another Liberal, he was "shadowed" by a Tory Town Councillor. The Tories will do these shady things. But let the Town Councillor take care, or he may find that he is himself " shadowed " by the "snap-shot' of the amateur photographer.

A " Conservative " sends us a Tory leaflet which he asks us to publish by way of reply to the lette r of our correspondent" Manlius ;" but, with what Mr. Bright once called the" measureless audacity" of Toryism,he entirely ignores our correspondent's proposal which is to take two equal periods of Tory and Liberal government, and let them adduce all the measures they can bring forward on their individual sides for those periods.

"Conservative's" idea of" two'equal periods" is I to take twelve years of Tory administration and set them against six years of Liberal administra- tion! The gross unfairness—not to say immorality —of such a proceeding is thoroughly characteris- tic of Tory modes of controversy. It may do for the deluded hangers-on of the Primrose League; but not for the ordinary newspaper reader. Let " Conservative " begin by comparing "two equal periods,"—say six years of each party—and our columns will be open to him as to all other in- vestigators. But no fraudulent devices, please.

A local Tory contemporary quotes the Prime Minister's speech at Hastings, and heads it— " Lord Salisbury on Free ' Trade. How the country is being ruined." This is a dainty dish to set before the people, seeing that Lord Salisbury has been in power for over five years, and is still in power. If this comes of having the Tories in office, the sooner they are turned out the better it will be of course for the country that is "being ruined."

This much is clear, that if Lord Salisbury and his ministers believe that " the country is being ruined" by Free Trade, and that Protection is the road to salvation they ought to be impeached for their criminal neglect of a plain duty. The man who allows his country to be" ruined " when he knows what will save it, is not a patriot : he is either a coward, an incapable, or a traitor. We do not say Lord Salisbury is one or the other. He is just a bit of a humbug who is laughing in his sleeve at the muddle-headed Fair Traders while giving them a free hand in angling for votes. What said Mr. Bright in May 1885, and the Tories ' are never tired of praising the views of Mr. Bright? —" There seem to be few men acquainted with the facts, and still fewer who can reason from them. An American asked me if I thought we should return to a policy of Protection. ' I said, perhaps so, but not till you return to slavery.' The feeble Fair Trade' cry is dying out, and even Salisbury and Northcote have discovered this."

The Duke of Argyll was the principal speaker; and with his usual confidence he set about the im- possible task of proving that Mr. Gladstone had been guilty of political deception. Well, there is this to be said for the duke that he has not deceived anybody of late, for nobody has believed in him. His grace complained of the Liberal policy of con- cealment as to Home Rule; and yet, although an outsider, he professed to know that the Home Rule Bill of 1886 will be revived "with more monstrous features." " God bless the Duke of Argyll," and may his features never become monstrous.

Another Warrington police prosecution against a publican, and another instance of a case dis- missed. The Chief Constable must feel that this is getting monotonous ; and we cannot wonder at his intimation that for the future he would take out no summons on his own responsibility. There was a time when convictions against members of "the trade" averaged a score in the year. At the presant rate the average will be one to a score of years. Is the town becoming a marvel of vir- tue P Or, is it as one magistrate has suggested, that there is lamentable laxity somewhere P.

In the ordinary way of dealing with the ordin- ary person who is fined ss. and costs, there does not seem to be any difficulty. It is only when the ordinary person is found in a public-house that a difficulty arises as to whether be is drunk or not. It is thus that circumstances alter police court cases. The magistrates really ought to agree on a definition of drunkenness ; and some of them, we are quite sure, would incline an ear to the definition of the Scotchman who said, "a man is not drunk so long as he can lie on the floor."

Good Templars are being asked by the Grand Lodge of England to make use of the opportunity afforded them by the forthcoming election to pro- mote their principles. A circular offering advice and instruction has been issued from which we take the following :—" Ascertain definitely the views of your respective candidates. This may be done by means of an interview by deputation, or by letter. The candidates' opinions should be taken upon the following leading questions :—(1). Will you, if elected, support a measure giving the people a direct popular veto on the issue or re- newal of all liquor licenses ? (2). Will you oppose any attempt to grant compensation, from the pubiic funds, to the holders of expired licenses who, in the public interest, may be refused fresh licenses? (3.) Will you support the English , Sunday Closing Bill ?" These are fair and pertin- ent questions, and there. should be no delay in laying them before candidates.

"The Liberal Roll Call" is the title of a refer- ence sheet which has been printed in two colours at the " Examiner " Office. It is adorned with an admirable portrait of Dr. Houston, Q.C., the Liberal candidate for Warrington. It gives reliable details of the work done in the past by the Liberal party, and it will be seen that the record is a splendid one. As it is being distributed i amongst the electors of Warrington, t will serve to counteract the grossly misleading leaflets which the Tories are circulating. It will be seen that "The Roll Call" not only deals with "the work of the past," but points to "the work of the future ;" and in this respect it is in striking contrast to the literature of the Tories, who have no programme. L We shall give extracts from the sheet in our next

RUNCORN COUNTY COURT. His Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes held a sitting of this court, on Tuesday, when the list comprised 10 judgement summonses, 65 pilints, six default sum- monses, and one adjourned case. In the afternoon he preached to a large con- gregation in Victoria-road Chapel, and in the evening he delievered a lecture on "Jonah, the runaway prophet." There was a capital audience. The rateable value of the township is £140,813, and it was estimated that the rate would produce £14,081 6s. Od. The whole of the old rate had been collected. WIDNES CASES AT LIVERPOOL ASSIZES. At the Assizes which are now being held as Liverpool, there are seven prisoners who have been committed for trial from Widnes on the following charges : Man- slaughter, one; highway robbery with violence, two ; and unlawfully wounding, four. The list is somewhat shorter than usual, but the charges are of a graver character. _ _ .

A boy named Patrick Daley, 13, of Moss-st., was brought before the Widnes magistrates, on Monday morning charged with stealing a vest from Messrs. Muspratts works on the 24th April. Defendant was bound over to come up for judgment when called upon. —James Devereaux, 10, and Edward Flanagan, 13,both of Victoria-st., were dealt with in a similar manner for stealing a quantity of iron washers from Widnes Found ary. If you want a lucky wedding ring go to 51, lusin-sT.,where yen will get a present with ft.—Advt. ASSAULT WITH A POKER AT WIDNES.

At the viTdi;Wil'etty Sessions on Thursday before Mr. G. Filkington and Lieutenant-Colonel Gaskell a young man named Henry White, 14, Peal-st., was charged with unlawfully wounding John Powell, early on Sunday morning by striking him on ths head with a poker, in- flictine a wound four inches in length which penetrated to the bone. Inspector Patterson produced a certificate from Dr. O'Keeffe stating that the injured man was unable to appear in court. A remand was granted until Monday next, bail being allowed. PRITCHARD'S have now stood the test for 50 years,and quality sad firot-class workmanship are still guaranteed.—Advt. SHOCKING DEATH OF A CHILD AT RUNCORN.

Mr. J. E. Worsley, the coroner, on Thursday after- noon, held an inquest at Runcorn Police Court on the body of Wallace Wilson, aged two years, son of John Robert Wilson, of Mersey-at. Catherine James of Mill- et., said on the previous afternoon she heard that deceased had fallen down the closet and she found him there head downwards. There was only one foot to be seen. She took him out, and Dr. MacLennan was sent for. The doctor pronounced life to be extinct.—Mrs. Wilson, the mother, said it had been stated that a little playfellow aged five years had pushed the deceased down, but in her opinion the child had overbalanced himself in trying to reach a slat* pencil.—The jury re- turned a verdict of "Accidentally suffocated." If you wantyour watch repaired by skilful workmen, bake lb to PXITOIAILD'II.—Adrot.
SUDDEN DEATH AT THE RUNCORN UNION WORKHOUSE.

A man, apparently about 45 years of age, whose name is unknown, died at the Workhouse, Dutton, shortly be- fore eight o'clock on Wednesday night. The deceased arrived at the office of Mr. Ward, relieving officer, Church-st., Runcorn, at half-past one on Tuesday after- noon when he was noticed to be very ill. Mr. Howard provided him with a chair. He was unable to give any account of himself. Dr. McDougall was summoned,but despite that gentleman's efforts no information could be obtained. The man ma in a comatose condition. He was removed, in accordance with medical instructions, to the Workhouse, where he died as stated above, with- out having regained consciousness. From his appear- ance he seemed to be a navvy engaged on the works of the Manchester Ship Canal. Jos SPX PRITCHARD keeps spectacles to suit all sights from a shilling a pair.—.Adrt. FUNERAL OF MR. SINCLAIR ARMSTRONG OF RUNCORN. The mortal remains of Mr. Sinclair Armstrong, for ten years landlord of the Hulls Head Hotel, Flalton-road, Runcorn, were interred in their last resting place at Runcorn Cemetery on Sunday. In front of the hearse walked many members of the Licensed Victuallers Association, and representatives from the Duke of Devon- shire and Duke of Edinburgh Lodges of Oddfellows and from the William Wrights Pride of Past Grands Lodge. The mourners occupied coaches supplied by Messrs. Yarwood Bros. The service in the church and at the grave side was conducted by the Rev. A. Riley, curate at Holy Trinity Church, and Mr. Slade of the Duke of Devonshire Lodge read the burial service of the Independ- ent Order of Oddfellows. The deceased, who was 35 years of age, leaves two children and numerous friends to mourn his loss. dom., PRITCHARD is prepared ta wind and keep ia repair private (docks from 10s. per annum.—Advt. ALTERING A WATER METER AT WIDNES.

At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday Edward Gandy, shipwright, of Terrace-road, was summoned by the Local Board for having on or about the 20th April altered a water meter without the cQnsent of the Local Board as required by the Waterworks Clauses Act, 1863.—Mr. George Allen (Oppenheim and Malkin), prosecuted and Mr. F. J. Poole defended. Mr. Poole said the offence was admitted, but he had repaired the meter with a god intention and with no desire to defraud. He had had a lot ot trouble with his meters' and this one burst- ing, like the others he ordered his blacksmith to put an iron plate on.—Mr. Alien said it was not suggested that there was any fraudulent intent, and the Board would be satisfied with a nominal penalty as they had brought this case merely to show people they could not do these things.—A fine of ss. an I costs was imposed, Mr. Pil- kington remarking that the magistrates did not think there was any fraudulent intention. JOBEPH PRITCHARD, Watchmaker and Jeweller, 51, High. st., and 4, Bridge-at., Runcom—ildvt.

FOUND DROWNED AT WESTON POINT.

On Thursday afternoon, at the Weaver Hotel, Weston Point, Mr. E. .1. Worsley held an inquest on the body of a man unknown, which was found in the Weaver Canal, on Wednesday evening. The body is that of a man ap- parently between 30 and 40 years of age, and it is sur- mised that his occupation was that of a navvy. He was of dark complexion, and measured 51t. 9in. There was nothing in the pockets to lead to identification, and there were no marks of violence. An open verdict of "Found drowned" was returned. THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c.
"Br AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT."

Considering lie very short notice on which the arrangements had to be made, the Liberal meeting on Wednesday evening was a very successful one Dr. Spence Watson, who was under a promise to visit Widnes, wrote on Friday that he could attend on the evening named, and Mr. Shores at once set about arranging for a meeting by ticket, advertis- ing being dispensed with. Consequently the Drill half fillea must be •considered highly satisfactory, but it would be well in future not to call such meetings without due and ample preparation.

The proceedings kad a narrow escape of not being reported at all. It is impossible to compliment the organisers of these meetings upon the arrangements they make for the Press,and on Wednesday evening there was a table but no seats, and follc,wing the course they have had to take on innumer- able previous occasions, the reporters took chairs from the platform. A man who was apparently in charge and who said he was " acting lunder instructions" gruffly demanded that the chairs should be given up, and on an attempt being made to argue the point, he uncere- moniously dragged them from beneath the reporters, who did not immediately rise. As a protest against the want of accommodation and this conduct, the reporters left in a body, but at the request of the candidate and Mr. Shores, who as secretary to the Liberal Association is always courteous and obliging, they returned and found that ample accoramodation had been provided in the meantime. The meeting which had been delayed some minutes, then proceeded. The incident appeared to afford the audience considerable amusement, and their sympathies were evidently with the Press, who have a difficult duty to perform even under the best conditions. Perhaps in future Widnes press- men will be saved the trouble and unpleasantness of hunting up a chair or stool on which to sit when they attend lature meetings.

Mr. Deacon delivered a speech which exhibited his usual careful thought, and full consideration of the "pros and cons" of the questions which are agi- tating the country at the present time. There is no uncertain sound about his wishes and convic- tions, and should he have the good fortune to secure a seat in the House of Commons he will be found fully capable of dealing with the various social and political problems of the time. And with united and steady work, I think the Liberals of Widnes Division will convert a minority into a substantial majority, and thus wrest the seat from the party whose past history shows them only as defenders of class and privilege and as barriers to the liberty of the people.

_ Mr. George Whiteley, the Conservative candidate for Northwich Division, paid a visit to Runcorn on Tuesday, and spent a very busy day in canvassing and seeing that the organisation of the party was as complete as possible. I have heard a whisper that he visited about 60 public-houses in the course of the day, and, if, like the parsons with their tea- drinking (if they are not libelled) he had a drink at each place, he must have been nearly " brasted " when his round was completed. However, he was able to deliver an energetic and able speech to his workers in the Conservative Club in the evening,so that he must have either carefully mixed his drinks, or there is no truth in the story. A capital portrait of Mr. Whiteley is being circulated through the division, and his features will soon be well known to the electors.

The advent of the charter of incorporation into Widnes ie evidently not to be signalised by those gala proceedings that at one time appeared certain to take place. The LioC4l Duurcl cuunot utilize the rates for a demonstration, and the ratepayers out- side seem unwilling to take any action to subscribe to the cost of a display of loyalty and jubilation. If anything is to be done,a Committee of townspeople should be formed at once.

div.head: RUNCORN INDUSTRIAL BUILDING SOCIETY.
div.p: RUNCORN INDUSTRIAL BUILDING SOCIETY.

The a7n-n-U-ai meeting of this Society was held on Wed- nesday at the Society's office, 10 High-st., Runcorn, Mr. John Poole presiding. The report and balance sheet, which showed a balance in favour of the society of £5l 3s. 9d. together with a sum of £335 10s. 11d, pro- spective profits on premiums were fully discussed, and were adopted on the motion of the chairman seconded by Mr. J..K. Digges. The following gentlemen, viz., Messrs. A. Jordan, Wm. Sutton, J. K. Digges, and John Gates were re-elected as directors ; and Mrs. Joseph Pritchard and D. S. Garner were appointed auditors. chairman said he was glad to be able to criticise the report and balance sheet favourably. He pointed out that the prospective profits from premiums gave the society a good sum in reserve. He deprecated the practice of withdrawing which he considered against the interest both of the withdrawing member and also of the society. lie drew attention to the fact that the working expenses had been kept within the lowest possi- ble limits, the whole of the working expenses for the year being only £6l 7s. 9d. and he exhorted the mem- bhrs to co-operate with the directors in their efforts to issue the remaining books.
