div.head: RIVERS POLLUTION INQUIRY.
div.p: THE RIVERS POLLUTION INQUIRY.

The Parliamentary Committee on the Lancashire and Cheshire Rivers Pollution Bill resumed its la- bours on Wednesday, under the presidency of Sir F. S. Powell. Evidence was given as to the pollu- tion cf the Rollin by the town of Macclesfield, and as to the deplorable condition of the Irk and the Medlock. A member of the committee caused some amusement by the ironical inquiry, "Can fish live in those streams ?" The inquiry was again ad- journed.
Lawn Tennis.—GARL.LND, ironmonger, Bridge-at., Warring- ton.
DEATH OF A CHESHIRE CONGREGATIONAL MINISTER. _ _

The Rev. A. W. Potts, pastor of the Congrega- tional Cburch, Crewe, died yesterday morning. The rev, gentleman was well known throughout Cheshire, and had been prominently identified with religious movements in the country for nearly twenty years. He had been pastor of Crewe Con- gregational Church for nineteen years. The cause of death was cancer. Some years ago Mr. Potts was a prominent figure on Liberal platforms, but afterwards became a Liberal Unionist. Cricketing Goods.—GARLAND, Sports' Warehouse, War- rington.

div.head: VYRNWY WATER AQUEDUCTS„
div.p: THE VYRNWY WATER AQUEDUCTS„

On a visit being paid on Thursday to Fiddler's Ferry, where a tunnel has been bored under the Mersey for the carriage to Liverpool of Vyrnwy water, it was ascertained that the work is progres- sing very satisfactorily, every effort being put forth to complete it by the time indicated by Mr.lleacon, —the 14th of July. The pipes that have been laid in the subway have now been jointed,and will soon be joined to the main, men having been detailed to work all night in order to push forward the opera- tion. In consequence of the present high tides of the Mersey, water has got into the shaft on the r Cheshire side of the river, but very little delay will , be caused by this circumstance, as the water can Boon be got out. Lawn Mowers.—Lleatartn, horticultural ironmonger, War, rington.

"THE MOLOCH OF PARAFFIN" AT RUNCORN. About nine o'clock on Monday night a fire occurred at the house of John Sanders, 8, White-st., and but for the prompt action of several neighbours, might have had serious results. For nine weeks Mrs. Sanders has been confined to bed, and at the time stated, her son Harry, aged seven years, whilst lighting a paraffin lamp near the bed occupied by the invalid,upset the oil on the bed,and the clothes became ignited. Learning what had occurred,seve- ral neighbours went to the woman's assistance, and carried her into an adjoining house before she had been injured by the fiames,which were also quickly extinguished. The bed was destroyed, and some of the furniture was badly damaged. Mrs. Sanders received a severe shock through fright and was seriously ill for some time afterwards. The Fire Brigade were summoned,but their services were not required. The damage is estimated at £2O. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. tV,Icl W. DUTTON, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. A GEOLOGFICAL CURIOSITY AT Sr. HELENS.

On Wednesday . afternoon, a curious monument was erected in the Quakers' Burial Ground, adjoin- ing the old meeting-house in Raven-st., St. Helens. The Society of Friends set great value upon the place, and frequently spend large sums of money upon its renovation and restoration. For some weeks men have been engaged in raising the ground, it having sunk a considerable distance by reason of mining operations, and in addition to this the wall facing Shaw-st. and the railway station has been to a large extent repaired by pointing and renewal where necessary. The ground in question forms but a smallportion of a valuable estate owned by the sect,and on a portion of their land in Oxford- street,which runs up to the summit of Cowley Rill, there has lain for thousands of years—geologists say hundreds of thousands of years— a huge con- glomerate boulder. Very few people apparently were aware of this interesting relic of the glacial period in Britain being at their doors, and Messrs. Hanson and Booth, surveyors, of Church-st., who are the local stewards or agents for the Society of , Friends, determined to bring it to the front. Accor- dingly the work was entrusted to Mr. John Heaton, contractor, and he on Wednesday brought a lorry with three horses and a large number of men into requisition, and the huge stone, which weighs be- tween three and four tons, was lifted and taken to the burial ground a mile away; where it was set up on a plateau in the centre, so that a good public view might be obtained from Shaw-st. UMBRELLAS RECOVRRED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-st., Warrington.— Advt.

div.head: ALLEGED WOUNDING AT WIDNES. _ _ACQUITTAL OF THE PRISONERS._
div.p: ALLEGED WOUNDING AT WIDNES. _ _ACQUITTAL OF THE PRISONERS._

At the Crown Court of the Liverpool Spring Assizes, on Thursday afternoon, before Mr. Justice Cave, three men named Thomas Griffin, James Meloin, and Peter Ryland surrendered to their bail on a charge of having wounded Danial Gilmore, at Widnes,ron the 25th April, with intent to do him griev- ous bodily harm. Mr. Collingwood Hope appeared to prosecute, and Mr. Swift appeared for the defence. Mr. Hope said that the prosecutor was a labourer, and that as he was returning home from his work on the night in question the prisoners met him and commenced to quarrel with him. They set upon Gilmore and threw him over some railings. They afterwards jumped over I after him and kicked him. The prosecutor received I severe injuries, and as he had one of his ribs broken he could not go to work for some weeks. For the defence it was contended that Gilmore provoked the assault, and made the men fight with him.—After hearing witnesses on both sides the jury found the prisoners not guilty,and they were accordingly discharged.

div.head: PROPOSED TREAT TO POOR CHILDREN AT RUNCORN.
div.p: PROPOSED TREAT TO POOR CHILDREN AT RUNCORN.

On Monday evening the General Committee of the Aged Persons' Treat Fund met at the Town Hall, to consider the report of the sub-Committee with reference to the proposed summer treat to poor children. Mr. H. J. Grice presided and there was a good attendance. Mr. W. Frith (one of the secretaries), read the minutes of the sub-Com- mittee, who recommended that Mersey View Grounds, Frodsham, was the most suitable place to visit, that the treat be given on Friday, June 3rd, and that they leave Runcorn Station at one o'clock. It was stated that the number of children would be about 500, the selection to be made from the School Board registers. It was also recommended that the tender of Mrs. Parker, of the Mersey View, to cater for the children be accepted, and that the children each receive a bun and orange before starting, and that 20 or 30 members of the Committee be requested to give their services to attend to the wants of the children. The probable cost per head was Is.—The Chairman, in moving the confirmation of the suggestions said the matter had received most careful consideration, and he thought that the course recom- mended by the Committee was the wisest possible.—Mr. W. M. Sowerly seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously.—On the motion of the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, seconded by Mr. Sowerby, the sub-Committee was authorised to make all necessary arrangements for the trip, and it was further resolved on the motion of Mr. W. Mundin, seconded by Mr. S. Taylor, that the adults who accompany the children shall pay their own I- expenses.

div.head: MR. WADE DEACON FOR WIDNES.
div.p: MR. WADE DEACON FOR WIDNES.
MEETING IN THE DRILL HALL.

A meeting in support of the candidature of Mr. 11. Wade Deacon, the Liberal candidate for Widnes Division, was held in Widnes Drill Hall on Wednes- day evening. There was a good attendance and, in the absence of the Chairman of the IS idnes District of the Liberal Association, Mr. F. H. Pankhurst pre- sided. Besides the candidate, there were on the platform Dr. R. Spence Watson, chairman of the National Liberal Federation ; Messrs. S. K. Muspratt, F. Gaskell, Stewart Deacon, F. Hartland and IL B. • Shores. .

Mr. Deacon, who received a cordial greeting, said he was glad to see so many preseat on such a fine night, and when there were other attra'iti a 3. (Hear, hear.) He proposed "That this meeting of Widnes electors hails with satisfaction the approaching dissolution, as affording an opportunity of expressing through the ballot box their continued support of Mr. Gladstone's Irish policy, and of reversing the hastily conceived and mistaken verdicts given by the constituency at the last two elections." (Applause.) The present Government had lived too long, and the future lay with the Liberals, and they in Widnes were cheerful and full of hope, and they intended to do their utmost to win the next elec- tion whenever they had the opportunity. (Applause.) But like reasonable beings they recognised that they had a hard fight before them. They had to pull down a very big majority, they had to defeat a man who had been twice successful, a man whom his party told them they were cocksure of carrying again to victory. What they had to do was to keep a cheerful heart and a cool head, to be united, and not be led to abstain from voting, or to vote on the wrong side if the candidate could not agree with everybody upon every conceivable subject. (Hear, hear.) They had one great cause to fight and other causes to help and they had a magnificient leader in Mr. Gladstone (applause), and they wanted to oust and utterly defeat the Government of broken pledges. (Applause.) He trusted that the Liberals would not be found wanting on the day of election, but would give a good account of themselves. (Applause.) They did not fight for Home Rule alone; there were other reforms which were awaiting Liberal hands to accomplish—great social questions which were rapidly coming to the front—questions of most vital importance and upon the proper solution of which de- pended the future welfare of millions of their fellow countrymen and countrywomen. They believed that these questions could be solved by the Liberals in a wider, freer and more sympathetic manner than they could be by the Tories. (Applause.) They were face to face with new social problems, and it was the duty of the Liberal party to face what was before it. If these problems were solved wisely—if the goose which laid the golden eggs be not killed by reform—then he believed there lay before the great masses of the people more leisure, greater hope, not less wages, he trusted, and not less happiness. (Applause.) But if great and serious mistakes be made; if in the enthusiasm of unsound benevolence trade be crippled and enterprise checked, then the work* classes would feel the effects most heaviiy. He had little doubt but that in future I they would act wisely and carefully, for he had great ; faith in the good sense of the people. (Applause.) He agreed with the principle of the direct veto. The power I was at present exercised by the landlords, who had the , power to close public-houses on their estates, and, if it be right for landlords to have this power, could it be wrong for the people of a locality to have the power tor themselves. (Applause.) Sunday closing and the ' sale of liquor to children would have to be attended to in the immediate future. As to the provision of pensions for old age. Everyone could join in a desire that every- body should have enough to live upon when they became old and enfeebled and unfit for work, but in his opinion there would have to be more thorough and careful con- sideration than it had already received before they could arrive at a satisfactory conclusion. They did not want to discourage thrift nor to discourage in any way the work which was being done by the friendly societies. (Applause.) Great injustice was at present worked be the Poor Laws. Decent men and women seeking relief were herded together with the worthless and depraved, and this state of things 'ought not to exist. (Applause.) Old couples who had spent their lives together, honourably and in hard work, should be allowed to end their lives together if they went to the workhouse. (Applause. i Their present system of pocr laws offered no inducement for thrift—a -man might as ' well save nothing at all as save less than was sufficient to support himself when he became old, because under the present law relief could not be given if a man had money to spend on his own account. This was wrong and must be clTsged. (Applause.) Then the receipt of temporary relief ought not to disfranchise a man from voting. A reform of the Registration laws was much needed. (Hear hear.) It ought to be as easy to get on the register as it was to get , on the rate book (applause) and it ought to be just , as easy to be kept there. (Applause.) As to the ques- tion of Home Rule, Mr. Edwards Moss was reported to , have said that he would not be surprised to hear that I the rank and file of the Gladstonian party were rather pleased if Home Rule were put back in the dim and • distant future. Now, he (Mr. Deacon) 63 a member of

the rank and file of that great party declared it to be impossible to make a statement wider of the mark than that (Applause.) If ever the Liberal party was pledged to anything in this world, in word and in honour they were pledged to the utmost to givc Home Rule to Ireland on the first opportunity. (Applause.) And speaking for himself, and he believed for hundreds of Liberal men in Widnes he said they desired nothing but the opportunity to give effect to their pledges. (Renewed applause.) Mr. F. Hartland seconded the motion and said the actions and deeds of the Liberal party in the past invited the working-men to place their -confidence in them in the future. (Applause.) Dr. Spence Watson supported the motion, and in the course of his speech said there was the true sound Radicalism running all through Mr. Deacon's remarks, and he urged all present who were anxious to see the reforms the Liberal party had undertaken carried into execution, to make himself in a political missionary for Mr. Deacon. (Applause.) He proceeded ta deal at length with the Irish question. The motion was unanimously carried, and the usual votes of thanks concluded the proceedings.

div.head: HOUSE-BREAKING AT PRESTON BROOK
div.p: HOUSE-BREAKING AT PRESTON BROOK

Yesterday, at the Runcoin Police Court, before Mr. Joseph Handley, John Massey, of the Albion Vaults ; Daniel Massey, coal dealer; John Brown, labourer, all of Nelson-st. ; and James Clayton, la- bourer, Ellesmere-st., were charged with breaking and entering the house of John Robinson, railway porter, Preston Brook, and stealing a wooden box containing a quantity of wearing apparel,some-time during Wednesday night. These men on Wednes- day afternoon went for a drive in a conveyance be- longing to Mr. Banks, furniture dealer, High-street, and at night when they were returning home the attention of P.C. Fryer was drawn to them at Hal- ton by a couiplaint that they had been trespassing in search of game. Afterwards, when it became known that the house of Robinson bad been robbed, the constable remembered seeing the box described in the conveyance occupied by the pri- soners, for a search revealed it in a hay loft in Nelson-st..occupied by John Massey.—The prisoners were remanded to Daresbury Petty Sessions, on Tuesday.

div.head: CONFERENCE OF LIBERAL AGENTS AT
div.p: CONFERENCE OF LIBERAL AGENTS AT
NORTHWICH.

The annual meeting of the Manchester district of the National Association of Liberal Secretaries and Agents embracing the counties of Cheshire, Lanca- shire, and Derbyshire, was held at the Gladstone Club, Northwich, on Monday. Mr. S. J. Harrison, (chairman of the district) presided, and the follow- ing members of the association were present : Messrs. B. L. Green, N. W., Manchester; Sim Schofield, Prestwich ;C. A. Walls, East Manchester ; Fred Monks, Rossendale ; T. Renshaw, North Salford •, J. Birtwistle, Accrington ; J. Lonsdale, Clitheroe ' • S. Cheetham, Mid- dleton ; W. Rawksworth, Oldham • J. Wigley, Stretford and South-West Manchester; J. W. Rylance, Leigh ;E. L. Kenyon, Altrincham ; A. Honey, Liverpool (u. B. Shores, Widnes ; J. J. Bellis, North Manchester : H. Gerrey, Bolton: Richard Vickers, Westhoughton ; S. Bancroft, Blackpool : J. Longworth, Farnworth ; T. Hampson, Radcliffe; W. Handley, Northwich ;A. Gould Jones,Excha.nge Division,Liverpool; T. W. Neale, Gorton; George Massey,Stockport ; E. W. Humphreys, Runcorn; J. Latham, Crewe; U. E. King, Northwich • J. Cart- ledge, Northwich; and George Shaw, Davenh'am. The annual report submitted by Mr. Sim Schofield and the bat:lnce sheet presented by Mr. C. A. Walls were con- sidered very satisfactory, it being shown that much useful work had been performed by the association. The report and financial statement were unanimously adopted. The following gentlemen were appointed as officers for the ensuing year: Messrs. S. J. Harrison (Darwen), chairman ; C. A. Walls (East Manchester), treasurer ; and S. Schofield (Prestwich), hon. secretary. All the officers, with the addition of Messrs. A. Gould Jones (Liverpool), William Handley (Northwich), and B. L. Green (Manchester), were appointed as the Exc. , cutive Committee, Messrs, S. J. Harrison, S. Schofield, B. L. Green, A, Honey, and William Handley were choSen as representatives to the Central Council of the Associatlon. The ordinary business having been dis- posed of, several points of great interest and importance relative to the coming election were discussed at length by the members, after which the company were enter- tained to tea by Mr. J. T. 13rupner, M.P. (president of the Cheshire Liberal Federal Council).

div.head: HORRIBLE CRUELTY TO A WIFE AT
div.p: HORRIBLE CRUELTY TO A WIFE AT

WIDNES. EXEMPLARY SENTENCE. At the Liverpool Assizes on Wednesday, before Mr. Justice Cave, Francis Gaynor (20,1abourer,was indicted for having maliciously wounded his wife, Mary Ann Gaynor, at Widnes, on the 2nd ult., with intent to do her grievous bodily harm. Mr. Squarey prosecuted. The wife of the prisoner, who was called, said she had 'n married about nine months. She resided in lodg- in ith the prisoner in Widnes. On the 2nd of April the prisoner came home and asked for his dinner. She replied that she had had no breakfast. He then asked for some tobacco, but she had none to give him. The prisoner then threatened her with violence, and said "If you are here when I come back to night there will be another Rainhill case." The prisoner then went away, and for safety she went into the house of a neighbour. She subsequently with her child went into an outhouse, and the prisoner hav- ing ascertained where she was from another child, went to the place, and seizing hold of her dragged her into the house. He then caught hold of her by the hair, knocked her against the wall, and beat her. He next seized hold of her by her ears and bumped her head against the wall. She cried out " Murder," and the prisoner put his hand upon her mouth to stop her cries. He next threatened to murder her. A neighbour burst , the door in, as the prisoner was dragging her by the ' hair across the room, and striking her with his fist. She ultimately got out of the place, and took refuge in a neighbour's house. On the next day the prisoner again I assaulted her, and kicked her with his clogs till she was insensible. He kicked her upon the small of the back, and also struck her with his fists upon the head. She had suffered great pain, and was lying ill for several weeks. Mrs. Oakes, a neighbour, said she went into the house of the last witness on hearing cries of "Murder." she saw the prisoner striking his wife and dragging her :by the hair across the floor. She told him not to murder his wife as she was only a woman. The prisoner then used an obscene expression, and ultimately his wife managed to escape from the house. Another witness proved that on the next day she saw the prisoner assaulting his wife and kicking her with I clogs. The wife of the prisoner had to be removed in an 1 insensible condition. The prisoner, who was undefended, did not ask any questions of the two witnesses. Mr. Squarey called several other witnesses' but as the prisoner said he did not wish to ask them any quest'ons they were not examined.

Dr. Hudson said he had attended to the wife of the prisoner. When he first saw her she appeared to be dying. She was suffering great pain and agony. She was bruised all over. Her spine had been injured, and she would never be a strong woman again. .The prisoner now said he did not know what he was doing. He asked the judge to have mercy upon him this time, and promised that he would never do such a thing again. He had been drinking on the occasion from nine o'clock in the morning.

The jury found the prisoner guilty. His Lordship, in passing sentence, said the prisoner had been convicted of wounding his wife with intent to do her grevious bodily harm. It was a mercy that the prisoner was not standing there to take his trial for murder. If he had been standing there on that charge, he certainly would have been convicted and hanged for what he had done. Fortunately for the prisoner, the woman's constitution had enabled her to pull through. The assault he was found guilty of was that of a savage rather than that of a man. People in the condition of • the prisoner must be taught that they were rict to give vent to their passions upon a woman, and those women their wives, whom they had sworn to cherish and pro- tect. The prisoner must go to penal servitude for 12 years.

div.head: IMPENDING DISSOLUTION.
div.p: THE IMPENDING DISSOLUTION.
PROMISED ANNOUNCEMENT.

The " Daily News" says :—We understand that the conversation which took place in the House of Commons on Thursday night between the leader of the Opposition and the First Lord of the Treasury followed upon communications that 'had taken place between the two Front Benches on the ques- tion of the date of the Dissolution. The Govern- ment will take a few days to consider the situation, but a definite statement on the subject will be forthcoming before the House adjourns for Whitsun recess.

The General Committee of the National Liberal Federation held a meeting in Birmingham on Tues- day. A resolution was passed expressing satisfac- tion at the prospect of a speedy dissolutfon of Par- liament, and a spirit of hopefulness and confidence pervaded the several speeches delivered. It is reported from Braintree that to avoid a by- election Sir Henry J. Selwyn-Ibbetson, Bart.,M.P. for the Epping Division of Essex, will defer until the Dissolution the acceptance of the honour con- ferred upon him by his elevation to the peerage on the Queen's Birthday. In the course of an interview on Thursday after- noon, Mr. Leonard Courtney, M.P., the Chairman of Committees, is said by the Press Association to have expressed the opinion that the Dissolution would come in about three weeks. In regard to the view that there would not be time to discuss the Local Government Bill for Ireland in Committee this session, Mr. Courtney said this was a very large question, and if the Opposition were organized I against the Bill, it was difficult to see how it could be passed. At a meeting of the Irish National party held on Thursday a permanent committee was appointed to sit in Dublin to make and direct arrangements for tie electoral campaign. The committee will enter upon its duties on Monday next. It consists of Mr. Dillon, Mr. Healy, Mr. O'Brien, Mr. Sheehy. Mr. 1 Murphy, Mr. Davitt, and the whips of the party.

div.head: SUNDAY TRAINS FOR RUNCOBN.
div.p: SUNDAY TRAINS FOR RUNCOBN.

It will be welcome news to many persons that next month the Railway Company intend to relax their rigid rule with regard to the non-running of Sunday trains at Runcorn. From the first Sun- day in June a train will leave Chester for Liverpool at 9.35 a.m., calling at Runcorn. The train will return from Liverpool to Chester at 5p.m., also call- ing at Runcorn. This is only a small concession, but it will be of great advantage to many people, and having now got in the thin end of the wedge we may hope for greater privileges in the near future.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.
BULL LOOSE AT PENKETH.

On Sunday afternoon last some excitement was caused by the appearnce of a large bull running wild through the village. The animal belongs to Charles Kilshaw, of Cuerdley, and had broken out of the field where it had been placed. Several men endeavoured to turn the bull towards his home but he leaped over the hedge into afield and from there he ran into the grounds adjoining the Mission-room. The animal attempted to leap over the railings but fell forward impaling himself on the spikes. He ' fell into the road dragging the railings with him. The bull was bleeding freely and was then driven home.

div.head: N'ARROW EscAPit.
div.p: A N'ARROW EscAPit.

On Saturday evening, about 8.30, *whilst traverS'- lug the gangway leading from the lightship to the shore atbFiddler's Ferry, a Mrs. Rowe was precipi- tated into the river owing to the gangway, which is only a plank ten yards long, turning on edge. It was high tide at the time, and Mrs. Rowe would ' assuredly have been drowned had it not been for the coolness of Mr. Johnson, jun. On hearing screams he immediately ran to the spot, and suc- ceeded in drawing the immersed woman close to the bank by means of a hook attached to a long pole. He then jumped in, and brought her safely to the shore.

div.head: FRODSHAM,
div.p: FRODSHAM,

TirmyrY SUNDAY Somer..—The annual services in aid of the funds of the Wesleyan school were held in the Trinity Chapel, on Sunday morning and evening, when the Rev. Robert Newton Barritt, of Bolton, preached. The rev, gentleman also conducted a special service in the afternoon for scholars, teachers, and friends. The services throughout the day were well attended, the evening one especially. Mr. W. H. Pickering officiated at the organ, and Mr. T. Sant conducted. The offer- tories realised £22 2s. PETTY SESSIONS—At these Sessions on Wednesday before Mr. C. Reynolds and Dr. Steele, Samuel SVorrall, Five Crosses, was summoned for being drunk and dis- orderly in Belle-Mont-road, Overton, on the 16th ult.— He was fined 2s. 6d. and Bs. 6d. costs.—George Griffiths, Ilapsford, was summoned for obtaining from the Railway Inn public-house, Dunham-o'-th'-hill, one pint of ale, by falsely representing himself to be a Londfide traveller, on the 3rd ult.—Defendant pleaded guilty. Griffiths obtained the ale by saying he came from Chester.—Fined 18s. including costs. SALE or PROPERTY. —On Tuesday evening, at the Bear's Paw Hotel, Frodsham, a very successful sale of property was couducted by Mr. Jones, auctioneer to the Frodsham Farmers' Auction Company. Two freehold shops with dwelling-houses, in Church-st., Frodsham, respectively occupied by Messrs. John Roberts and James Hough, were started at £4OO, and ultimately advanced to £1,025, when Mr. Youd was declared the purchaser. Three freehold dwelling-houses, in Main-st., Frodsham, in the occupation of Mr. Thomas Maddocks, Mrs. Janion, and Mr. Henry Lewis, passed into the posses- sion of Mr. Hunt at £7OO. A freehold shop and dwell- ing-house, is Main-st., tenanted by Mr. Frank Harrison was purchased by Mr. Gleave for £250. Six dwelling- houses known as Albert-terrace in Main-st., were sold to Mr. Youd, for £7OO. The solicitors acting in the matter re Thomas Gorst, deceased, were Messrs. Linaker and Linaker, Runcorn and Frodsham. FLASIT BANK NOTES Al' FRODSHARI. —At the Frodsham Police Court, yesterday week, before Mr. A. Thomas, a charge was preferred against John Fordham, aged 67 years, of shabby genteel appearance, of loitering in Main-st., Frodsham, with intent to commit a felony, on the 10th and 12th inst.; also refusing to give any ac- count of himself, and being in possession of a money order fer £7 which had had the date altered, and was supposed to have been:stolen from the Wandsworth Post Office, London.—P.S. Doyle stated that at 1.30 p.m. on the 10th inst. he saw the prisoner in Main-st.,Frodsham, standing about and reading a paper. From information received on the 12th inst. he went to the house of H. Limbeth, Church-st., and examined a parcel left there by the man on the Tuesday previous. In consequence of its contents he went in pursuit of the prisoner, found him, and the same night at the police station charged him. He declined to give his name and address, or, in fact, afford any information. In his presence he his property, and found correspondence from various towns in different names, and several dash" bank notes—two for £lO, and one for £s.—Prisoner stated that he visited Frodsham in order to get lodgings, which were cheaper there than in Chester during the race week. The money order was not one in reality, but simply a counterfoil for an amount sent to India_ The " flash " notes were such that a blind man could not be deceived. There was no trickery about the bills; they were simply advertisements, given away in the streets of London. The letter registering patent was a real one, for an invention sof his own.— The prisoner was discharged, the Bench ordering the detention of the sus- picious notes.

Mr. William Fl. Vanderbilt, eldest son of the mil- lionaire, died on Monday night, in New York. I It is said that Captain Osborne has sent in his papers. to the War Office Authorities, with a view to resigning his commission. At Kilquaro, near Tralee, a herdsman named Dono- ghue, aged 60, was on Sunday gored to death by a bull of which he had charge. The survivors of the crew of the schooner Edward, of Portmadoc, were landed on Saturday at Southampton by the Havre mail boat. On Saturday the Durham coalowners refused the men's offer to resume work at 10 per cent. reduction, declining to accept a smaller reduction than 131 per cent. On Thursday an attempt was made at Coventry to sell goods seized for non-payment of Vicar's rate, but some 20,000 persons assembled and prevented the sales and the auctioneer, who hailed from Birmingham, left the scene under the protection of the police.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
FIIRIGGS DRIVING AT WARRINGTON.-ALDERMAN HARRI-

SON DEFINES DRUNKENNESS AND INTOXICATION. Alexander Dunlop, chemist, 52 John-st., was charged at the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday, with furiously driving a horse and gig on Saturday night.—A witness, Mr. Brice, described the defendant as intoxicated.—Alderman Harrison : Do you think he was drunk or only intoxicated, because there is a broad distinction ?—Mr. Brice : He was intoxicated. —Alderman Harrison : A man is said to be intoxicated hhen he knows what he is doing but does not care, and drunk when he neither knows nor cares what he does. —The defendant was fined 205., including costs. ANOTHER. THIEVISH JUVENILE. At the Borough Magistrates' Court, on Monday, John Stanton,a boy,l2th appearance, was charged with steal- ing, at about half-past ten on Saturday night, in the Market Place, 2s. 6d. the property of James Longshawo. Musgrove had been exhibiting two half-crowns he had to the prisoner and they fell, on which the prisoner stooped and then ran away. A man asked him where the half-crowns were and he winked at him. Stanton was apprehended by P. S. Monaghan in company with a lad named Bamford amongst the stalls in the market about half-past 11 the same night. They had 2s. 7d. between them, and he took them both to the Police Station, though Bamford could not be proved to have had anything to do with the theft. Stanton was also charged with stealing oranges, evidence being given by Bamford and other witnesses.—The Bench considered there was a doubt in the casesand dismissed the lads with a caution.

CIWZGE OF NON-MAINTENANCR. At the Borough Police Court, on Saturday, Richard Bushell was summoned by his wife, Alice, for non-com- pliance with an order made at Runcorn, to contribute towards the support of his three children. Mr. Percy Davies defended.—The complainant said that they had been married 22 years. Her husband was employed by the Bridgewater Navigation Company at Birkenhead. Ldant had not complained of her conduct. Last . .
The defeiii ‘)e,

Novemi ton. Isaac Bostock had been living with her since she came to Warrington. The Bridgewater Company had discharged him at a minute's notice, she did not know why.—Bushell said his wife while at Runcorn was lead- ing an improper life, and on that account he had broken the house up several times.—Mr. J. Sutcliffe, foreman for the Manchester Ship Canal Company at Birkenhead, gave the defendant an excellent character.—Thomas Carlson, captain of the flat Rija, said he saw Mrs.Bushell coming off Bostock's flat the very day that Bostock was discharged.—Mrs. Hatton, 146, Manchester-road, War- rington, said she was landlady of the house in Cross-st. at which Mrs. Bushell lived. She understood that Mr. Bostock was her husband. Had she known the truth, then she would not have allowed them to live there.— Mr. Davies said he thought it was a piece of impudence for complainant to summon her husband for money which, if paid, would go towards supporting, Bostock and herself.—The magistrates decided to discharge the order.

CHARGE OF CRUELTY TO A SHEEP.—ALDEEMAN HARRISON ANIMADVERTS ON BUTCHERS. At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday, Wm. Worrell, butcher, of 47, Wash-lane, was charged With cruelty to a sheep,by allowing a dog to worry it in Rnutsford-road, on the 6th inst. Mr. Browne defended. P.C. Bell deposed to seeing the defendant's dog worry- ing the sheep by tearing wool from its hind quarters, the dog's mouth being full of wool. Witness put up his hand for the defendant to stop the sheep to examine it, but though he saw this he would not stop it. He turned the sheep into a field, the dog continuing to worry it. The defendant never took any notice of the worrying, and said he did not see the constable put up his hand. The sheep was exhausted and frothing from the mouth. He went afterwards with Mr. Dowty to see the sheep, but could not tell whether a sheep he saw there was the same or not. Richard kliller,who was with the constable on the occasion of the alleged worrying, corroborated. --Mr. Browne called William Caskey, who said the dog was only barking at, not worrying, the sheep.—Robert Fairclough, retired butcher, said he examined the sheep's carcase and skin after it had been slaughtered, and found no indications of worrying. There was a bit of hair off the neck which would be caused by pulling it aleng.—Alderman Harrison said there was a good deal of cruelty in permitting dogs to run at sheep.—Mr. , Browne said in that case every butcher in Warrington would be subject to prosecutien.—Alderman Harrison said butchers were a very cruel race of people. At one time they were prohibited from sitting on juries, be- cause it was thought that on account of their business they would not be able to appreciate what cruelty was. —Mr. Browne: Thank goodness that was in a bye-gone age.—Alderman Harrison said he was afraid butchers by reason of their occupation were very liable to be cruel. He considered the evidence in the case clearly proved cruelty.—The Mayor concurred in the last re- mark, and the defendant was mulcted in the costs,
12s. 6th

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE coma. SATURDAY.—Before Alderman Burrss and Mr. Geddes. THEFT OF PIGEONS.—Thomas Farrington, a young man, residing with his parents in Pierpoint-it., was charged with stealing two pigeons from a cote in the yard of his brother Michael, a married man, living in Cartwright-st. The prisoner had sold them to a Mr. Locker for 10d. He pleaded not guilty, and was sent to prison for 14 days with hard labour. DRUNKENNESS'—Emma Williams was fined for this offence. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Greenall), and Aldermen Francomb and Harrison. A DRUNKEN WINDOW SMASHER.—Martin Mulhall, labourer, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-St., on Saturday night, an wilfully breaking a window in the shop of Wm. Gallop, doing damage to the extent of 105. He put his back against the window to break it and not succeeding the first time, did so a second time. When apprehended he told the constable if he let him go he would do it again. He was sent to gaol for a month in the first case and two months in the second. DRUNK.—Daniel Crosby, drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-St., on Saturday night, was dismissed with a caution.—John Parry was charged with being drunk and disorderly, also with assaalting P.C. Bell :in Buttermarket-St.lle struck the officer several times and kicked him on being arrested, and at the station re- fused to be searched. He was sent to jail for a month's hard labour.—Michael Chasey, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bridge-st.,on Saturday night,also with assaulting P.C. Meacock at the Police Station. The constable said he was drunk playing a tin whistle, and causing an obstruction, and refused to go, using abusive language, and on entering the station assaulting the officer. He was sent to jail for a month's hard labour. —John Duffy, labourer. 3, Ship Yard, drunk and disor- derly in that yard t hat morning,was fined ss. and costs.— Martin Cassidy, labourer, was charged with being drunk and disorderly at Bank Quay Station, and with assault- ing Bennett, the ticket collector, on Saturday night. • The prisoner and three companions, all drunk, came to the station at half-past ten p.m. and wanted to go to • Earlestown, but Bennett told them they were too late,

and if they had not been he would not have allowed them to go in their condition. The prisoner then struck Bennett, and the other three dragged him about and when he got up, the prisoner hit him in the mouth and nose and made them bleed. He was fined 10s. and costa, THEFT OF A WAISTCOAT—John Scott, navvy, lately of Wigan, was charged with stealing, on Saturday night, a waistcoat, value 4s. Bd., from the shop of Edgar Valentine Morton, pawnbroker, Winwick-st. He went to the shop and enquired for a pair of earrings, and while the man in charge was getting them, took the , vest from the counter and put it under his coat.—P.C. ' Corcoran apprehended him, and he said a man put it under bis coat.—The prisoner said he was the worse for drink and did not know what he was doing.—He was fiaed 10s. including Costs. TRAVELLING WITHOUT A TlCKET.—Michael Devine, labourer, of Widnes, was charged with travelling on the London and North-Western railway from Widnes to Warrington on Saturday night, and with assaulting Railway-Detective Osborne, at Bank Quay Station, on the occasion. He was asleep in the carriage, and on Osborne arousing him to get his ticket struck him and knocked him on to his back. He had a ticket from Liverpool to Widnes, but could not be got out of the train at the latter place. He wasfined 10s. and costs. UNSEEMLY CONDUCT.—Sarah O'Brien, 3, Naylor-St., was charged with unseemly conduct in Church-st., on Saturday night, and with having been previously com- mitted of the like offence. She was dismissed on con- dition that she left the town. Ficarrnsa.—Mary Ann Hulford, for fighting in Sankey- st., on the 14th inst. was bound over in £5 to keep the peace six months, and had to pay Bs, 6d. costs.—Wm. Nicholson, bricklayer, 4, Aiken-st., and Michael Foy, forge labourer, 39, Leicester-at., were each bound over in 25. THROWING A BRlM—Thomas Savage, 33 School Brow, charged with throwing a piece of brick, to the annoy- ance and danger of passengers, on the 12th inst., was dismissed with a caution. STREET OBSTRUCTION BY A TRADESMAN.—Frank Gar- rett, 6, Rylands-st., who was fined for a like offence last week, was charged with allowing on the 19th inst., goods to stand a,nd hang so aa to be en obetruetiou to the footpath.—The Chief Constable remarked that he did not wish to press the case too much, but the defendant was a hard learner. He was ordered to pay the costs, 7s.—Frances Mellor, widow, pork butcher, Bridge-st., was fined ss. including', costs, for depositing refuse in front of her shop on the 19th inst. TUESDAY.—Before Mr. R. Garnett and Mr. E. J. Guest. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—John Moran, in Butter- market-st., on Monday night, 10s.—George Deakin, at Latchford, the same night, 2s. 6d.—Mary Douglas, in Stanley-st., 2s. 6d. including costs. EDUCATION CASES.—The following persons were fined, at the instance of Mr. Riley, school attendance officer, for not sending their children to school :—Thomas Chrimes, Portland-st. ' • David Dunbobbin, 23, Nicholson- st. ;Eliza Eripath, Eldon-st. ; Mary Garrity, rag sorter; Wm. Rennan, 12, Robinson-st. ; Seth Travis, 91,School- brow •, John Sankey, 23, Hind-st. ; Richard Moore, 24, Glazebrook-st. ; James Bibby, Daniel-. ; and John Bracegirdle, 39, Warburton-st. THEFT BY A MILITIAMAN.—Peter 0' Brien, militiaman, was charged with stealing ss. Bd. on Monday night,from the tunic of another militiaman at Orford Barracks. The prosecutor went to bed leaving the money in the pocket and got up again, and found that the amount had been stolen. Sergeant Craythorne was acquainted, and the prisoner was apprehended.—He was sent to prison for 14 days. THURSDAY.—BeforeXaptain Ridgeway (chairman) and Councillor James Fairclough. TRAVELLING WITHOUT A TlCKET.—Frederick Lyon was charged with travelling on the Cheshire Lines Com- mittee's railway, from Liverpool to Widnes the previous night without a ticket, and had to pay 10s. and costs, and the railway fare; in default 14 days imprisonment. FEraet.—Before Captain Ridgway (chairman), Alder- men Wright and Harrison and Dr. Gornall. NON-MAINTENANCE.—Arthur fames Bailey, a married man, of Birchall-st., was charged by Mr. Shearer, on behalf of the Guardians, with refusing to contribute 2s. a week towards the maintenance of his father. An order for allowance of the amount was made.—G. Ball, 2, Gorsey-lane, was icharged with non-payment of £7 arrears due for the maintenance of his wife, Catherine, of 4, Orford Avenue. Mr. Jenkins defended, and sought to show that she had been consorting with other men, but she denied having been guilty of misconduct. The case was adjourned for a month, he saying he would obtain evidence on the matter.—Alderman Harrison desired it to be understood that a previous charge of assault on her by her husband was dismissed, because not proved, not on the ground of immorality. CRUELTY TO A HORSE.—Joseph Owen, Glazebrook-st., was charged with cruelty to a horse by working it while in an unfit state on the 16th ult. Mr. Browne appeared for the detendant.—lnspector Dowty, R.S.P.C.A., said he saw the defendant in charge of the horse, which was attached to a spring coal cart, and which was lame on the near fore leg, suffered from contracted tendons, and had its fetlock partially overshot .—William Owen, of Bank-st., the defendant's brother, ana owner or the horse, said he had known the horse 11 years, and it was always weak on its legs. It had won a trotting match, running five miles in 181 minutes. It was not a bit worse now. There was no cruelty in working it. It could do a mile in 4, minutes now. He did not suppose there were three horses in Warrington that could do this. —Mr. Browne said Mr. Jenkins had just reminded him that the celebrated horse Vespasian won a race with its fetlocks absolutely touching the ground.—Mr. Browne requested the magistrates to proceed to examine the horse below, and the Chairman and Alderman Wright did so.—On their return the bench dismissed the case, but the Chairman said the horse would have to be used very gently.—lsrael Ball, farmer, of Edge-lane,Golborne, was charged with working a horse while in an unfit state, on the 28th inst.—lnspector Dowty said the animal was suffering from ringbone and inflammation of the joints.—Mr. Dowty remarked that the defendant looked like a pauper, but was worth thousands. He was a regular old miser. He was reckoned one of the richest men in Golborne.—The defendant: My brother left me seven children—(laughter)—l had to keep them. —He was fined 2s. 6d. and costs. CHARGES OF ASSAULT ON A FARMER.—John Johnson, farmer, of Sankey, was charged with assaulting John Domville, farmer, of the same place, and Thomas Clare, 1, Dickenson-street, Warrington, carter for Mr. Monks, grocer,Warrington. Dosnville and Clare were cross-sum- moned on charges of assaulting Johnson, at Warrington on the 11th inst. Mr. A. Browne appeared for Dom- villa and Clare and Mr. Longton for Johnson. Mr. Browno withdrew the charge by Clare he being, he said so severely hurt that the question was really one of damages. Mr. Lengton therefore withdrew the cross-summons against Clare. Mr. Domville, said he was at Warrington on the 11th inst., and put up at the Wool Pack Inn. Ile was about to leave the inn with his horse and trap, when Mr. John- son said " How do you do," and witness replied " I don't want anything to say to you," because they had had a few words a few months back. Johnson swore and said witness had had drink, and added-' Look at your horse, why don't you feed it ?" Witness replied that he did not want anything to do with him. While witness was stooping in the cart fixing the seat, Johnson came behind him and pulled him out, and thumped him on the head till he was almost insensible. The ostler and Mr. Clare came to witness's assistance. Johnson afterwards tried to waylay them, in his trap, and when to escape him the complainant drove mrather way, drove furiously after him, though that was not the defendant's way home, the com- plainant only getting away through Johnson's horse backing.—Miss Domville, Mrs. Clare, wife of Thomas, and other witnesses gave evidence for the defendant. The substance of this was that on the defendant saying "How do you do ?" Domville answered him nastily, then twice called him a wastrel, and suddenly struck him several times with the whip, cutting his head. The defendant pulled him to get the whip from him, and then drove after Domville to go to his house for an explanation.—Dr. Murray, of Penketh, deposed to dressing bruises on Johnson such as might have been caused by a whip stock.—After other evidence,the Bench fined Johnson £5, including costs,and dismissed the case against Doraville. AN ABSENTEH APPRENTICE.—The adjourned case of Mary Dunn, 10, Silver Square, charged by Thomas Oakes, fustian cutter, Haydock-st., with absenting her- self from service as apprentice, was brought, up, and as she had lost 61 days during the month since tho adjournment an order for her commitment to prison for seven days was made, but suspended to allow her the chance of doing better, in which case it would not be executed. ASSAULT ON A WOMAN.—Wm. Oakes, 8, River-road, was bound over to keep the peace for six months for assaulting Kate Knight, of 8, River-road.

div.head: SENTENCE OF DEATH.
div.p: SENTENCE OF DEATH.

At the Leeds Assizes on Thursday, Henry Picketing (29), mechanic, was indicted for the murder of his wife, at Holbeck, on April 23. The evidence showed that the crime was the outcome of jealousy, for which the pri- soner does not appear to have had any foundation. The accused pleaded guilty, but acting on his lordship's advice withdrew the plea, with the remark that he did not know what to do, and the trial proceeded. It was stated that the parties had been married only three , months, and tkat the deceased lived uncomfortably with the prisoner by reason of his idle habits. During a quarrel he attacked his wife with a carving knife, and almost cut off her head. When arrested he said it was caused through jealousy, and that he intended cutting his own throat. He was found guilty, and was sentenced to death.

HOUGH GREEN.—This match was played at Hough Green on Saturday, and resulted in a victory for the visitors, mainly owing to the bowling of Crompton, whose analysis read five wickets for seven runs. GRAMMAR SCHOOL.—The above match was played on Saturday on the ground of the latter,the result being a win for the Brewery by two runs. For the visitors 'l. WARRINGTON v. BOLTON.—History repeated itself in the first engagement between the above clubs on Satur- day. and as was the case last season, Warrington had to retire defeated. Both sides were exceptionally strong, the homesters having the assistance of a prominent amateur, who, for reasons best known to himself, played under the nom de plume of" Captain Moggridge." Win- ning the toss, Bolton had a distinct advantage in bat- ting on a wicket which certainly had not a tendency te improve, whilst the heavy rain of the day previous naturally helped the attack. Walker and Staton faced the two Crosfields. With ten runs on the board, the home captain brought about Staton's dismissal, whilst at 16 and 19, both Woodhouse and Mallett were sent back. Walker and Ellis forced a little more life into the came, and at 34 Captain Manson took the ball from J. J. Crosfield. The change worked Immediately, for with his first ball Walker was easily taken at point—five for 43. Ellis next left at 56, but Stanley continued to hit away, and receiving valuable assistance from Williams and Laidlaw, a double change was tried at 84, J. J. re- lieving the captain, whilst Captain Manson went on again at his original end. Previous to this S. M. Cros- field had bowled Stanley with a beauty, for a clinking 23. The venture realized 105. "Captain Moggridge" and R. Smith were the first representatives of Warring- ton with the willow. Both soon got to work, six runs coming from Ellis's first over. However, with only eight runs on, the home umpire no-balled Halley for throwing. To effect a remedy against this Laidlaw relieved Ellis, and Halley then sought protection under the Bolton um- pire, a proceeding which did not meet with the approval of true cricketers. Halley continued to bowl in the un- satisfactory way, and with no small amount of success. At 15 he bowled Smith, whilst Lee, when he had totalled eight, also fell a victim to one of Halley's peculiar de- liveries. "Moggridge" continued to bat stylishly, but S. M. Crosfield played on the second ball he received. Three wickets were down for 34 runs, and on Captain Manson coming in, some vigourous batting was seen. " Moggridge " however, gave two distinct chances when he had made 18, but the mistakes did not alter the aspect of the game, as with only another run added, he was caught and bowled by Halley. Captain Manson was bowled off his pads at the same score, 51, whilst at 56 George Clarke was dismissed. Bell and Voisey made a vigorous attempt to save their side, but Ellis got the better of Voisey, and the remainder lending little assist- ance the innings closed for 83,0 r 22 runs in arrear. The fielding on both sides was very close, whilst the wicket- keeping of Clark was good, not a bye being chronicled against him. Score and bowling analysis:— BOLTON. WARRINGTON. RuNcona T. CHESTER.—This match was played at Runcorn on Saturday, before a good number of specta- tors. Chester won the toss, and commenced batting against Woods and Wilson! They made a good start, the first wicket realizing 32 runs, and the second wicket falling at 48. After this, the batsmen did not give much trouble, the innings closing for 76. Griffiths played exceedingly well for his runs, and carried his bat right through the innings. Stanyer and Bamford also batted well for their respective scores. Woods bowled splen- didly for Runcorn, taking eight Chester wickets for 32 runs. Runcorn commenced their innings with H. Wright and J. M. Frith, the latter being dismissed when he had scored three. Wilson then joined Wright, and the score was raised to 48, when Wright was bowled for a well-played 15. The Chester score was passed for the loss of only three wickets, and when stumps were drawn the score was 115 for six wickets. Wilson, the new professional, played a splendid game for Runcorn, hiq score of 56 being well put together. They included some brilliant drives. The following are the respective scores of each team :

The "Athletic News " has the following note : Captain Moggridge. Who's Captain Moggridge ? " was the inquiry at Warrington. The " lintleman " was numbered among the home eleven, and the aristocra- tic, if not ornamental, name puzzled everybody until it was discovered that it was the pseudonym of a young county amateur. He could not hide his identity when he appeared on the field. The Warrington team was rather warm with "Captain Moggridge,4 S. M. and J. J. Crosfield, Reginald Smith, Captain Manson, and Fred Lee, the ex-Yorkshireman, included,, but they found Bolton a trifle too good for them nevertheless.

div.head: CYCLING.
div.p: CYCLING.

On Saturday Mr. Charles Lucas, of the North Liver- pool Gymnasium Bicycle Club, succeeded in lowering the London record held by Mr. Bennett, of the Anneld Club, by one hour and forty-one minutes. Leaving the General Post Office, Liverpool, at 3.45 a.m. Mr. Lucas reachld St. Martin's-le-Grand, London, at 6.58 p.m., thus averaging a distance of aut miles in fifteen hours thirteen minutes. Mr. Lucas worked on his old lines of dispensing with pacers, &c., in every part of the journey, and obtained fourteen checks. The rider nearly suc- ceeded in breaking the twelve hours' record (161 miles), as on arriving at Little Breckle at 3.45 p.m. he found he had covered a distance of 1591 miles. Mr. Lucas shortly intends establishing a record from Liverpool to Edin- burgh..

Dealing with cycling', the " Manchester Guardian" says :—The really large numbers of wheelmen to be seen outside of Manchester every fine Saturday afternoon affords proof of the surprising extent to which the sport is being followed, and leads to some curious reflections as to the amount of capital that must be employed in providing the numberless types of machines that may be seen on the road. A class of tradesmen that have reason to rejoice at the development of cycling is the roadside inkeeper. In many cases houses that had teen left high and dry by the disappearance of passenger traffic on the high roads ate now renewing their youth, So to speak ; and the "licensed victualler" has again be- dtime what he was originally intended to be, namely, a purveyor of food and not of drink exclusively to the wayfarer. Houses, of this kind are now to be found in many picturesque villages in Lancashire and Cheshire, and they fin I their account in ministering to the wants of the clubmen who scud out of Manchester in their fifties- and theio hundreds every week. The principal clubs each have their headquarters at some country farm, where the members may enjoy their Saturday afternoons, or, better still, their " week end," as their means or inclination may dictate.

One of the principal local clubs—the Wheelers—has an" active" list of nearly ninety members, who have made the white cap a familiar object on many roads in Cheshire, Derbyshire, and even Staffordshire. The club has a journal of its own, published monthly, and in this we find some good advice given to wheelmen in regard to the too prevalent hetbit of " scorching "on frequented roads. "We owe it to ourselves," says the Mentor of the Wheelers, "to set a good example, for the Bowdon road is our great outlet to the country, and it depends upon our friendly relations with the police whether our frequent use of it is to be enjoyable or the reverse. Our distinctive white caps make us readily recognisable,and I our conduct, good or bad, is conseqnently brought more prominently before the public and the police than that of any other club in the city. There is a great deal of bunkum, of course, talked about the recklessness of cyclists and the right of pedes- trians and drivers; but allowing that we have far greater claim to consideration than the correspon- dents to newspapers seem disposed to admit, there is no earthly reason why wearers of the white cap should endeavour to obtain a little cheap glory by scorching past new riders on hired machines through the most frequented parts of Bowdon-road, or why they should consider it highly clever to whirl down St. Margaret's Hill and round past the Sheaf corner with their backs in the ridiculous horizontal position which many of our riders seem to consider necessary to the attainment of high speed. Let our scorching be done where it is safe." This is advice of a kind to which no good cyclist can object.

A strange poisoning case is reported from Stratford, Essex. On Sunday the wife of a small shopkeeper named East, made a plum pudding in which she used ~
to be flour from rs jor thr-rhop.- - •• • • ir "

After eating the pudding the family became ill ; in tfie evening the husband died, and on Monday morning the wife expired at the hospital whither she had been re- moved. A son, aged 18, is in the hospital in a critical condition, and a boy aged 10 was also affected, though not seriously. It is believed by the doctors that the case is one of arsenical poisoning.

div.head: LABOUR ELECTORAL ASSOCIATION.
div.p: THE LABOUR ELECTORAL ASSO- CIATION.

The fifth annual conference of Labour Electoral Asso- ciations opened at Leicester, on Monday, under the pre- sidency of Mr. Kelly, of Manchester,a number of labour organisations being represented. The Chairman urged the importance of forming a labour party in Parliament, and the Committee's report stated that the movement had of late made great progress. A discussion took place on help to labour candidates at the general elec- tion, State payment of members and returning officers' charges. On Wednesday the discussion of a general Eight Hours Bill was resumed, and a resolution was moved in favour of such a measure for all trades where the majority of the workers are in favour of it. Resolutions were also adopted protesting against, royalty rents and way leaves calling for various amendments of the Employers Lia- bility Act, and for the establishment of a system of [industrial pensions.

div.head: ALARMING ACCIDENT TO LORD SALISBURY.
div.p: ALARMING ACCIDENT TO LORD SALISBURY.

Lord Salisbury had an exciting experience on Thurs- day. Driving along St. James-street, London, OR his way to the Foreign Office, the horses bolted. The brougham, dashing against the Refuge opposite King- street, was overturned and greatly damaged. The coachman was flung off the box and seriously injured, and the Premier was severely shaken and narrowly escaped injury to the head, his hat being much broken. Lard Salisbury afterwards transacted business at the Foreign Office, and happily was little the worse for the mishap.

div.head: LOSS OF A BRAZILIAN MA.N-OF-WAR
div.p: LOSS OF A BRAZILIAN MA.N-OF-WAR
AND 125 LIVES.

The news was received at Rio de Janeiro, on Sunday, that the monitor Solimoes, one of the vessels of the naval flotilla despatched by the Brazilian Government to suppress the insurrection in the province of Matte Grosso, was wrecked on the previous night off Cape Polonia, on the Uruguyan coast. It is reported that 125 of the crew were lost and only five saved. Captain Castro, the commander of the Solimoes, is among the drowned. It is supposed that the ill-fated vessel must have been driven aground during the prevalence of a southerly gale, and stranded too far from shore to estab- lish communication.

div.head: HEAVY THUNDERSTORM.
div.p: HEAVY THUNDERSTORM.

A heavy thunderstorm, accompanied by very vivid lightnining, passed over London about five o'clock on Thursday morning. Rain also fell in torrents, and the streets were flooded. I Braintree correspondent states that a terrific thunderstorm visited East Essex early on Thursday morning, and lasted for several hours. The storm closed with a heavy fall of hail,which did much damage to the fruit trees.

A hailstorm of extraordinary severity, preceded by flashes of sheet lightning and thunder, broke over Ips- wich at 10.40 on Wednesday night. Hailstones, formed of sheer pieces of ice as large as bantam eggs, fell thickly for some eight minutes, and the damage to glass in greenhouses and to fruit blossoms proved very serious.

div.head: DEWSBURY TRAGEDY.
div.p: THE DEWSBURY TRAGEDY.

At Leeds Assizes, on Thursday, Haley Walker, a res- pectably-dressed and intelligent-looking young man, was charged with the wilful murder of Mary Ann Chatman, at Dewsbury,on the night of May 9th. Prisoner pleaded not guilty. On the day named prisoner had been in the company of Chatman, and as they were crossing Savile Bridge at night, he lifted her up bodily and rolled her over the bridge. She was drowned. Evi- dence showed that Walker was helplessly drunk at the time of the occurrence. The hearing of the evidence oc- cupied considerable time, and at ''the conclusion the charge was reduced to one of manslaughter, his lord- ship sentencing the prisoner to twelve months' hard labour. There was cheering in court when the jury's verdict was announced.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.-TIIESDAY.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.-TIIESDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at five minutes past two o'clock. MRS. MAYBRICIL—Mr. STUART WORTLEY informed Mr. Dalziel that the Home Secretary had no information as to new facts in the case ot Mrs. Florence Maybrick. He was always prepared to give careful consideration to such facts relating to convicted persons when presented to him. Intsn LOCAL GOVERNMENT.—The debate on the second reading of the Irish Local Government Bill was resumed by Colonel Nolan, who found the measure so thoroughly bad that all the Irish members were united In opposing it. Mr. T. W. RusseLL,, while not agreeing with all the details of the Bill, supported its principle, and said it was an honest effort to redeem the Government promise to reform county administration in Ireland. Mr. GLADSTONE declared that the measure as framed falsified the pledges of the Government, and ,stamped Ireland with all sorts of inequalities. It was a miser- able Bill offered in place of the Home Rule upon which the people had set their hearts. Ile found in the Prime Minister's language as to Ulster and civil war not only a prophecy, but a distinct encouragement to the mis- guided men capable of imbibing his doctrines to the use of unlawful arms against the constituted authority of the country. He declared the franchise of the Bill to be unreal, and the power given to the Lord Lieu- tenant excessive, and said he did not believe a man with a grain of self-respect would sit on a council liable to be hauled up before the ccurt and suppressed on any loose charge. He stigmatized the Bill as legislative refuse, and urged that its object was to hand over the majority to landlord and minority control. Mr. BALFOUR, in his reply, first denounced the reckless misrepresentation of the utterances of the Prime Minis- ter, who, he said, had stated three propositions as a forecast of what would be likely to happen in the event of the Ulster loyalists being handed over to an Irish Parliament; and he entirely agreed that any attempt on the part of the British Parliament to coerce Ulster by force of arms, as contemplated by the Opposition, would rend society in two. He contended that the Bill was a perfect fulfilment of the Government promise,and that if provided local government on simpler lines than in the cases of England and Scotland, with only such modifica- tions as were necessary to suit the exceptional state of society in'the sister isle. The House then divided with the following result For the second reading 339 Against .. 247

Government majority 92 The aanouncement of the figures was received with loud and prolonged cheering. SCOTCH DISESTABLISHMENT.-Mr. CAMERON moved a resolution at the evening sitting for the disestablish- ment and disendowment of the Church in Scotland, which was defeated by 265 to 209. The House adjourned at one o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. In comparison with previous Wednesdays, the House of Commons presented a most lively appearance when the Speaker took the chair at a quarter-past twelve o'clock. div.head: BILL.
div.p: BILL.

The second reading of the Electors' Qualification and Registration Bill was the first order of the day. Mr. STANSFSLD, in moving that the Bill be read: a second time, expressed the opinion that no member of the House would question the accuracy of his statement that the system of Parliamentary registration was in ur- gent need of amendment, simplification and reform. He explained that the Bill proposed to amend, simplify, and reform the existing system of Psrliamentary Regis- tration by placing it in charge of a public officer, by reducing the qualifying period of ownership and occupy- ing voters to three months ending on the 24th June, abolishing the necessity for the payment of certain rates and taxes as a qualification for admission to the register, allowing persons removing from one kind of qualifying premises to another in an electoral area during a year to retain their franchise, and making provision for keep- ing on the register lodgers who had once established their right, without their bein,, required to make a fresh claim each year,the new register to come into operation on the Ist Nov. in each year. Mr. Jas. Lowther, believing the bill would make many undesirable alterations in the law, moved that it should be read a second time that day six months. General Goldsworthy seconded the amendment. The bill was supported by Mr. Shiress Will, Mr. Heneage, Mr. Parker, Mr. Waddy, Mr. Hol- den, Mr. T. D. Sullivan, Mr. Chance, Mr. F. Stevenson, Sir William Harcourt, Sir Henry James, Mr. Stuart, and Sir A. Rollit ; and strongly opposed by Mr. Baumann, Mr. Tomlinson, Mr. GainsfGrd Bruce, Mr. Bousfield, and Mr. R. G. Webster criticised various provisions of the bill which they considered objectionable or defective. The SOLICITOR..GENERAL said that al- though the bill contained proposals affecting the franchise to which the Government could not as- sent, still, as it was essentially a registration bill, the Government did not feel bound to oppose the second reading. Mr. BALFOUR, speaking some time after the Solicitor-General, said the Government would take part neither for the Bill nor against it, nor would they ask any of their supporters either to vote for or against it. On a division the second reading was carried by 207 votes ; the figures being 295 for the second reading and 88 against. VEXATIOUS. LITIGATION IN SCOTLAND.—Dr. Cameron obtained leave to bring in a Bill to amend the law as to vexatious litigation in Scotland. It was read a first time. The House adjourned at ten minutes to six o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THURSDAY. The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock.

Mrs. He-afield-entreated", commanded, reproacnea, denounced us both. She wept, raved, stormed ; all in vain. The man I loved folded his arms around me, and drew me—almost dead with grieving—to his breast. "I love Ethel, mother," he said, gently and firmly, "as you loved my father long ago. Look baek, I beseech you, to the happiness of your love- marriage, and do not refuse the same bliss to your son." But she would not yield. She declared that if we married, we should have her curse, and ordered me from her sight, saying that she should send me home to-morrow. To-morrow she had changed her mind. "1 was wrong," she said, wearily. "If you are necessary to each other's happiness, why should I interfere 1 Only don't marry until you have better prospects, Robert. Ethel, don't drag my boy down to poverty." So sudden a conversion was bewildering. I found my.elf involuntarily doubting if it could be real and true. I knew Mrs. Delafield (with all her gener- osity and pride) could stoop to deceit, sometimes, for her own ends. But Robert never doubted her. He held her in his arms, and kissed her handsome old face again and again. She was his "own darling mother" once more. Was it for me to come between them with a bare suspicion? So I held my peace, and tried to be content, and Robert promised all his mother wished. We were to be parted for one year. Robert had had a position offered him with an uncle in San Francisco. It was agreed that he should accept it, and, meantime, I should continue to live with Mrs. Delafield. So said, so done, and we parted. Alas my love! the misery of that one year I I can scarcely tell how our estrangement grew, so gradual it was, and so unaccountable. His letters, so loving at first, grew cold, grew few in number, at last ceased altogether, and his mother, kinder than ever to me now, began to regard me witk pity. One day she came into my room with a newspaper In her hand, her face very pale and grave. "Ethel," she said, "there is something in this paper which you ought to know, but which I have not the heart to tell you. I blush for my own son. Alas! child, I knew what his fickle nature was when I opposed your wishes. Had yeu but followed my advice you might now be Mrs. Goldman." And she laid down the paper and went away. I took it up, trembling like one in an ague fit. It contained a notice of Dr. Robert Delafield's mar- riage in San Francisco. For hours I suffered alone in that room worse than the torments of death. My love was false, my heart was broken.
Then I compelled myself to be calm and went to her.

"I will marry Mr. Goldman whenever you choose," I said, "if he still wishes to have me." It appeared that he did. I was too wretched to think about it at the time; but afterwards I learned how she had kept his hopes alive, and counselled him to have patience. I left everything to her to arrange. She provided my trousseau most generously. She ordered a wed- ding dress worthy of the wealthy Mr. Goldman's bride. I submitted to all, cared nothing at all for what they did with me. I felt as if that newspaper had been my death-warrant, and all these prepara- tions were making for death and the grave. My promised husband asked me for no protesta- tions of affection when he placed the magnificent solitaire ring on nay finger. "At last this fair band is mine," he said, and I answered him never a word. _ _

And so the days went on. And at last the morning came that was to witness my "prosperous marriage," and doona me to misery for life. Such was my thought, at least, as I awoke from an uneasy slumber. rt,„ tood bdside me. "'Online I submitted with the same dull apathy. "It Won't be for long," I told myself. "I sha'n't live long ;" and I yielded myself to their hands. Just as they were putting on the bridal veil a servant came into my room. She was a new girl The house was all confusion. "There's a gentleman waiting in the missus's boudoir to see the bride," said she. Mrs. Delafield answered her. "Say that she will come to him immediately," said she. "It's Goldman, my dear. I promised him a sight of you in your wedding dress before you went to church. Come down." I obeyed in silence. She threw the door of the boudoir open wide, and let me in. "There 1" she said, triumphantly. your bride. Is she not beautiful 7" And placed me face to face with—Robert I Robert stern and pale. He looked from one to the other 91 us questioningly. "What does this mean 7" he demanded. But he got no further, for, with a scream of horror, his mother fell fainting at his feet. That was no time for explanations. Her con- dition needed all our care. Only, when she began to recover consciousness, he turned to me and took my hand. "I have been true and faithful to you. Can you say the same 7" he asked. And I clung to him, and thanked God for so much happiness, weeping on his breast. Our letters had been tampered with, intercepted, suppressed, we never really knew by whom. There was, indeed no need to ask. Robert said: "We are happy, after all. Let us forgive and forget. She is our mother, dearest." She was, indeed, our mother, for we were married the very day after his return. And Mr. Goldman gave up his claim with an excellent grace, and begged me to retain his diamond ring as a wedding gift. Moreover he became one of my husband's best patients, and recommended him to many others. Altogether. I don't know but what he had a good deal to do with making ours— what even my mother-in-law allowed it to be at last—a truly prosperous marriage
