THE HEAVY RATES OF WARRINGTON.

Sir,—Will you kindly give me space to enter my pro- test against the iniquitous rates we have to pay as struggling tradesmen, my Improvement Rabe being for two shops e? ss. I don't know how my fellow-labourers fare, but it is hard work to make an honest living in the face of such taxes and bad trade. Is there no one in our Town Council who will lift his voice against this heavy taxation 2—Yours truly, WM. BESWICK. 48, Horsemarket-st., Warrington, May 2Cth, 1892.

COLLECTIONS FOR WALKING- DAY. - Sir,--it has come to my knowledge that some one is collecting on behalf of Emmanuel Sunday Schools for Walkina Day treat, who is not authorised to do so. Will you, therefore, kindly allow me to tell the public, through your columns, that those only are authorised to collect for our Schools who present a book, haying, in addition to the efEcial stamp of the Chnrch, my own signature, and that of our superintendent, Mr. John Allen.—l am, dear Sir, yours truly, ,EDWARD F. REED, Minister, Emmanuel Reformed Church of England. 17, Museum-st., Warrington, May 24th., 1822.

div.head: DRINK ON LICENSED PREMISES.
div.p: DRINK ON LICENSED PREMISES.

Sir,—l hope my fellow townsmen,especially those who are interested in promoting the moral welfare of the people at large, have carefully studied the remarks of , Alderman Harrison in reference to the case tried at our Borough Police Court a few days ago. If such an inter- pretation of the law as the alderman indulged in must be taken as correct, well may we endorse the opinion of that illustrious prototype of Mr. Elarrison,who emphati- cally declared that" the law's a bass." I fancied I could hear the lucky publican exclaiming (with his tongue in his cheek) a " Daniel come to judgment," as he hurried out of court to indulge in the laughter which this unexpected display of " justice's justice " must have provoked in him. In the face of this extraordinary expression of opinion, how can we expect ear police to do their duty ? The Chief Constable may well say that (after such a farce) he will be extremely cautious as to what summonses he applies for in the future. Alderman Harrison's charac- teristic effusion may be taken as a direct suggestion to those in the trade, who are disposed to " sail near the wind," to continue doing so. Well may our town con- tinue to be a "bye wora and a reproach" when we have magistrates capable of such idiosyncracies.—Yours, A DISRUSTED TOWNSMAN.

THE WARRINGTON CANDIDATES, AND QUES- TIONS BY RAILWAY MEN. Sir,—l notice in your issue of last Saturday, that the local Secretary of the Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants has submitted a number of questions te the two local candidates for Parliamentary honours, and, as many may perhaps think that the Society represents and expresses the views of the majority of railway employes in Warrington, the following figures will show its real strength, and how far it gives utterance to the thoughts and views of local railway men :—ln the locomotive department L. aridNW. thew. are upwards of 250 men and youths employed ; out of these the society cannot claim more than 20. lam not quite conversant with the number employed in other departments, but the number of employes of all railways in Warrington is not far from 500. Out of these the society has a mem- bership of about 90. These figures need no comment: they speak for themselves. Thanking you in anticipa- tion, for insertion, I am, yours sincerely, JOSEPH DAKIN. Padgate, May 26th, 1892. [lt will be noticed that our correspondent does not say that he disapproves of the questions. They are being put in the interests of railway servants throughout the kingdom. It is nothing new for the workmen in a trades society to have to struggle for themselves and those who are outside the society.—En. Ex.

div.head: RUNCORN TOWN BAND.
div.p: RUNCORN TOWN BAND.

Sir,—May I trouble you with a few remarks with re- spect to the brass band which aspircs to be known by the above comprehensive title. I think the public whom I understand have up to the present liberally subscribed towards the fund for obtaining a set of new instruments are entitled to some information and explanation on the position of affairs. Nine months have elapsed since first the appeal was made, and during that time a consider_ able sum must have been collected by means of the cards which were spread broadcast through the town and also .by means of collecting books, and subscribers have a right to know to what practical use their contributions are being put. Why is not a financial statement issued setting out the subscriptions in detail, and showing how many instruments have been purchased with • the money? Again, when may we expect the prize drawing to take place? Originally fixed to take place in March, it was postponed to May, and we are now near- ing the end of this month, and there are no signs of the draw yet being made. Is this fair to those who have held tickets for so long a time? In my opinion these • m atters require immediate attention and explanation? I am sorry to hear that the band has recently lost 'nearly one half of its members, but as to the cause of ‘such, a wholesale desertion I am ignorant, and with many .others would be glad of enlightenment by those in auth- ority. A few more withdrawals Sand it appears to me that _Runcorn Town Band will be but a memory of the past, and what Will be done with the instruments then ? --i Yours truly,

div.head: •SUBSCRIBER.
div.p: A •SUBSCRIBER.
TIM CLOSING OF PHI IC FOOTPATHS.

Sir,—A great many of your subscribers will be pleased at the interest evinced by you in the above subject. The petty pilfering that has been and is being carried on, especially in the rural districts, is alarming,and as a rule tis done by those whose position secures them from interference, unlecs by an organisation. As you ask for information concerning the closing of footpaths, I may be allowed to call your attention to a case in the parish a Grappenhall. Time was when a person going from Grappenhall to Daresbury would naturally tate the faapath opposite Mr. Fletcher's, and near Mr. Parr's lodge, through the field now rented by the Grappenhall Cricket Club. This path brought you out on to the Appleton Thorn road to the right of Mr. Farr's house. From thence you crossed the road, and by the path, which is still open; you went down to the brook, which flows through The Dingle, crossing the brook by the wooden bridge. By-the-bye, the bridge has been recently washed away, and a new one is re- quired. You proceeded through Mr. Lyon's farm and out on the Stretton road. This was one of the most pleasant walks, and one of the roost convenient in the whole ,district, but it is now practically closed to the public. The wicket gate opening on to the .road near Mr. Parr's lodge, and which I presume is supplied by the parish, is still there ; the stone parapet is still visible by the fence ; but after proceeding through the first field you lose all trace of the path. In fact, the field rented by the Cricket Club has been divided by a new fence, and no stile or gate has been placed in it for the con- venience of pedestrians. Mr. Parr is the County Council member for Grappen- hall and district, but it would seem that he or someone on his behalf has deprived the public of a right, a con- venience,. and a pleasure. I hope, sir, that the day is not far distant when we shall have our parish Councils, and when the rights of the public will be defended by , themselves, in their own House of Commons, and when the filching of public rights will be.come a thing of the jpast.—Yocra, Ake., BETA,

div.head: RUNCORN AND THE SUNDAY QUESTION.
div.p: RUNCORN AND THE SUNDAY QUESTION.

Sir,—The observance of the Sabbath day at Runcorn is not sufficiently strict ;so thinks the Conference of teachers who assembled to consider the advisability of appealing to the magistrates to close the sweetmeat dealers who dare to open on Sunday—to collect money to assist them to deal honestly with their landlord and the various tax collectors, who call upon these wicked shopkeepers at various periods during the year. lam at a loss to know whether the teachers are really in earnest respecting the influence it has upon the moral character of the children, or the deficit in the collection boxes. Perhaps it would not be out of order for them also to appeal against men being employed in chemical works, and men driving conveyances conveying people to places of worship on the Sabbath. It is a fact that some offi- cials in connexion with schools will allow their boats to carry lime, coal, &c., on the Sabbath day. It is not a bad act of any person or number of persons to correct themselves first before they chastise others. If it was possible for the teadlears to gain the desire of their hearts, it would be a great injury and injustice to these struggling shopkeepers who are not in a financial position to join a syndicate where they could gain large profits from other people's labour. Christ used moral suasion not coercion. I have never heard or read of Him appealing to magistrates to compel people to sub- mit to him or accept His views. There is not another town in England where there is so much of the external aspect of " Goody Goody." If the teachers have any powers of a persuasive kind let them use them in school. Will these teachers please read, mark, learn, and in- wardly digest the teaching of their Master, which is to do unto others what they would like others to do unto them. For the information of teachers who seem igno- rant of the system by which some people live, viz., by license, I beg to inform them that each shopkeeper has a license for which he pays to the Inland Revenue 10s. 6d. So you will see we are the privileged few who are per- mitted to make a collection on the Sabbath toward de- fraying the " exes." I do hope the teachers are not so morally low as to admire such men as Charles the Second, who enforced such rigid laws as compelling every person to desist from their calling on Sunday, whilst he himself conducted his life as he liked it. What is desirable in Runcorn as elsewhere, is liberty to earn a shilling honestly, and deal with our own affairs as best suits us on Sunday as on other days in the week, as there is no difference only in name. lam a strong believer in the policy of owe no man anything but love, which means, I like to pay my way. —Humbly yours,
JUSTICE.
TORY STUPIDITY, MINING ROYALTIES, &c.,

Sir,—On Saturday last, while looking in the " Observer " for a brief report taken by me to the office of that paper, I found my report of a temperance meeting was supplemented by a "Tory Enquirer's" heartless cunning letter, penned solely to mislead work- ing-men voters. ' • "

Some time since , I was requested to write that source of light and freedom, by some victims of an employer of labour. That letter was also suppressed, and a lot of rubbish given in its stead. Therefore lam prevented from replying to the "Tory Enquirer " in the "Observer," and trust that you will permit me to do so through your columns. Now, Sir,—" Tory Enquirer" continues a number of questions under four headings :—(1) " As to the ques- tions put to Mr. Pierpoint." (2) "As to the Drink Traffic." (3) " Workingman Champions." (4) " Min- ing Royalties." The vital points have been cleared up repeatedly of late in every local newspaper, save in the Tory lamps of light. " Tory Enquirer "in the begin- ning of his epistle declares that he does " not intend to try to answer" what I have hitherto stated concerning the drink question, &c., and ends his crafty letter by saying :—" I am not concerned about the elegance and culture of his remarks about religion and its ministers." This subtile foe of humanity is afraid lest ministers and their flocks, as well as some tern- perance workers, be led to see and feel that if they continue to vote as some of them have done hitherto, to send men to make laws and rule the Empire,whe an un- willing to go against "Sunday Trading," and for" Direct Veto," and prohibiting the sale of the cursed drink to little children, the souls of such as perish thereby will . finally be required at the hands of such voters; such thoughtless voters, who put, or keep, such a heartless class of rulers in power, as permit the shameful number e of drinking dens to abound to the right and to the left, y in order to allure men, women, and children into the le ruinous habits of intemperance, and enrich a few brewers and their allies. None but Shyrocks such as "Tory ts Enquirer" could write so heartlessly about drink, and ts also " Mining Royalties," which are ruining the iron and steel trade of England. Mr. Maskell Peace, secretary and iw solicitor to the Mining Association of Great Britain says: be —" The result of the existing state of things, is far from he what was anticipated when the leases were made. : certain rents and royalties have to ,be paid to the land-
ord annually-, and are tenant, while i;eeking to recoup I these -

himself for 1. ....e payments will pull.every ton of mineral he can out of the mine, and if this royalty is leased from several landlords, he may also be tempted to work the minerals with a view to a payment rather than in a work- manlike manner, and in the safest way." Therefore, follow four results :—(1) Markets become glutted with over production. (2) Small or no profits are reaped by the employers, who have sunk their capital in the working of the mine. (3) Small or starvation wages are paid to the miner, (4) followed by a terrible increase of accidents, and loss of human life and limb. Many very narrow escapes from losing my life during nearly 30 years' labour in the mines have I undergone; and been thrice victimised ; simply because I dared to speak the truth concerning ventilation, and other vital matters, as to the safety of the mine. At one colliery where I was working, firemen were dismissed appar- ently for no other reason than that of faithfully report- inn discoveries of gas found in the working . of the mine. Shortly after this kind of thlng, one day while in the mine, a deathly stillness prevailed for a moment; then a mighty rush of wind and dust. " What's that ! what's that Dick ?" exclaimed another miner who was working about 20 yards where I was. " It's fired! it's fired ! down with thee; down with thee," I replied, hav- ing instantly stretched myself out at full length with my face to the floor,knowing that the flames always made for the highest point. He however ran to me,and stood over me for about a half minute speechless. Fortunately the flames did not make us their prey. We rushed towards the pit shaft,and there the scene was heartrending. I may not here describe all the wild commotion among the lads and young men ; some were crying for their mothers, sowe praying. I inspired some by saying—" Look to the Lord—He will save you." Now, "Enquirer," such is the " religion of a sort" that suited me then, and suits me still. It then enabled me, after hastening homeward and informing the underlooker, whom I met going towards the pit with slow heavy steps,of what had occurred. He pleaded with me to go and tell his wife " and make it as light as you can." The poor woman burst into tears. Was she thinking she had looked upon her husband's living form for the last time—heard his last fond word. Alas !it proved but too true. Oh! Hew she pleaded with me to stay longer.; while I pleaded to go home and comfort my wife, that mylife was prolonged. After a moment's stay at home I ran about a mile into the village for the doctor for him to haste with all speed to the scene of the terrible calamity. In spite of my dear wife's appeals that I should not risk my life among the explorers, I was quickly at the pit baadr, now crowded with mourners, and guarded by police, who for a moment prevented my access to the Pit brow ; but could not prevent me calling out to one of the men on the brow "Do you want any help ?" I was soon again amongst stifling fumes, and, broken coal boxes. The first victim whom I laboured to restore to. respiration and life, was the said underlooker whose Wife I had tried to comfort but left in tears. I, by God's help did what I could to cheer her,and save him. Near by lay also stretched in death two other officials. Who will dare to say that " Mining Royalties" had net been the cause of the mine not having "been worked in the safest ! way," in order to meet the landlord's greed of £s d ? " 600,000 persons are employed in the mines of Great Britain:"" The capital invested isalmost £100,000,000." The landlords charge an iniquitous rent for that whereon they have bestowed no labour—and run no risk, accept "an annual income of about £10,000,000." "Who," says Ruskin, " was ever the better Or having coffers full of ' gold? But who shall measure the guilt that is incurred to fill them," Let raV " Tory inquirer" remember that the main things should be settled first. In the year 1880, the Liberal Government gave us the Employers' Liability Act, which came in force in the beginning of 1881. But our colliery masters locked tens of thousands of us out cf eriaplovrnent because we would not contract ourselves out of the Act. The struggle lasted about (eight , weeks. No sooser had some poor families been thus forced into idleness and starvation than if tne police caught them begging they imprisoned them or threatened to do so. The aim of miners' agents in struggling for years and spenditg thousands of pounds to secure a , passing of the bills was mainly to save human life and limb. a' But no,"Eaid our employers, " your lives are ' as nothing to us and our rich landlords, who will have ' their rent royalties. E[en cost us cothing. £ S. d. we ) must and will have !" " Skin for akin, yea all that a . man bath will he give for his life:' What under the , heavens, human, social, intellectual, moral, or divine, . can be cf value if life is not to be held sacred above all I price? Therefore, to save my fellow-men from reckless slaughter on the one hand and starvation or imprison- ment for seeking bread from door re dear., on the other, . I addressed scores of miners' rneetings,somatimes three in one day,and, as my Tory friend now compiains, " poured out my soul over" the matter. I was victimized, and have since had great difficulty in obtaining sufficient means to keep the wolf from my door. Still " hone of these things move me." High above the scorn of any human being, comes the clear voice of Him, in whose love and fear, and strength, I have endeavoured, but too often failed to do all I ought to have done for His glo,rY, and the welfare of humanity.—Faithfully yours, 1 RICHARD SPOREY. Warrington, May 19th, 1892.

(MIXED.) Br Tux 0' DICK o' BOB'S. "Cleanliness is next to Godliness." Aw dorn'd know whooa id wor as uttered them true words, but aw say ditto to 'em; an' aw dorn'd , know whooa id wor as quoted 'em an' said they I explained th' reeason o' weshin' day comin' next to : Sunda.' Th' words may meean cleanliness i' lang- wige as weel as aleeanliness o' th' body, but tekkin' 'em to nobbut meean th' last they're varra wise, an' aw'm fain to see as there's some agitatisn gooin' on we a view to hevin' baths put r cottage-heawses. , This is as id owt to be, an' law_ hooap no builder's plans 'll be passed r th' future except there's plans shows on 'em, becose a ten peawnd nooat 'll do th' job when they:re buildin', an' iv th' builder wants , six per cent for his brass thrippence a week on th' rents 'll pay thad extry, aw'll bet. Yo'll nooatice as some o' th' wedgeheyds as write letters to th' noospappers on th' subject try to mek id eawt as ,th' werkin' men are wimmen corn'd affoord this thrippence a week extry, an' aw'm su'prised they dudn'd gooa a bit forther bi sayin' as we're too lazy to tek a bath, or too tired, or too ill. Yo' know there was wonst two chaps hevin' a bathe th' seea—aw'll nod say wod teawn they coom fro' —an' one on 'em lookt at t' other an' said: "Aw tell tha wod, Jem, tha'at dard nasty !" Aw think them's th' soort o' chaps as tawk an' write this nonsense abeawt nod affoordiu' a ferthua' —or say a ho'p'ny a bath; they'd rayther spend th' thrippence in a extry flat pint every week—that's any opinion. A poor beggar were browt up last Tuesda' cherged wi' beggia', an' th' poleece fun on him a little memoran- dum book—ealy th' beggars bizness-book—aa hod ' th' names o' th' teawns as he'd bin an written In; "the book was 'posted up' in a most business-like fashion," says th' repoort o' th' case. This dialogue took place between th' tramp an' Mr. Leresche (th' magistrate at Manchester): Magistrate : You don't put down how much you get at each place. Prisoner: I have no need. Magistrate: Will yvu leave this book behind you? Prisoner : Oh, I have use for it. (Laughter.) Magistrate ; This is obviously a chart of your beg- ging places. Prisoner : Sometimes I forget where I have been. (Laughter.) Magistrate: You might go twice in one week and runthe chance of getting locked up. You had better apply for this book to Mr. Bent when you come out. He in the meantime will make entries of these towns and then the police will know something about you. You mast do 28 days,"—etsettera. That's shabby, iv yo' like, for a Beak to gooa an' chaff wi' a poor chap,an' then pile id on thad thick. Aw wish yo' a Merry Wissenda' when id comes Some on us may ha' gooan for h bit ov a halladay afoore we see one another ageean ; iv sooa aw hooap we shall hey a bit o' nice weather. Beawt thad there mich pleasure i'th' pathless woods, or rapture on th' lonely shore',an' th' only gainers bi thad soort o' weather is th' public-houses, an' there's plenty o' them at hooam. THE SHIP CANAL. THE NEW BILL. The Bill to confer further powers on the Manchester Ship Canal Company came on Tuesday before a Select Committee of the House of Lords, presided over by Lord Dude. It contains, among others, clauses with the view of obtaining alterations in the provisions for the protection of the trustees of the River Weaver Navi- gation, which interfere with the construction of the works ;to extend the time for the completion of the Western Mersey lock ;to extend the time for the con- struction of the Warrington dock ; to secure exemption from the payment of tolls to the Upper Mersey Commis- sioners for vessels entering or leaving the canal by the 'entrance channel at Eastham ; and to enable the com- pany, as owners of the Bridgewater Canal, to make a charge for the use of barges propelled otherwise than by animal force, and also for tugboats towing vessels thereon. 4 The first part of the Bill considered was the proposal to exempt vessels using the canal from the payment of tolis to the Upper Mersey Commissioners, and to meet the objections of the Commissioners on this point. Mr. Pember, Q.C., offered to insert a proviso preserving the income which the Commissioners now receive for the pnrpose of buoying and lighting of the channel. The promoters further offered to aceept from the classes al vestels using Ellesmere Port, Weston Docks, and Run- corn Docks. It was urged on behalf of the company that in the stress of passing the original Act a great many thinhs had been inserted that had to be recon- sidered in the public interest,and that the power granted to the Commissioners was one of them, for its enforce- ment would mean 'a serious injustice to the shipping *going to Manchester. It was further pointed out that the Commissioners had simply a public duty to perform that they had made no money out of the tolls, and that there could be no use in their having a great surplus. Mr. Bythell, deputy chairman of the company, and Mr. Leader Williams, the engineer, were called in sup- port of the proposal. Mr. Sinclair, one of the Mersey Commissioners, in the course of his examination, stated that he thought the income guaranteed by the company should be at least £2,800 a year, and that the traffic on which the Com- missioners should be allowed to levy a toll should include not only that going to Weston Point and Runcorn, but that going further inland through those ports. Mr. Cripps, for the promoters, said the company were prepared to leave the committee to decide what was a fair minimum guarantee. After consultation a clause was provisionally adopted to the effect that all vessels going to Ellesmere Port, Weston Point, and Runebrn should pay toll. Similarly, all vessels going along the Weaver or the Bridgewater Canal should also pay, but all vessels going up the Ship Canal itself should go free. The company offered to make good any deficiency in revenue below £2,800. The Committee, having decided to accept a clause carrying out the agreement, adjourned. The Ship Canal Company's Bill was further considered by a Committee of the House of Lords on Wednesday. A clause brought in by the promoters establishing a schedule of tolls in respect of steam haulage on the Bridgewater Canal, in addition to the tolls upan cargo, was struck out. The Committee then went through the unopposed clauses and reported the bill to the House. EXTENDED APPROACHES I:0 MANCHESTER. At the meeting of the Improvement Committee of the Manchester City Council held on Wednesday some important proposals were adopted for improving the approaches to the Ship Canal Docks at Pomona. It was decided that Cornbrook-road, which runs from Chester- road a distance of about 400 yards to the docks, should be made of a uniform width of 25 yards. This extension will necessitate the widening by the Corporation of the railway bridge which crosses the road. Another thoroughfare to be widened is Hulme Hall-road, which runs from the westerly side of Chester-road to the Woden-street bridge, a distance of about 300 yards. The most important of the series of improvements agreed , upon on Wednesday connects Oxford-street, from a point opposite the Palace Theatre of Varieties, with Deansgate, at the point where it is crossed by the rail- way viaduct. THE WHEAT TRADE AND WEAVER POOL. On Thursday afternoon the Spanish barque Francesco • Gotusso, Genoa arrived in the Weaver Pool, of the Ship Canal, from Rosario in South America. The vessel carries a cargo of 650 tons of wheat consigned to Messrs. • Fairclough, of Warrington, and it is being rapidly tran- shipped, under the superintendence cf Mr. W. H. Smith, into flats which will convey the grain to Warrington via the Mersey. In the ordinary course this cargo would have been transhipped at Liverpool.
BY WILFRED B. OLDING.

The natural gullibility of mankind in general, and Tories in particular, is so well established that it hardly needed the additional evidence recently furnished by St. Petersburg in the person of a cer- tain M. Gatchkowsky. This adept in the proper study of mankind is, you must know, what we in these parts would call a "'quack"; and by a tre- mendously-unheard-of-African-Chimese-Skiek-half- a-crown sort of aconcoction termed " vitaline," he has succeeded in gulling thousands and poisoning ' not a few. Rather a harmless sort of a mixture when examined, however,—borax and glycerine in •homcepathic quantities. Oh, poor, stupid, Ens- sians,thus to part with your hardly-earned copecks at the bidding of the first soft-tongued mounte- bank that parades his political—ahem ! medical, I should have said--nostrunis before your weary, heavy eyes. Quit you like men,arfd seek no longer the elixir of life in the borax pills and glyzerine draughts administered by the gettle, soothing, hands of Primrose Dames. Bless_me! Bless me!

1;T:1-Mixing Warrington and St. Petersburg! Having cleared the way thus far, I proceed to state it as my candid opinion that Toryism is a " Gospel of dirt." The shade of Carlyle threatens me,but to no avail. What I have written I have written, as Deeming said when he directed, that his frozen brains should be sent for medical inspection to Europe. A pretty pass indeed are we coming to, when a murderer's brains are to be hawked about Europe. To be frozen are they ? Well I'd just pack them in cement. The savants would be quite as wise at the finish of their inves- tigations. When these venerable fossils with their scalpels and microscopes get the brains they won't get the man. No, as Kingsley put it, he will have gone to his own place. That iseo ! Carlyle applied the phrase" Gospel of dirt" to the doctrine of evolution. Nothing offensive is meant in its present application. Jr. conveniently and tersely expresses the actual value or Toryism. Dirt is matter out of its place, and the best thing I can at present advise is that the doctrines and prin- ciples of Toryism should be frozen into portable form and shipped off to Central Africa. I don't expect the " Observer" and its friends will take my advice. It is, perhaps hardly natural to expect them to do so. Deeming didn't part with his brain until compelled. Toryism has its root deep in the land, monopolis- ing the national heritage, filling its coffers with the "unearned increment," taxing honest capital, and depriving honest labour of its rightful reward Its foreign policy is one of Grab and Bluster. Its Irish policy consists in stirring up the mud of religious dissension.; and in England it maintains its status only by the constant throwing of dust in the eyes or the working classes. How can a working-man be a Tory? I remember M. Gatch- kowsky and human nature in Russia, and am silenced. Allow you to object? Of course I will. " Gospel of Dirt" very vulgar ? Well, suppose we adopt the following definition.—Toryism is a privileged system ot Borax and Glycerine. How will that do? Wonderful compound is Glycerine. Combined with nitric acid it forms anarchy; but, combined with borax, Toryism. Anarchy and Toryism have a common basis in Glycerine. That is something like a discovery. I shall apply for the medal of the Society of Arts forthwith. In the meanwhile, I will betake me to Sankey-St., and keep my weather eye open. One never knows what may happen. What then is Toryism ? A system of pure politi- cal quackery—a thing without an idea, without a conscience, without a soul—a dust-throwing organ- isation, a generator of Anarchy—an unjust, un- sympathetic class doctrine. No man ought to embrace Toryism unless possessed of a wooden head and a thousand a year. When these qualifi- cations are wanting, alas! M. Gatchk owsky, or Dr. Rentoul, has been at work.

LIBERAL MEETING AT PENKETH LAST NIGHT. Last evening a largely-attended meeting was held in the Wesleyan Schoolroom, Penketh, in sup- port of the candidature of Mr. W. Neill, the Liberal candidate. Mr. J. T. Gumersall presided, afid amongst those present, besides the candidate, were Mr. W. C. Gully, Q.C., M.P., Mr. G. W. Rawlins, Mr. R. Garnett, Mr. C. E. Parker, &c. The CHAIRMAN asked what the Tory party were offer- ing to the country. Aa a Government they offered no- thing. The Government appeared to be quite con- tented with what they had done during the past six years, and perhaps they thought it would be better to offer nothing than to offer a great deal as they did six years ago, and then finish up with it practically un- fulfilled. (Hear, hear.) Mr. R. GARNETT moved "That this meeting of the electors of the Sankey polling district expresses its entire confidence in Mr. Gladstone and the leaders of the Liberal party, and emphatically affirms its conviction that no permanent settlement of the Irish difficulty can be secured except by the concession of a measure of self-Government which shall give the Irish people con- trol over their own domestic affairs." (Applause.) He admitted that they had had some very fair measures from the Conservatives, in fact won- derful measures considering the Government they had had, but he thought those measures were indebted for their best parts to the Liberal party, who helped to pass them and refrained from obstruction, (Hear, hear.) Oae of the most important of these measures had been that of assisted education, and yet he believed it had been a bitter pill for many of the Conservative, party. For his own part he thought a Tory workingman was an anomaly. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Mr. JOHN PEERS seconded the motion. Mr. W. NEILL was received with much applause. He said that what they had got to consider when they were making up their minds as to whom they wished to vote for was, what set of principles and which policy of the two great parties was more in conformity with their desires and their opinions of what was good not only for themselves but also for the great nation to which they belonged. (Hear, hear.) The Liberals offered them what was known as the Newcastle programme, but the Conservatives had absolutely no programme. Mr. Balfour had himself told them that the Conservatives promised nothing, and that therefore, they were more likely to give them something. (Laughter.) Dealing with the Irish question, Mr. Neill said that, speaking as an Ulster man and an Ulster Protestant, he could assure them that there were many Protestants, in Ulster in, favour of Homo Rule, which he regarded as a simple measure of justice to Ireland. He had been shocked by the deliberately wicked speech of Lord Salis- bury, in which he incited Ulstermen to re- bel and to defy an enactment of the Impe- rial Parliament. It almost struck one as though Lord Salisbury hoped that when the Convention was held in Belfast there would be such an outbreak and such a riot as would appeal to the unfounded fears of the British electors. (Hear, hear.) He (Mr. Neill) did not fear that there would be the slightest armed resistance on the part of Ulster. He believed that the Ulster men would settle down and endeavour by political means to get the greatest amount of power possible in any Parliament which might be established in Ireland. (Hear, hear.) But, in any case, he contended that England should not allow herself to be dictated to by a small knot of MU) in one corner of the Empire.(Applause.) Turning to the Irish Local Government Bill of the Government, he said it was an insult to every self- respecting Irishman. It was a bill that had already been sufficiently condemned by the very way in which Mr. Balfour introduced it. He did not know whether the Government intended to try to pass it into law, but he did not think they did, for the simple reason that nobody wanted it. (Hear, hear and applause.) Mr. Neill next advocated "one man one vote," reform of the registration laws,and a revision of taxation by which progressive death duties might be imposed so that a man who inherited £lOO,OOO would be called upon to pay a larger rate per cent. than the man who only got £5O. They wanted also to bring into taxation a number of sources of revenue which at present paid nothing such as mining royalties —and ground rents. (Applause.) Unearned increments should also be dealt with, and land which was held out of cultivation and use for the purpose of raising its value should also be taxed. (Hear, hear, and applause.) In conclusion Mr. Neill spoke favourably of dealing with the large number of important questions which are lumped under the name of "labour questions." On resuming his seat he was loudly applauded. The motion was then carried. Mr. C. E. Partaxa next moved a resolution pledging, the meeting to support the candidature of Mr. Neill, and this resolution was also adopted enthusiastically by the meeting.

CONFERENCE OF WARRINGTON CHURCHMEN. A conference of Churchmen "of all shades of political opinion," was held in the Masonic Rooms, Sankey-st., on Tuesday evening, the chair being occupied by Mr. C. S. Burgess. The object of the meeting, as stated in the circular convening it, was "to consider what are the duties of • Churchmen at the present crisis." There was a small attendance, which included the Rector (the Rev F. W. Willis), the Revs. E. C. E. Carleton, M. Stevenson, J. J. Longhorn, F. Slater, and W. E. Glenn; Captain Buckton, and Messrs. John White, Herbert Woods, John Hesketh, Aaron Brimelow, H. J. Westbrook, John Coxon, McGregor, A.J. Jolley, and Peter Edgar. • —The CHAIRMAN contended that if the interests of the Church were to be protected, local organization ought to be established, through which Churchmen could maws their voices heard and their power and influence felt whenever public questions arose, whether directly or indirectly, affecting the Church's welfare. (Applause.) Then the idea had occurred to them of forming a Church I party, free entirely from politics, taking an independent line of their own, and having no connection with either Liberals or Conservatives. (Hear, hear.) Undoubtedly the members of such a Church party would expect, and had a perfect right to expect,complete liberty of action,and no attempt would be made by any one to dictate as to how any member should vote at a Parliamentary election. Disendowment, denominational education, the establish- ment of parish councils, and the adjustment of tithes, Church discipline, and other matters were still within the range of practical politics, and social questions were 1 cropping up upon which the Church should be prepared to speak unitedly and harmoniously. (Applause.) The idea of the promoters of the Conference was that a local Church party or society should be formed. They should ' suggest a very broad general basis, so that there might be little or no difference of opinion. The principal work ,of such a seciety would be educational. They should I organize public meetings, and whenever a Bill was be- fore Parliament which seemed to affect the Church; 1 have lectures upon public questions affecting the Church, and endeavour to instruct the working classes in these subjects. They would thus be able to impress upon their Parliamentary representatives the importance or votlog for or against any particular measure, and they might also influence very largely the representa- tives of neighbouring constituencies. They should en- deavour to exercise an influence through the Press in their favour; watch the correspondence and paragraphs in the public papers; read the speeches and utter- ances of their opponents, and arrange for replies to be made to anything that appeared necessary.—Mr. Herbert Woods moved "That it is the duty of Churchmen to see that the interests of the Church are, as far as possible, safeguarded at all times, and especi- ally during the agitation of Parliamentary elections." —The Rev. Morley Steveason seconded the motion, and Mr. 11. J. Westbrook supported it.—lt was then put, and carried unanimously.—The Rector moved "That a Church Society be formed in Warrington, con- sisting of Churchmen of all shades of political opinion, and having for its object the proper safeguarding of the interests of the Church. at all times." (Applause.) He observed that he had always shrunk from taking part in political matters, but he felt that duty compelled him to do so in the present instance. He felt deeply on the question of education. He felt that God had given into their hands the instruction of the young, that it was their absolute duty to preserve their Church schools, and to teach their children, the children of Churchmen, the faith which they believed to have been committed to the saints. (Applause.) Captain Buckton seconded, and Rev. E. C. E. Carleton supported the motion. The motion was also unnanimously agreed to.—The Rev- J. J. Langham moved "That the following gentle- men be appointed a Provisional Committee, with power to add to their number: The Rector, the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, the IlPv. M. Stevenson, the Rev. J. J. Lang- ham, and Messrs. C. S. Burgess, Herbert Woods, R. • Dobson, jun., H. J. Westbrook, .J. D. Buck- ton, John Coxon, J. A. McGregor. and Frank Appleton." He contended that they were led too much by party, and too little by conscience.— Mr. McGregor seconded the motion, which was carried. On the motion of Mr. Coxon, a hearty vote of thanks, was accorded to Mr. Burgess for presiding, and the meeting terminated.
THE PROPOSED NEW PUBLIC HALL.

The proposal that the Corporation should under- take the provision of a new Public Hall for War- rington was, on Tuesda3, under the consideration of a special committee of the General Purposes Committee, Alderman Chandley being the chairman. The Committee, in the end, came to the conclusion that at the present time the scheme was not feasible, inasmuch as they were advised by the Town Clerk that the Corporation could not under- take the erection of a concert hall or assembly room except in conjunction with, or as part of, a building required for municipal purposes. The Committee will, consequently, report to this effect to the General Purposes Committee. A suggestion was, we believe, made that a Corn Exchange should be erected over the present Market Hall which could be utilised as a concert and assembly hall.

div.head: CHARGE OF MURDERING A SWEET-
div.p: CHARGE OF MURDERING A SWEET-
HEART.

At Oldnill, Staffordshire, a young man named Harry Pugh, has been arrested on the charge of murdering his sweetheart, named Ann Gill. On being taken into cus- tody he asserted that on Wednesday he and the young lady decided to commit suicide together in Pig-lane Poo!, but after entering the water he swam out. It is alleged, however, that he admitted holding the woman under the water until the died. Her body was recovered on Thursday morning. An inquest was held at Oldhill, yesterday, touchicg the death of Ann Morris Gill, widow, who, it is alleged, was drowned in a pool atll on Wednesday by her lover, Harry Pugh. The father of the deceasei . said he was not aware she was in any trouble. The inquiry was adjourned for a grost-inortem: examination,

The deattris announced of the Right Hon. Sir Charles Butt, President of the Probate, Divorce, and Admiralty D:wision of the High Court of Justice. The immediate canse of Sir Charles Butt's death, was paralysis of the heart. Lady Butt was with her husband when the sad event occurred. Sir Cnarles was called to the bar at Lincoln's Inn, in 1854, and joined the nurthern circuit. He obtaino a silk gown in 1868. He unsuccessfully contested Tamworth in Pebruary, 1874, und sat for Southampton, in the Liberal interest from 4ril 1880, till March, 1883, when he was appointed to the judge- ship in the Admiralty Division of the High •Court of Justice. div.head: NEW NATIONAL INFANT SCHOOL,
div.p: THE NEW NATIONAL INFANT SCHOOL,

LAYING OF THE FOUNDATION STONE. On Thursday afternoon the laying of the founda- tion stone of a new infant school in connection with . the Parish Church took place in Ellesmere-st., the ceremony being performed by Mrs. Beamont, widow of the late Mr. W. m. Beamont, in the presence of a large assemblage. Among those present were the Rector (the Rev. F. W. Willis) and Mrs. Willis, the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton and Mrs. Carleton, the Revs. W. E. Glenn, J. E. Richards, J. Phillips, H. V. Pigot, C. E. Jackson and F. W. Cook: Mr. R.Pierpoint,Mr. R. Davies, Alderman Wright, Dr. White, and the Misses White, Councillor R. Fairclough, Mr. Moores, Mr. Dewhurst (master of the boys' national school) and Mrs. Dewhurst. Mr. Dewhurst accompanied on the harmonium the hymns, which were sung by the surpliced choir of the Parish Church. The Rector read the usual service for the occasion of a foundation stone laying, after which a hymn was sung and Mrs. Beamont then, at the request of the , Rector, laid the stone and she was subsequently presented by Miss Willis, daughter of the Rector, with a bouquet of flowers.—The Rector then de- livered. an address. He said it was four years since he came to Warrington, and he always kept the memory of the late Mr. Beamont in his heart. One of the first letters which came to him to Northampton- shire after his appointment to the rectorate of War-, rington was from Mr. Beamont, and he always considered it a great privilege to have known such a man. It was 60 years since the National Schools were built, by his last predecessor but one, Bishop Powys, on land given by the late Colonel Blackburne. In 1832, Bishop Powys built the rectory, and afterwards, about 1844, the present Mount schools and the clergy daughters' school. The people gave very liberally at the time towards their erection. Amongst benefactors of the school now to be built were Lord Lilford, Lord Winmarleigh, and the present Colonel Blackburne. The present scheme was to build two schools, oue in Ellesmere-street and the other in Manchester-road, these to accomodate 1,000 children, 300 in Ellesmere-street, and 700 in Manchester-road. The schools would cost about £6,000, £5,000 of which had already been promised, that was, £2,500 by the Training College, and £2,500 by other donors. £l,OOO therefore remained to be raised. The rector urged that the provision of more school accomodation was now becoming all the more necessary from the danger of a School Board being established, which would entail a large amount o, f expense. The national schools, had, he said, a high name both with the school inspectors and the diocesan representative. It was necessary not only to teach the children reading, writing, and arith- metic, but also to pro vide teaching to meet their spriri- tual needs. Ile himself went to the schools each morning for an hour and read the scriptures to and prayed, with the children so that their spiritual education might not be neglected.—Another hymn having been sung, and a collection made, the Rector pronounced the benediction, and the proceedings conclude d.
LORD ROSEBERY AT BIRIIIN GRIM.

Lord Rosebery, addressing a Liberal gathering at Birmingham on Thursday night, alluded to the position taken up by Mr. Chamberlain with regard to the politi- cal representation of that city in the House of Commons. He pointed out that Mr. Chamberlain, althoo,;li pretend- ing in all Liberal matters except Horne .Rule to be the voice of Birmingham in the House of Commons, invari- ably voted on the Tory side, and thus stultified the character of Birmingham, once the strine of Liberalism. In regard to Home Rule, he ridiculed the recent speeches of Lord Salisbury, remarking that the dangers which the Premier had taken upon himself to warn the country of fare merely fancied perils. He also accused the Prime Minister of endeavouring to obscure the main issue— namely, the Irish Question, by references t) Protection. He was glad that the Irish Local Government Bill had been introduced, because it would enable them 'to raise a definite issue between the policy of the Government and the policy of -Home Rule. GLADSTONE AND THE EIGHT HOURS QUESTION. Ata meeting on Thursday night, of the Executive Committee of the London Trades Council, the letter of Mr. Gladstone asking for further information on the question of the legal eight hors proposal was considered. It was ultimately resolved that the society be instructed to forward Mr. Gladstone .copies of the resolutions passed at the Newcastle Trades Congress and in Hyde Park, on May Ist, and that he be referred to the speeches delivered in Hyde Park, as expressing the arguments and desires of the London workmen, which it was the intention of theiproposed deputation to lay before him,

div.head: LATEST' NEWS.
div.p: LATEST' NEWS.
LOSS OF A STEAMER.
The London steamer Harley struck the Itundlestones yesterday morning during a fog, and sank. The crew saved themselves in the boats, and landed at Penzance.
A MURDERER RESPITED.

Lord Provost Muir, of Glasgow, has received an in• timation that Archibald Robertson, sentenced to death for murdering Annie Campbell, is respited by her Majesty, pending the further signification of her pleasure.

div.head: CABINET COUN/CL.
div.p: CABINET COUN/CL.

Yesterday all the Ministers, excepting Mr. Stanhope, attended the Cabinet Council. Lord Salisbury appeared none the worse for his accident. and Mr. Ritchie seemed to have recovered from his recent indisposition. CHARGE OF KILLING A NIGHT WATCHMAN. William Thomas was remanded at Pontypridd yester- day, charged with the manslaughter of a night watch- man on the sewerage works. The accused is already committed on the coroner's warrant. THE DURHAM COAL STRIKE. RESULT. OF THE BALLOT.

The Press Association West Hartlepool correspondent telegraphs that throughout the eastern district of Durham the iesult of the ballot just taken shows a fully five-sixths majority against the coal-owners demand for 1.31 per cent., and a similar feeling prevails through- out the county. AU hope of an early settlement has been abandoned. ATTEMPTED DOUBLE MURDER.

Yesterday, at Strood, Kent, Frederick Marrs, shoe- maker, attempted to murder his wife as she lay in bed, by attacking her with a hammer. She was terribly injured, and became unconscious. After a similar un- successful attempt upon his son, Marrs was arrested. He made a desperate effort to strangle himself in the cell.

div.head: SAD FATALITY TO A WORKMAN.
div.p: SAD FATALITY TO A WORKMAN.

Two men named Roberts and Platt, were emptying a sewer intercepting pit, at Newport Pagnell, yesterday, when Roberts fell in. Platt, in attempting his compan- ion's rescue, succumbed to foul gas, and was taken out dead. Roberts was removed by some workmen, and now lies dangerously ill. A ROMANTIC MARRIAGE.

The Rev. J.l. Howells, Baptist minister at Meresteg, who recently received £l,OOO from the Taff Vale Railway Company for the loss of his leg in the Pontypridd colli- sion, has m3rried the nurse who attended him at Ponty- pridd Union Infirmary.

div.head: ANOTHER- PARISIAN SCANDAL.
div.p: ANOTHER- PARISIAN SCANDAL.

An Exchange Company's telegram from Paris yester- day reports that another social drama has been enacted in that capital, this time in the aristocratic neighbour- hood of the Faubourg Saint Honore. A banker's clerk named Conor fired a revolver at his mistress, Blanche Laval, and then blew his own brains out. The girl is expected to recover. RAILWAY COLLISSION IN PARIS.
PARIS, FRIDAY AFTERNOON.—A collision took place thN morning at the St. Lazare terminus by which 21 persons were slightly injured. --- •
BOATING FATALITY AT RAMSGATE

A gentleman named Jarvis went for a sail at Rams- gate yesterday morning with two ladies. The boat capsized id Pegnell Bay, and one of the ladies was drowned. The other lady and Mr. Jarvis were rescued in an exhausted condition.

div.head: CRICKET.
div.p: CRICKET.
Oxford University beat Lancashire by seven runs ; Notts 86 for eight wickets ; Cambridge all out, 100.

div.head: YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT.
div.p: YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS.-FRIDAT.

MISCELLANEOUS.-- Tile House met at a quarter past four.—The MARQUIS of SALISBURY received congratu- lations of his friends on his escape from the carriage accident yesterday. The Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire extension to London Bill was read a second time.—The Earl of DUNRAYEN raised a question, based on the motion agreed to in the Canadian House of Commons, referring to preferential trade with the United Kingdom. His Lordship enforced Protectionist views.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS._
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS._

The Speaker took the chair at five minutes past two. TREATY WITH SPAIN.—Mr. J. W. LOWTHER, answering Mr. Lenz, said negotiations were in progress, between Her Majesty's Government and the Spanish Government for the conclusion of a treaty. AGRICULTURAL HOLDINGS.—The consideration of the Small (Agricultural) Holdings Bill was resumed as ' amended. The bill was read a third time, &lad the House resumed discussion on the Vote on Account. THE VOTE ON ACCOUNT.—The House resumed discus- sion on the vote on account, Mr.WINTERBOTHAM initiat- ing a debate upon the question of the employment of Polynesian !abourers in Queensland which he strongly condemned.—Mr. J. A. BRIGHT suggested that a warning he sent to Queensland stating that public opinion in this country would carefully observe whether abuses continued.—Earl COMPTON thought if necessary the bill of the Queensland Government should be disallowed.— Mr. BALFOUR felt confident the present discussion would tend to check the evils which admittedly occurred under the system. Mr. Mowrois next moved a reduction of the vote relating to Newfoundland by £lOO. He called attention to the alleged alteration of the Newfoundland Fisheries Bill. The question was being discussed when, at six- fifty, the House resumed. BILLS ADVANEED.—The Customs and Inland Rev,enue Bill was read a third time. The Merchant Shipping Acts Amendment Bill was being considered in committee when at 7 o'clock the House adjourned till nine.
WARRINGTON AND THE SHIP CANA L.

The Bill promoted by the Manchester Ship Canal Company, has been before the Rouse ot Lords Com- mittee this week. Warrington Corporation was represented by Mr. Vesey Thompson, Q.C. One Of the proposals of the promoters of the Bill was with regard to a toll that should be levied upon steam barges and vessels propelled by other than animal power on the Bridge- water Canals. This was opposed by the Warrington Corporation and the Rochdale Canal Company, and the Lords Committee ultimately struck the clause out of the Bill. It was stated during the discussion of the clause that the matter should be brought for- ward again in the revised classification of rates which the Ship Canal Company are obliged to Submit to the Board of Trade under the Railway and Canals Traffic Act, 1888, but, no doubt, in that ease the Corporation will again look after the interests of the traders of Warring= ton: In the Bill it is now provided that the proposed lock at Walton shall be made available for traffic by the time any portion of the canal between "P.nncorn Bridge and Latchford is open for traffic. With regard to Warrington docks the Bill merely 'repeats the provision in the Act of 1885 which pro- vided for the construction of the docks within three years from the opening of the canal for traffic be- tween Eastham and Latchford, though a few words have been added, at the instance of the Warrington Corporation, to give the provision additional de- ufiniteness.

div.head: CULCHETH.
div.p: CULCHETH.

FUNERAL OF MRS. Amax HUNT.—The funeral of Mrs. Hunt, wife of Mr. John Runt, of Beech mill, and Hob- hey-lane, Culcheth, whose death occurred after an ill- ness of several months, took place at Nevvton,on Monday afternoon. EastaY PRYSBYTERIAN CHURCH.—The annual sermons were preached in the above place of worship on Sunday afternoon and evening, by the _Rev. John Warnock, of St. John's Presbyterian Church, Warrington, in aid of the Wilds of the church. There were good congrega- tions, and appropriate anthems and hymns were sung by the choir. The collections amounted to £5 7s.,beiog 13s. less than last year..
TERRIBLE GUNPOWDER EXPLOSION.

SIX SOLDIERS BLOWN INTO TUE AIR. A Paris correspondent says a terrible accident hap- pened on Wednesday at the Chalons camp. Six soldiers had been ordered to convey a chest of gunpowder to the. firing ground. They were all sitting on the chest, smoking cigarettes, when the gunpowder exploded, blowing them into the air. The surgeons hope to be able to save the lives ot two, but despair of the other four.
At the usual meeting of the Water Committee of th Liverpool City Council, en Tuesday, Mr. Deacon said he had no doubt the aqueduct tunnel under the Mersey would be Aniabed by July 13th.

NOTICE. THE SHOP ASSISTANTS' HALF-HOLIDAY. Furniture Warehouse, Bridge Foot, Warrington, May 25th, 1892. MY attention having been called to the fact that tbereis some uncertainty as to my position with regard to the Half-Holiday Movement, I beg to remind my 'Customers and the Public generally, that I close my Establishment on Thursday afternoons from one o'clock ; and that I have done so since the first day on which the holiday was adopted. I hope my Friends and Customers are put to no inconvenienee or trouble on account of my closing. for I can assure them that I have adopted the Half-Holiday not from choice or because my shop-people wish it, but because the majority of the shopkeepers having identified themselves with the move- ment, Ido not wish to be thought a stumbling-block to Its success. I think it necessary, however, to exp!ain that so far from desiring to have the Thursday after- nom holiday, my shop-people prefer te be on the old footing, which was, and had been for some years, that one half of them in turn ceased work on Saturday after- noons at one o'clock. While sympathising with the Shop Assistants, many of whom have to work up to late hours at night, both I and my-shop.people would prefer every other Saturday afternoon or at one o'clock. It is, therefore, reluctantly . that I have felt it my duty to help the Shop Avis- tents' movement, by falling in with the Thursday Half-Holiday, and I trust that the agitation to reduce thehours of Shop Assistants en ordinary working days, and on Saturday in particular, will go forward, as I am strongly of opinion that the long hours worked by many is not only necessary from the point of view of the public, but is a source of danger to the health of those concerned. R. W. MARSH.

Gentlemen,—l have now had your Marsh's Patent Smoke- oonsurning Stove for 18 months in constant use, and the longer we use it the better we like it, and for cleanliness and comfort it is a great contrast to the open fire. THISTLETHWAITE. 322, Leeds Road, Bradford, January 15, 1892. Gentlemen,—j have two of your Marsh's Patent Smoke. consuming and Fuel-economising Fires at work continuously in my establishment. One fire has been fixed for fourteen months, working two large ovens (one heavy cast iron and one sheet iron), and the other is applied to a complete bakers range, with large ovens, side boiler, and hot plate, and they have both given every satisfaction. After getting the fires well started with nuts, we use practically nothing but smudge on the two-decker, and nuts and smudge on the range, for the remainder of the day. The heat obtained from this inferior coal with this Patent fire is really marvellous ; indeed, one can hardly realise tfie fact of being able to bake bread and pastry with common smudge. Previous to having these Fires we had to sweep the chimney every two months, but it is now fourteen months since we had it swept, and so far as I can judge, there will never be any necessity to sweep it again.—Yours truly, E. "ONE OF THE ORDINARY TRICKS." Mr. Sidney Halifax, Liberal and Labour candidate for North-East Kent, has called Mr. Gladstone's attention to a statement made at a Conservative meeting that, in the event of the Liberals being returned to power, Sheerness Dockyard would be reduced. Mr. Gladstone has replied stating that he knows of no undertaking to reduce Sheerness Dockyard, and he characterises the statement as " one of the ordinary tricks of the party." MR. MORLEY AT HUDDERSFIELD. -- Mr. John Morley, M.P., was present at a great Liberal I demonstration in Huddersfield on Saturday night, and gave an address, in which he replied to Lord Salisbury's recent speeches on Ulster and the fiscal policy of England. He remarked that in the House of Commons at present they were living in an atmosphere of sham, because they all knew that before six weeks were over the country would have to decide whether the Irish Local Govern- ment Bill or any other Bill coming from the same source was to pass and become the law of the land. Be did not, of course, know as much as the newspapers, but if he were a sporting man, he should be prepared to bet 100 to one that the dissolution would take place before the end of the first week in July. There was nothing, he con- I tinued, that the Liberal party more earnestly desired than that labour representation in the coming Parliament ahould be as large as possible, and thor who were respon- sible for the matters, had done their best to make that desire effective. His own belief was that in matters of hours and of wages for adult male labour the interfer- ence ot Parliament would be a bad and mischievous thing : but this was a question on which there should be the fullest liberty of discussion, on one side and on the other. Referring to Lord Salisbury's sneers at the religion of Free Trade and its Rabbis, he said : A more reckless set of remarks than those qf Lord Salisbury, in view of what was going on in America and France were never made. Turning to Ireland, he ridiculed the idea that because strong language had been used at a share- holders' meeting in Dublin the Irish were to be consid- ered unfit for self-government. Nothing had happened since 1886 to shake his confidence in the capacity of Irish- men to govern themselves, and he had no doubt that -when the time came they would prove themselves as tit for self-government as Frenchmen, or Norwegians, or Swedes, or Englishmen, or Scotilmen.
